World.title: On Ukraine's front lines, female soldiers testing Canadian-designed body armour
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Ukrainian soldiers fighting on the front lines of Russia's war are now testing curved body armour designed specifically for women so they're better protected against bullets, shrapnel and drone strikes.

Ukrainian MP Iryna Nykorak said the majority of the more than 10,000 women serving in combat in her country are wearing ballistic plates for men that are too bulky, heavy and don't fit their chests. Some decide not to wear the plate at all, which makes it useless, she said.

"Right now, women must adapt to the current system, not vice versa," Nykorak told CBC News. "It's a respect to women's dignity.... She left her home, her family, sometimes in the majority of cases children, and joined the army. She sacrificed a lot."

Many countries around the world, including Ukraine and Canada, issue servicewomen standard body armour that isn't shaped specifically for them. Last month, Ukraine started handing out its first round of female body armour vests, saying there's a need for this protective equipment as the number of women serving grows.

In June, the U.K. also separately donated 2,000 sets of body armour to Ukraine that include curved female-specific ballistic plates by Canadian company NP Aerospace, paired with vest carriers designed by Logistik Unicorp, also based in Canada.

More than 75,000 women are serving in Ukraine's military, including more than 10,000 in combat roles on the front lines, according to Ukrainian MP Iryna Nykorak. (John Moore/Getty Images)

CBC News spoke to a female officer with the National Guard of Ukraine who's been serving for almost 15 years and is being identified only by her call sign, "Kudriava," in accordance with Ukrainian military rules.

She served in major combat operations across eastern Ukraine, including Bakhmut, Sievierodonetsk, Lysychansk, Chasiv Yar, and the Serebryansky Forest. Today her role on the front lines includes managing drones, electronic co-ordination and signal jamming.

Kudriava said she was on duty in eastern Ukraine when Russia invaded its neighbour on Feb. 24, 2022, and she wore standard body armour designed for men for the first year of the war.

"I have a typical body like slim man," she said. "But a lot of women have a different type of body, and it was hard to do something in the front line when your uniform and your armour are not for you — if you have a big chest, big hips or other types of body."

Kudriava says body armour should fit like a 'second skin.' If it doesn't, it leaves vital areas like the chest and torso exposed, which could be deadly. (Serhii Moos/CBC)

Kudriava started sourcing her own uniform and body armour over the years so that it's more comfortable during her operations, but she said it isn't ideal.

Military gear should fit like a "second skin," she said, and if it's uncomfortable, soldiers can become distracted instead of focusing on their mission.

"When you're in operation and you have some tasks [from] your commander, you shouldn't think about your uniform, you should think to save your life, to save life of your personnel and to do best in this operation," she said.

'Women are not just small men'

Michael Sandercott, part of a team at the NP Aerospace factory in Coventry, England, where the armour is manufactured, said women often size up so that men's body armour fits their breast tissue. This burdens them with extra weight they don't need, so they may give up other items like ammunition, water and rations, he said.

Flat ballistic plates rest again female soldiers' chests, causing the plate to angle outward creating gaps near the neck and lower torso.

"You're much more exposed to the risk of being struck with top-down munitions," he said. "A bullet or shrapnel or anything along those lines. You're less covered."

Erin Grieve, left, a sales manager at NP Aerospace, holds a standard flat ballistic plate for men to her chest to show the gap that it creates. (Lyzaville Sale/CBC)

Erin Grieve, a sales manager for the company's personal protection team, said that "women are not just small men" and body armour shouldn't shrink to fit them. It should be designed to accommodate their breast shape to protect the organs they need to survive.

"You've got your heart, greater vessels, liver and spleen," she said. "So if you were to take an impact, you've got less than 20 minutes to get to a hospital. So what body armour is designed to do is make sure the impact doesn't happen in the first place."

Grieve said her company's ballistic testing and research show that its curved body armour fits tighter to women's bodies, providing better protection.

"So our modelling shows that wearing a curved plate, you are 48 per cent more protected than a flat plate," she said. "So in Ukraine, for example, where you've got drone threats and elevation threats, that gap is really significant."

WATCH | Making armour that fits women: Ukrainian women don't have armour that fits. That's about to change | Duration 1:37 Ukrainian women soldiers are fighting in body armour that doesn't fit — because it was designed for men. NP Aerospace, a Canadian company in the U.K. is trying to change that by making body armour specifically designed for women.

MP leads charge for female body armour

Ukrainian MP Iryna Nykorak has spent years pushing for change. She founded Arm Women Now, an NGO supported by NATO that has provided 350 sets of female body armour with lightweight plates to servicewomen. She's also been donating uniforms, boots and gear to fit woman in the battlefield.

"Despite the fact that at the state level they don't have female body armour which will protect their body, their health and their lives, we support them," Nykorak said.

In 2024, Ukraine started giving women jackets and pants for the spring and summer designed for their bodies, she said. But Nykorak said dozens of other pieces of the uniform are not yet tailored to women's bodies.

Ukrainian officials said in July that women are performing in combat missions on an equal footing with men, so it's consistently implementing female-specific protective equipment.

Nykorak said she hopes her country's efforts to get combat soldiers gear that properly fits will lead to other allies, including the European Union, Canada and the U.K., following suit.

"Our experience teaches us a very important lesson that women's participation today is a matter of national resilience," she said. "So it affects a country's ability to defend itself and to survive."

Canada's Department of National Defence said last year it's working on releasing its first body armour system, with darting around the chest, shorter plates and tapering for women, this year for the army's light forces.

Plans are also underway, Canadian officials said, to procure more female-specific personal protective equipment.

World.title: 'Worst-case scenario': Ships blocked from the Strait of Hormuz pose invasive species threat
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Ships stalled in the Gulf region because of the closure of the Strait of Hormuz could trigger a "super-spreader" event, with long-term environmental consequences, according to a paper published last week.

The paper, published July 22 in Biological Invasions, warns that algae, barnacles, tunicates and other organisms growing on stationary vessels in the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman could pose an "immense international biosecurity threat" once the ships resume travelling.

"If you had to design a biofoulic spreader event and you really wanted to get as many species moved around as possible, this would be it," said lead author Mario Tamburri, a professor at the University of Maryland Center for Environmental Science.

The Strait of Hormuz lies between the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman. There are over 1,500 ships stalled due to the closure of the Strait as a part of the U.S.-Iran war, researchers estimate. (The National/CBC)

The researchers estimate about 1,500 ships are stalled in the Persian Gulf and hundreds more in the Gulf of Oman because of the strait's closure amid the U.S.-Iran war.

Biofouling — the accumulation of organisms on ships hulls, propellers and other external surfaces — could allow invasive species to spread to ports around the world if the vessels are not properly managed, the paper says.

Why the ships could become 'super-spreaders'

Tamburri and his co-authors describe the closure as a "worst-case scenario."

Ships generally remain in port for one to three days and may go years between hull cleanings. Some vessels in the Gulf have been stationary for at least 40 times as long as usual, the researchers said.

Hull coatings designed to prevent biofouling also become less effective when ships remain idle, Tamburri said.

WATCH | Canadian ships stuck in Strait for months: 2 Canadian freight ships stuck in Strait of Hormuz for months | Duration 5:48 Pascal Larose is the vice-president of Desgagnés, a shipping company that has had two vessels stuck in the Strait of Hormuz since hostilities between the U.S., Israel and Iran broke out. Larose says it's uncertain when the ships will be able to complete their voyages.

The number and size of the vessels, their proximity to one another and the timing of the closure increase the risk of a "super-spreader" situation, Tamburri said. The ships became stranded as waters were warming and many organisms were beginning their growing and reproductive seasons.

Species that tolerate the Persian Gulf's high temperatures and salinity may also be effective invaders elsewhere, particularly as ocean temperatures rise, Tamburri said.

Cleaning the vessels before they leave would be difficult. In-water cleaning companies are not equipped to handle so many ships in a short time period, he said, and sending workers into the water during a conflict would pose safety risks.

"Ideally they would all clean before they left, but most of these ships are just going to have to leave," he said.

Shipping's ecological issue

Species can move between ecosystems through cargo and ballast water, but researchers say biofouling has received less attention.

After zebra mussels appeared in the Great Lakes in the mid-1980s, governments and the shipping industry focused on species transported in ballast water, said Meghan Mathieson, director of strategy and engagement for ClearSeas, a non-profit aiming to raise awareness about marine shipping.

"There just was less awareness of the fact that organisms can cling to the outside of a ship and then drop off in new systems," she said.

The N.W.T. will be getting a boat washing station similar to this one installed next spring. It's part of an effort to stop invasive species like zebra mussels from entering the territory. ( Invasive Species Centre)

This zebra mussel was one of 19 pulled off the Mactaquac Dam by Bruce's team during last year's survey of the Saint John River. (Submitted by Meghann Bruce)

Organisms can detach or release larvae when a ship reaches another port. If they become established, they may out-compete native species.

Tunicates, or sea squirts, are one example. The slimy invertebrates, which spread through biofouling and ballast water, compete with mussels on farms along Canada's East Coast.

The International Marine Organization released an updated set of guidelines around biofouling in 2023. Unlike for ballast treatment, Mathieson said there are no mandatory regulations yet but they are in the works.

WATCH | East coast shellfish face tunicate invasion: Slimy and spreading fast: Shellfish farms face biofouling 'invasion' | Duration 3:02 Scientists are monitoring dozens of sites in Nova Scotia and southern New Brunswick to see if the latest warm winter in Atlantic Canada accelerated the spread of slimy biofouling marine invertebrates. Paul Withers has the story.

Such species are nearly impossible to eliminate once established, said Anthony Ricciardi, a biology professor and director of McGill University's Bieler School of the Environment.

"There's a chronic cost to having an invasion once it's entrenched," he said.

Ecological invasion

Ricciardi compared marine invasions to a hub-and-spoke network: Ships carry organisms to ports, that may become new hubs for further spread.

With so many vessels stalled in the Gulf, he said, they are likely to collect an "abundance and diversity" of organisms, increasing the risk of invasions elsewhere.

The situation shows how geopolitical events can have ecological consequences far beyond the region where they occur, he said.

The scale and impact of any spread remain unknown.

"What happens in the Strait of Hormuz will probably fuel a legacy that will keep unfolding," Ricciardi said. "You have to look at it as not just a one-off, but as a major step change in the marine invasion risk worldwide, at least in areas that can accommodate these particular species."

World.title: The web is being redesigned for AI. What does that mean for human readers?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Artificial intelligence is fundamentally reshaping how humans use the internet. For The National, CBC’s Nora Young breaks down the future of search and what happens to information when bots do most of the reading online.

Say goodbye to the internet as you know it

Deb Perelman has seen a lot of change online.

The food blogger's popular site Smitten Kitchen turns 20 years old this summer.

"I've always had the philosophy that I would just meet people where they were," Perelman said, which is why she established a presence on social media platforms from Twitter to Instagram to TikTok — but always took readers back to the recipes and stories on her website.

Now, she faces a new challenge: AI summaries.

Deb Perelman, creator of the food blog Smitten Kitchen, has seen AI summaries eat into her website's traffic. (Submitted by Deb Perelman)

Perelman said she's seen "a summary or a chunk of my own recipe in the AI blurb that you have in the top of search results."

"It's honestly shocking to me that somebody can publish my work ... without my permission," said Perelman, who is now pursuing AI-limiting protections for her site.

Google recently reimagined the search box for the first time in 25 years, with "AI Mode," a conversational back-and-forth that's similar to using ChatGPT or other AI chatbots. This Google function has surpassed a billion monthly users .

This screen grab shows the landing page for Google's AI Mode. (Nora Young)

Beyond that, Google is also prioritizing extensive AI summaries over links to websites — the result being that people increasingly don't need to leave Google's main page to get an answer.

Similarly, you can rely on Claude, ChatGPT or other LLM chatbots to provide answers, recommend products or take on more complex tasks, like creating an itinerary for a trip.

It's convenient, but it means big challenges for site creators who rely on human traffic. The web is being fundamentally reoriented to accommodate the bots that scrape websites for the information we seek.

Websites for machines as well as humans

Human web traffic is declining. Data from Cloudflare, a U.S. company that provides a range of internet services for websites and apps, found declines in human traffic across retail, software, IT and finance websites. Some hardest hit categories declined by up to 40 per cent between June 2025 and April 2026.

"The biggest impact is … machines going to read your content," said Hamzah Khadim, co-founder of Toronto-based internet marketing service Logik Digital .

Khadim argues that as search has moved "from keywords to conversations," the main goal for any website is not turning up in a list of links but being part of an AI's answer.

Logik Digital has long specialized in SEO (search engine optimization), so that websites turn up in search results, but it's now also focused on GEO (generative engine optimization). That means adding specific information that both indicates a site's credibility and answers the questions a user is likely to ask AI.

Sometimes, that means adding a lot of text to a website — for example, in its "About Us" section.

"People aren't gonna necessarily read all of that, but AI definitely will," Khadim said. "And it'll help establish trust."

The AI chatbot ChatGPT is shown on a smartphone in Mulhouse, eastern France. (Sebastien Bozon/AFP/Getty Images)

Getting paid for content and for the cost of scraping

While many independent content creators monetize their content on social media apps, through moves like brand partnerships, a lot of websites rely on selling ads or subscriptions to fund their content. So what happens if website visitors are AI bots and not humans?

Mark Surman, the president of Mozilla, best known for the Firefox browser, is concerned that "if those incentives to create original, creative, independent content disappear, does content just come from big and powerful companies, or from governments, or from AI itself?"

Even if a publisher is content to let AI have content for free and doesn't rely on advertising, there are real costs associated with AI accessing web content.

Wikipedia is one of the most-visited websites in the world. Lane Becker is president of Wikimedia Enterprise, which makes Wikipedia content accessible to organizations at scale. From an access-to-information perspective, Becker is enthusiastic about AI spreading Wikipedia's content.

Wikipedia articles are free for anyone to access, but the server infrastructure providing that content costs Wikipedia (or any website) a tiny bit of money. The sheer volume of requests from bots means that can really add up.

Lane Becker, president of Wikimedia Enterprise, says just one bot can click on 50 articles in under a second. (Submitted by Wikimedia Foundation)

Becker says just one bot can click on 50 articles in under a second.

"It's easy for one robot to show up and say, 'Hey, I want to scoop every single page out of every single Wikipedia [edition] and every single language, and I'm going to do it in under half an hour.'"

So Wikimedia Enterprise has deals with a number of AI companies — including Google, Microsoft, Amazon and Meta — to pay for direct, bulk access to Wikipedia's data.

A new deal for the AI-native web

Other media companies may start pushing back, too, if the decline in web traffic continues. According to reporting by the Wall Street Journal , Reddit and some other prominent publishers are considering cutting off or changing their relationship with Google.

USA Today's CEO recently said the "traditional Google search business model is dead … that traffic is declining … so we are going to be in a position soon where we have to block Google." He seemed to signal a willingness to forego showing up in Google search results at all.

But hope remains for a model that would preserve the open web and its diversity of voices.

For Deb Perelman, AI summaries miss something you can only get from the individual perspectives of creators.

"The context of a recipe is really important," she said, arguing "you're not going to get that from a blurb on top of a search result that has been extracted, perhaps correctly, perhaps incorrectly, from the actual recipe."

World.title: Canada built its nuclear industry to avoid foreign fuel. Its new reactors will depend on it
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The first reactors in Canada's planned nuclear expansion will depend on foreign suppliers — including the United States — to enrich and fabricate their fuel, even as Prime Minister Mark Carney argues Canadian sovereignty depends on the country's ability to supply and control its own energy.

It marks a sharp departure from the Candu reactor system, which gave Canada — the world's second-largest uranium producer — a largely domestic nuclear supply chain for more than half a century.

Ontario has begun building the first of four planned BWRX-300 small modular reactors, or SMRs, in Clarington, Ont., called the Darlington New Nuclear Project. The American-Japanese-designed light water reactor uses low-enriched uranium, unlike Canada's Candus, which use fuel made domestically from natural uranium without enrichment.

Ontario Power Generation (OPG), the Crown corporation that operates provincially owned electrical utilities, expects the first BWRX-300 at Darlington to be connected to the grid by the end of 2030. The other three are planned for the mid-2030s.

Cameco, the Saskatoon-based uranium mining and nuclear fuel company, will mine uranium ore in Saskatchewan and convert it in Port Hope, Ont., before it is enriched in the United States. France's Orano and Britain's Urenco are also listed by OPG as a supplier of enriched uranium, and an American company will manufacture the finished fuel assemblies in the United States.

Against Candu's founding logic

Experts say the shift reverses the founding logic in Canada's nuclear program.

A 1993 Library of Parliament background paper said the reason Candu was created was "to design a reactor tailored to Canadian circumstances" that used natural uranium to avoid "the difficult and expensive process of enrichment or, alternatively, dependence on foreign sources of enriched uranium."

A graphic from a Candu promotional video is seen at a trade show in 1982. Candu reactors use natural uranium produced in Canada without enrichment. (The National/CBC Archives)

By placing that step in foreign hands, experts say, the new reactors undermine claims of energy soverignty and expose Canada to long-term geopolitcal risk.

Mark Winfield, a professor at York University who studies sustainable energy, climate change and energy policy, said by relying on imported enriched uranium, Canada would give foreign governments the ability to disrupt its nuclear fuel supply during a political dispute.

"It turns the original rationale for the Candu program completely on its head," he said. "The whole idea was, going back to the 1950s, that we would have an all-Canadian fuel supply chain that would not be the subject to those kinds of geopolitical risks."

OPG said spreading the work among suppliers in the United States, Britain and Frnace creates a "robust and resilient supply chain," but the company still leaves both enrichment and fabrication — the two steps Canada cannot perform for the BWRX-300 — in foreign hands.

Why Ontario went global

Speaking at a recent news conference in Nanticoke, Ont., provincial Energy Minister Stephen Lecce said the province chose a foreign reactor because no Canadian alternative was ready to generate electricity at the required scale.

Ontario Energy and Mines Minister Stephen Lecce speaks to reporters on July 29 in Nanticoke, Ont., about the province's integrated energy plan. (Government of Ontario/YouTube)

"There is not a Canadian grid-scale, commercially viable small modular reactor technology to procure," he said. "So we had to go global."

He said Ontario chose the American-Japanese BWRX-300 because it was the most advanced option and offered the best chance to reduce the risks associated with building a first-of-its-kind reactor.

Canada does have a new domestic reactor under development, but it was not an alternative for Ontario's SMR project. The Candu Monark is not an SMR and is currently under assessment by Canada's nuclear regulator.

The decision to "go global," as Lecce put it, leaves Ontario dependent on foreign enrichment, but Lecce said the province has reduced the risk by arranging access to suppliers in the United States, France and Britain.

SMRs would use 'modest' amount of fuel

Winfield said multiple enrichment suppliers reduce the risk of disruption, but do not eliminate it. Every enrichment facility is outside Canada, while the only company identified that would make the finished fuel assemblies is American.

"I think that's still a risk. Particularly if the United States decides to use its supply of various uranium for geopolitical leverage, which is clearly not beyond the thinking of the Trump administration," Winfield said.

A rendering shows a BWRX-300 SMRs at Darlington, where Ontario is building the first of four planned units. Saskatchewan and New Brunswick are also evaluating SMR projects, while Alberta is developing a nuclear roadmap that includes potential SMR deployment. (Ontario Power Generation)

Even with France and Britain as backup suppliers, Winfield said, it opens the door to "all kinds of vulnerabilities relative to an all-Canadian supply chain. You are at the mercy of whatever external geopolitical events may be occurring."

The federal government says foreign enrichment doesn't present a significant supply risk, especially in the short to medium-term.

In an email, Natural Resources Canada said the four planned Darlington SMRs will require "a very small amount" of enriched fuel, which is "modest" compared with the global market, but did not provide a quantity.

Why being first is 'not a good thing'

While there are other SMRs active in China and Russia, the Darlington facility will be the first SMR in the G7.

"That's not a good thing, in my opinion," said M.V. Ramana, a University of British Columbia professor who studies nuclear energy and international security.

An aerial view shows of construction at Ontario Power Generation's Darlington New Nuclear Project in Clarington, Ont., where Canada's first BWRX-300 small modular reactor is being built. (Patrick Morrell/CBC)

"Nuclear power is a very expensive way to generate electricity and the small modular reactor is even more expensive."

Ramana said SMRs sacrifice the economies of scale available to larger reactors.

A 2014 study suggests they are more expensive per unit in generating capacity unless savings from shared infrastructure can offset the disadvantage, which is what OPG intends for its four-reactor Darlington site.

BWRX-300 designer GE Vernova says smaller reactors can overcome some of that cost disadvantage because they require less machinery than conventional reactors: water circulates through the reactor without powered pumps, while emergency cooling functions use gravity and natural circulation.

The company says this reduces the amount of equipment that must be manufactured, installed and maintained.

However, because Darlington is the design's first deployment, those projected savings have not yet been demonstrated by a commercially operating unit.

WATCH | First Nations sign deal for Darlington project: 7 First Nations sign $715M nuclear reactor deal | Duration 0:52 Several First Nations communities will receive minority ownership in the Darlington New Nuclear Project. This historic agreement, made between Ottawa, Ontario and seven First Nations communities in the province, is the largest Indigenous loan guarantee issued in Canada, worth about $715 million. The first modular, out of four, is expected to be completed by 2030.

Could Canada enrich its own uranium?

The only way for Canada to eliminate its reliance on foreign suppliers is by establishing its own uranium-enrichment industry.

Yellowcake uranium, a concentrated powder produced from mined uranium ore, is an early stage product in the nuclear fuel supply chain. Canada is the world's second-largest uranium producer. (Daniel Acker/Bloomberg News)

Lecce said Ontario would be open to discussions, but he acknowledged the decision ultimately rests with the federal government.

Natural Resources Canada said Ottawa has made no decision on commercial enrichment but plans to create a "Nuclear Fuels Table" with the provinces and industry to examine future needs and opportunities.

Ontario is currently the only province committed to building SMRs, but Saskatchewan is advancing plans for the same BWRX-300 technology, while New Brunswick and Alberta are evaluating potential nuclear projects that could include SMRs.

Ramana said Canada would need to enrich its own uranium to control the entire fuel chain, but such a facility would cost billions to build and require extensive security, regulation and international safeguards througout its life.

"In the enrichment business, again, there are economies of scale," he said. "It would be much more uneconomical for Canada to develop one just for this small modular reactor design."

Ramana added that the new reactors also create another long-term liability. Canada's current $26-billion nuclear waste plan was calculated around fuel from the existing Candu reactor fleet.

New reactors could change both the volume and type of spent fuel requiring disposal, but Ramana noted there has been no cost estimate from Canada's Nuclear Waste Management Organization for adding the spent fuel from four BWRX-300s.

World.title: 2 killed after helicopters battling Greece wildfires collide
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Two Greek firefighting helicopters collided in midair on Sunday as they were battling a wind-driven wildfire west of Athens, sending one aircraft crashing to the ground, footage showed. Two crew members died in the crash.

The dead crew members were one Greek and one Danish national, while the two who were recovered alive were one Greek and one British national.

The collision laid bare the danger at the most volatile front of Europe's wildfire emergency. Strong winds drove flames deeper into the region of the Greek capital and forced fresh evacuations, France guarded a still-burning scar four times the size of Paris, while Spain's major fires stopped advancing.

The aircraft were Bell helicopters operating over the Psatha area west of Athens, each with a two-person crew. Foreign firefighting and helicopter crews are often deployed in Greece to help tackle wildfires during the country's hot, dry summers.

Flames spread rapidly through western Attica, threatening communities and an industrial district outside Megara as violent gusts prevented firefighting aircraft from collecting water from the sea. The advance carried grim resonance in a region where the 2018 Mati wildfire killed 104 people, Europe's deadliest blaze this century.

WATCH | Fires burn in Crete: Wildfires burn on Greek island of Crete | Duration 0:23 Wildfires raged on the Greek island of Crete this week, AFP reports, leaving two firefighters dead. The fires in Greece come as Europe faces a hot and dry summer, with fires also raging in France and Spain.

Nearly 500 firefighters and 23 aircraft were deployed, but gale-force winds drove flames through dry forest and crippled the response, preventing some aircraft from reaching the sea to collect water.

Authorities ordered the evacuation of Kandili, Agia Skepi and Toutouli as smoke rose over the mountains. Crews were particularly concerned about Porto Germeno, a seaside community on the Gulf of Corinth. Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis was briefed on the operation.

The fire began Friday near Agios Vasileios before sweeping toward Porto Germeno and into the forested mountains west of Athens. Firefighters evacuated 254 people by sea Friday and another 12 Saturday — often the last escape route when fire and smoke cut the few roads from coastal communities.

Wildfire meteorologist Theodore Giannaros estimated the blaze had affected 40 to 50 square kilometres, although authorities had issued no official figure.

Firefighters battle a blaze near Porto Germeno, Greece, on Sunday. (Michael Varaklas/The Associated Press)

Elsewhere in Greece, flames threatened homes on Kefalonia, forcing evacuations from inland communities as aircraft made water drops over the Ionian island. Firefighters battled another blaze near Nea Tenedos in Halkidiki.

Earlier this week, two firefighters died fighting a fire on Crete, while a third was killed in the Peloponnese.

"A pristine forest, a paradise, was surrendered to the hands of the fire," local farmer Minas Tzortzanis said Saturday. "There are no words to explain what has happened. Destruction. Total destruction."

Mass evacuations in France and Spain

Together, fires in France and Spain have driven roughly a third of a million people from homes and vacation sites, emptied communities at the height of the European summer and stretched emergency services across simultaneous disasters.

The mass evacuations in France and Spain are the latest measure of a wildfire threat growing across Europe.

The continent entered 2026 after its worst fire year on record, with more than 10,000 square kilometres burned in 2025. Over the past four decades, wildfires have been linked to nearly 800 deaths across much of Europe, according to the European Environment Agency.

WATCH | Europe's wildfires are creating their own weather systems: Europe’s wildfires are creating their own weather systems | Duration 1:58 Wildfires in Europe have become so powerful they have created their own thunderstorm-generating weather systems. This has officials in France and Spain urging more be done to prevent the fires from starting.

Europe is the world's fastest-warming continent. It has warmed more than twice the global average since the 1980s, according to the European Union's Copernicus Climate Change Service.

Human-caused climate change made the extreme fire-weather conditions behind this year's French blazes at least twice as likely, scientists at World Weather Attribution found in a rapid analysis conducted while the fires were still burning.

'Fire is now fixed' in France

France's largest wildfire remained held within its perimeter after forcing 224,000 people to flee in what may have been the country's largest civilian evacuation outside wartime.

Hot spots still burned within a 420-square-kilometre scar, thousands remained unable to return home and nearly 3,000 firefighters were deployed against the Gironde megafire and a second, still-uncontained blaze in Provence.

In southwestern France, the Gironde megafire remained held within its perimeter Sunday but continued to burn after scorching 420 square kilometres of forest in 10 days.

"The fire is now fixed, which does not mean that the fire is extinguished," the Gironde prefecture said, using the French firefighting term for a blaze whose advance has been stopped.

WATCH | Bordeaux residents survey devastation: Bordeaux residents survey devastation after wildfire torches village | Duration 3:08 Residents of Le Porge in France's historic Bordeaux region show CBC News what's left of their community after a devastating wildfire tore through the village, destroying over 180 homes.

The region remained under France's highest red forest-fire alert. Dry conditions, soaring temperatures around Bordeaux and afternoon winds threatened to rekindle the flames.

In Le Porge, local officials said about 150 homes were destroyed. Mechanic Matthieu Plessis returned Saturday to the ruins of a house that had been in his family for seven generations.

"There are places I don't even recognize anymore," he said. "You don't even know what was here anymore, or who lived where."

WATCH | Drone footage of destroyed homes in southwestern France: Drone video shows homes reduced to ashes, rubble by wildfire in southwestern France | Duration 0:51 A massive wildfire in southwestern France has left parts of the town of Biscarrosse in ruins, with drone footage from Tuesday revealing burnt homes and forest. Fires across France have forced the unprecedented evacuation of tens of thousands of people.

Firefighters from Ukraine, Lithuania and French Polynesia were expected Sunday and Monday to reinforce the operation.

In southeastern France, nearly 1,500 firefighters battled a separate blaze in the Var department that tore through about 18 square kilometres in little more than a day.

The Gros Bessillon fire was stabilized Sunday after its perimeter held overnight, but it remained uncontained. Some 2,500 people were evacuated as flames threatened nearby communities.

WATCH | Are wildfires becoming worse?: Are wildfires becoming worse? | Duration 5:34 With wildfires dominating headlines across parts of the world, many may be wondering whether this is the new normal. The CBC's Dan Burritt spoke with author John Vaillant — who wrote the award-winning book, Fire Weather — about this year's wildfires worldwide.

It was the fourth major fire to strike central Var since July 19. A smaller blaze near Brignoles earlier in the week forced actor George Clooney and his family, along with about 700 other residents, to evacuate before it was brought under control.

Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said France's fires were generally under control but warned that conditions remained volatile. He appointed a national co-ordinator to oversee reconstruction in fire-ravaged areas.

More than 1,170 square kilometres have burned across France this year.

Fire eases in Spain

Spain's major fires — part of a season that has killed at least 13 people, produced the country's largest recorded wildfire and prompted a national emergency — were no longer advancing Sunday.

In Zamora province near the Portuguese border, more than 20 ground and aerial units guarded the perimeter of the Fermoselle fire against flare-ups in the rugged Arribes del Duero landscape. Most evacuees had returned home, according to local media.

Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez has called for a national pact to confront wildfires, warning that climate change is making them increasingly destructive.

World.title: Kyle Reyes wins Canada's 4th gold, 7th medal overall in judo at Glasgow 2026
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Kyle Reyes continued Canada’s judo medal haul at the Commonwealth Games with gold in the men’s -100-kilogram weight class on the final day of competition.

Reyes took down England’s Max Gregory just over two minutes into Sunday's final with a strong ouchi-gari throw, driving him backwards while hooking the right leg for the instant ippon win.

It’s Canada’s fourth gold and seventh medal overall in judo at Glasgow 2026.

WATCH | Reyes captures judo gold at Commonwealth Games: Kyle Reyes wins Commonwealth Games judo gold via an ippon | Duration 6:04 Toronto's Kyle Reyes beat England's Max Gregory in the men's -100 kg gold medal judo final, at the Glasgow 2026 Commonwealth Games.

The 32-year-old Reyes defeated The Gambia's Abdourahman Ceesay in his opening match and Georgios Kroussaniotakis of Cyprus in the semifinals, both by ippon.

Reyes, who was born in Brampton, Ont., but lives in Tokyo, took silver medals at the 2022 Commonwealth Games and 2022 world championships.

Canada's Coralie Godbout reached the podium earlier Sunday with bronze in the women’s -78kg division, defeating India’s Ishroop Narang 1-0 in the golden score extra time period after taking her down on her side for a yuko point.

The 25-year-old Godbout was the aggressor throughout the match, forcing Narang to hold on and survive as both athletes expelled energy for over six minutes before the finish at the Scottish Event Campus.

She defeated England's Shelley Ludford in the quarterfinals before falling to Australia's Maria Swan in the semis. The Saint-Charles-de-Bellechasse, Que., native is ranked 15th in the world in her weight class.

WATCH | Godbout claims bronze: Coralie Godbout grabs Commonwealth Games judo bronze | Duration 13:10 Coralie Godbout of Lévis, Que., defeated India's Ishroop Narang in the women's -78 kg bronze medal judo bout at the Glasgow 2026 Commonwealth Games.

Fellow Canadian John Messe A Bessong lost his bronze-medal match in the men's +100kg division to Tonga's Paula Monta by yuko later Sunday.

The Laval, Que., native began the day with a Round of 16 victory over Pakistan's Shah Hussain Shah before defeating Gerard Takayawa of Fiji in the quarterfinals. He fell to Australia's Kayhan Ozcicek-Takagi in his semifinal.

Canada finishes with 62 medals in Glasgow (19 gold, 20 silver, 23 bronze), good for third overall in the standings behind Australia's 170 and England's 110.

World.title: Lurkers in the deep: How Canada's new submarines will be used in peace and potential war
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

"Canada's next submarine fleet will secure our coastlines and waters," Prime Minister Mark Carney said early last month in announcing the choice of Germany's ThyssenKrupp Marine Systems as the preferred bidder for the country's new underwater fleet.

Patrolling Canada's three coasts will be part of the job for the fleet of up to a dozen state-of-the-art diesel-electric 212CD submarines, says retired vice-admiral Darren Hawco, who commanded Canada's Atlantic Fleet and served as the nation's military representative to NATO until 2020.

"With three oceans, the Arctic responsibilities, they're one of those strategic assets that we want to have."

But Hawco says the subs — which are intended to replace the navy's aging Victoria Class fleet and could be ready by 2034 — will also travel the world.

He expects to see them used in global hot spots from the Taiwan Strait and the nine-dash line in the South China Sea to the Mediterranean and the Baltic.

Protecting the seabed and everything on it

Nearer to home, the subs' job will include protecting underwater infrastructure and resources that many Canadians are only dimly aware of, like the fibre-optic cables that carry trans-oceanic communications.

"Most people do not appreciate that 90 per cent of global telecommunications actually runs across the seabed," said retired vice-admiral Mark Norman, former commander of the navy. "Everybody thinks it's satellite based."

"In the early days of the [current] Ukrainian conflict, we saw the vulnerability of underwater infrastructure."

Even for these more domestic tasks, the submarines' range of 7,000 nautical miles (13,000 kilometres) will be needed "because the distances are so vast," said Norman.

The new subs "have lots of endurance. They are not designed to go anywhere particularly quickly, but they are designed to stay at sea for relatively long periods of time, get into a patrol area, and basically stay there."

Their air-independent propulsion lets them remain submerged for about three weeks, allowing them to operate invisibly in areas such as the eastern and western approaches to Canada's Arctic coast and archipelago.

A scale model of the TKMS 212CD submarine at the Canadian Association of Defence and Security Industries annual defence industry trade show CANSEC, in Ottawa, on May 27. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

Riches under the sea

Hawco says the immediate threat in the North is the fact that Canada and Russia have overlapping undersea claims.

There would be little return for Russia to invade Canada's Arctic archipelago, much less its mainland, he said. But the ocean floor is a different matter.

"I think the return for them is to say, 'I own the entire Lomonosov Ridge and all the resources that are there, and there's nothing you can do,'" he said, referring to the 1,800-kilometre-long ridge under the Arctic Ocean that's the subject of a territorial dispute.

The answer to that kind of threat, Hawco said, is "having a submarine that can operate at that kind of distance, that's covert, super-quiet and can sink anything that comes close."

WATCH | Canadian submarine torpedoes decommissioned ship off Hawaii: Canadian submarine torpedoes decommissioned ship off Hawaii | Duration 0:56 As part of a bi-annual exercise, Canada's HMCS Corner Brook torpedoed and sank a decommissioned American vessel, a former guided missile cruiser called the USS Mobile Bay, on July 12.

As undersea mining becomes more important, said Hawco, the subs will be called on to make sure resources on Canada's continental shelf aren't pilfered.

He cites reports on the amount of rare earth minerals Japan has found by surfacing mud offshore. "That's just an indication of how much unexplored, unidentified and arguably unexploited critical minerals there are in seabeds," he said.

Protecting those resources in the future will involve submarines and a major investment in undersea technology, including "a whole bunch of sensors, whether sitting on the bottom or mobile," Norman said.

A needle in a haystack

A major role for the submarines in NATO's new Cold War with Russia and other adversaries will be intelligence-gathering and surveillance, including the covert insertion of special forces troops.

"They could be trailing other platforms, be they surface ships or submarines. They could just be doing general surveillance, including surveillance of land-based targets," said Norman.

Norman says he sees the subs working in concert with a fleet of underwater drones, and doesn't believe drones will render the submarines obsolete. Instead, their stealth will keep them relevant.

"Technology is not going to solve this problem in our lifetimes. It still will continue to be like finding a needle in a haystack, and nobody's figured out how to do that yet," Norman said.

Stephen Fuhr, secretary of state for defence procurement, speaks on his phone at CFB Esquimalt on Vancouver Island following an announcement July 6 about TKMS's winning bid to supply the Royal Canadian Navy with a fleet of submarines. (Chad Hipolito/The Canadian Press)

Fear of what lurks in the deep

That stealth is the key difference between the new submarines and the current Canadian fleet.

"It's hard to hide on this globe today with space surveillance being what it is," said Hawco. But the new submarines "are able to operate in a very dead zone of water where sound doesn't propagate well."

The goal is to create a mystery about where they're deployed.

"One of the greatest challenges in naval operations for an adversary is the knowledge that a submarine is out there somewhere, but you don't know where," said Norman.

When a Canadian frigate begins a deployment, there is typically a sendoff with fanfare. Pictures of the mission are posted to a Facebook page or the DND website and the frigate can be followed through online ship trackers.

Canada's new underwater fleet will be much more secretive.

A submarine "could be just sitting on the seabed off its own home port," said Norman, "but it doesn't matter because it's the fact that it's at sea," and therefore invisible. "It becomes an asymmetric consumer of resources to try to find a submarine.

"When you have a larger fleet, which we're hoping to get, it has a multiplication effect on an adversary. If they know that Canada has six submarines deployed at a particular moment, in a crisis, then where the hell are the submarines?"

Canada skips chance to get strategic weapon

Canada's choice of the German 212CD submarine over the larger South Korean Hanwha KSS-III wasn't a purely technical decision, but also took into account economic and strategic factors, including the Carney government's desire to integrate into European supply chains.

In an active war, the classic role of the submarine is to hunt and sink enemy shipping. The 212CD can accomplish that either with torpedoes or by launching cruise missiles through its torpedo tubes, which break the water's surface to strike a ship or a target on land. The subs will likely use a yet-to-be-developed supersonic cruise missile with a range of about 800 kilometres.

But in rejecting the Hanwha option, Canada also turned down what would have been its first real strategic weapon — one powerful enough to change the whole war calculus for a potential adversary.

One difference between the two subs is the South Korean one's ability to vertically launch ballistic missiles — in its case, the Hyunmoo-4 — a capability normally seen in nuclear-powered submarines.

WATCH | Carney announces Canada to buy up to 12 submarines from German shipbuilder: Canada to buy 'up to 12' submarines from German shipbuilder | Duration 1:14 Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canada is negotiating to procure 'up to 12' submarines from German shipbuilder Thyssenkrupp Marine Systems. Speaking to reporters in Halifax on Monday, Carney called the reported $24-billion procurement the 'largest in Canadian history.'

While the Hyunmoo-4 may not ultimately exceed the 212CD's cruise missile in range, it is a true ballistic missile that reaches into the exosphere and comes down at 10 times the speed of sound, making it very difficult to stop.

Moreover, its warhead weighs two tons, or about 15 times as much as the cruise missiles proposed for the TKMS submarine, and a sub in the Gulf of Finland could strike Moscow.

In fact, the KSS-III and Hyunmoo-4 package looks very much like a submarine designed in a country that's thinking about nuclear weapons.

In Canada's current strategic situation, Hawco said, it expects to fight as part of the NATO alliance, and "the military expectations of NATO for Canada don't today include such a capability."

"It would have been transformational in some respects from a war-fighting perspective," said Norman about the South Korean option. "But that doesn't mean the absence of that capability is in and of itself a vulnerability or a problem."

In a different future, though, in which NATO and NORAD might continue to fray and Canada finds itself more alone, the choice to forego a strategic weapon might come to be regretted.

"There's no denying that we won't have that capability," said Norman. "And I can't sit here and tell you categorically that not having it is not a problem. But we didn't specify it as a mandatory requirement."
