Remittances from the US to Jamaica amounted to more than US$2.6 billion last year. Since January this year a one per cent federal tax was imposed on such remittances. What if the tax on remittances to Jamaica were increased to 25 per cent or disallowed altogether as a form of punishment? We don’t have to pause to wonder what that would mean to thousands of families that cannot survive without it.

Our correspondent bank arrangements are tied to the US financial system. That’s what facilitates transactions between Jamaica and the rest of the world. What if those arrangements were cut off? Our economy would be literally paralyzed.

What if companies that want to do business with us were told that they would be penalized if they did so? What would that do to our investment flows?

Scores of people gather at the US embassy every day hoping to obtain a visa so they can visit their family members in the US or seek better opportunities here. What if the US were to restrict the granting of visas to Jamaicans as has been done to countries like Sierra Leone and Haiti?

And we are not alone in this; all Caribbean countries are at risk and all of us are extremely vulnerable. If our governments say or do anything that the White House finds displeasing, punishment will be meted out to us as sure as night follows day. Tariffs have become the weapon of choice and retribution a foreign policy tool. Canada was recently threatened with a 50 per cent tariff because smoke from wildfires there had drifted into America.

So, when Caribbean governments adopt a measured, cautious approach in dealing with America’s bullying tactics, it is because they understand the pickle we are in. Make a wrong move, defiantly defend the Cuban assistance programmes and our partnership with China and they pay the price. They understand how careful they have to be when their hand is in the mouth of an angry lion.

And, sadly, we have been placed into a position where Caribbean unity is of no avail. Our individual sovereignty and regional leverage are under siege. It is now every man for himself….every country on its own!

Some of us, in the national interest, have to be restrained in what they say; others of us, in the national interest, have to say what needs to be said and I will continue to voice my concerns as to how America’s dictates affect Jamaica and impair the hopes and aspirations of our people. Putting America first should not mean putting Jamaica in jeopardy.

I cautiously cling to the hope that this will pass, that the hemisphere will once again be a neighbourhood of peace, mutual understanding and respect, where true friendship prevails, where all of its people can pursue their own destiny with dignity and purpose and where we can look upon America as a friend indeed.

God bless all of you as you continue to make us proud and keep the black, green and gold flying. God bless the United States of America which, if it is so minded, can hold hands with us in a spirit of true friendship. God bless the land we love – Jamaica – and guide us with His mighty hand through these troubling times.

World.title: US embassies urge citizens to consider departing Middle East
World.content:
Smoke rises from Israeli bombardment near the village of Kfar Tibnit as seen from nearby Marjayoun (Marjeyoun) in southern Lebanon on June 14, 2026. Israel struck Beirut's southern suburbs on June 14, killing three people, in response to what it said was Hezbollah fire at northern Israel, while its military also carried out broader strikes on southern Lebanon. The latest escalation came amid expectations that a deal between the US and Iran to end the Middle East war could be imminent, but Iranian chief negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said there was "no point" in continuing peace talks with Washington after the strike. (Photo by AFP)

DUBAI, United Arab Emirates (AFP) —United States (US) embassies in capitals across the Middle East on Saturday warned their citizens to beware of “unforeseen escalation” in the regional conflict and urged them to be ready to leave.

The warning, posted online by US embassies in Bahrain, Egypt, Iraq, Israel, Jordan, Kuwait, Lebanon, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, came a day after US President Donald Trump threatened to hit Iran “very hard”.

Iran and the United States have been at war since February 28. A period of calm followed a ceasefire, though that collapsed with a return of strikes.

With no end in sight, the war has for months upended the lives of people across the Middle East and rattled global energy markets.

“Americans in the region should consider departing, or be prepared to depart should there be escalation,” said the security alert.

The messages urged citizens to check flight details and to follow safety advice from local authorities.

“Americans currently in the Middle East should exercise caution and heightened vigilance and should be prepared for flight cancellations, periodic airspace closures, and potential travel disruptions,” it said.

US citizens in Jordan were told not to visit military bases in the country, which have recently come under Iranian missile attack, and in Israel they were urged to seek the location of the nearest bomb shelter.

“The Iranian regime is unpredictable, as seen by its recent decisions to attack areas in the region without warning or provocations as well as to expand attacks to areas not previously targeted (such as Egypt),” said a post on the US Embassy Jerusalem site.

The US embassy in Beirut said the mission remained on “ordered departure status”, meaning that family members andnon-essential US government personnel were still relocated outside of Lebanon.

– ‘Defensive shield’ –

Iran’s military on Saturday accused Washington of “escalating tensions” in the region.

“Any country serving as defensive shield for criminal and aggressive America will be engulfed by the flames of war,” Ali Abdollahi, head of Iran’s military central command, said in a statement read on state television.

Mohammad Mokhber, adviser to Iran’s supreme leader, also warned against any attacks on Iranian infrastructure.

“You calculate through military equations, but we respond with the logic of history,” he wrote on X.

“Attacking Iran’s infrastructure directly awakens the fault lines on which 250 years of your hegemonic architecture have been built.”

Iran and the US resumed overnight exchanges of fire last month after a days-long lull in fighting, although there were no reported strikes overnight Friday to Saturday.

– ‘Unknown projectile’ –

On Wednesday a drone struck a US-owned gas vessel moored in an Egyptian port, causing a fire. Egypt is investigating but has not yet accused any group of launching the attack.

Meanwhile an “unknown projectile” struck a tanker off the coast of Oman, a British maritime agency said on Saturday, as the United States and Iran vie for control of the Strait of Hormuz.

Iran has effectively maintained control over navigation through Hormuz since the outbreak of the war on February 28, requiring vessels to obtain permission and pay transit fees before using the waterway.

Maritime trade tracking firm Kpler said on Friday that traffic through the Hormuz strait has dropped “sharply”.

“With US and Iranian public positions still at odds, operators are closely monitoring traffic volumes, routing behaviour and any diplomatic developments that could reshape risk across regional shipping lanes in the days ahead,” the firm said on X.

On the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, another waterway that has gained increasing importance as a transit route for Saudi Arabian oil, the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen on Saturday denied seeking to charge ships for passage through it.

The narrow waterway connects the Red Sea to the Indian Ocean and, via the Suez Canal, the Mediterranean.

The Middle East war broke out when the United States and Israel launched strikes on Iran, which has retaliated with missile and drone strikes across the region.

On the Lebanon front, Israel’s military on Saturday said it killed three Hezbollah fighters in southern Lebanon, while one of its soldiers was moderately injured during a “close-quarters encounter” with Hezbollah militants.

World.title: Hungary faces energy crunch as drought shuts down Paks nuclear plant, PM says
World.content:
“Due to the further drop in the Danube’s water level,” Magyar wrote Saturday, “tomorrow it will be completely shut down for the first time in 44 years."

The Soviet-built Paks facility remains the backbone of the country’s power system. The loss of output has triggered national energy-saving measures and offers of support from regional neighbors.

A prolonged outage would cripple Hungary’s electricity supply at a time when temperatures are forecast to rise above 40 degrees Celsius in Budapest next week amid an ongoing heatwave and drought across Europe.

Magyar warned the shutdown could trigger an emergency at a time of high summer demand: “An energy crisis situation may arise from Monday. Coordinated steps and self-restraint will be needed to avoid more severe consequences.”

The government has urged households and businesses to reduce electricity consumption during peak hours between 5 p.m. and 10 p.m., calling on people to limit their use of air conditioning and washing machines. Authorities have also prepared an emergency plan to temporarily restrict consumption at industrial facilities on a rotating basis, while increasing output from other power plants.

The European Commission said Friday it was closely monitoring the situation and was prepared to convene an emergency meeting of its Electricity Coordination Group over the Paks shutdown.

World.title: Trump cancels strikes on Iran, says deal imminent
World.content:
Donald Trump speaks during a Cabinet meeting at Camp David in Maryland, on July 31, 2026. | Aaron Schwartz/ AFP via Getty Images

Tehran has not responded to the U.S. president’s announcement and has not confirmed an agreement to end the Middle East conflict has been reached.

U.S. President Donald Trump said late Saturday that he was canceling planned strikes on Iran pending a rapid agreement with Tehran to end the conflict in the Middle East.

“We have just been asked by Iran, and other Middle Eastern Countries, to hold off any attack in that the perimeters of a deal has been agreed to,” Trump announced in a post on Truth Social.

He said the agreement would include the “Immediate, Complete, and Total OPENING OF THE HORMUZ STRAIT” and “an end to Iran’s nuclear threat.” Trump added that Israel supported his commitment to pause strikes, contingent on “being able to rapidly make a DEAL.”

World.title: Ceuta crisis: 22 EU leaders gang up against Spain’s Sánchez over his migration policy
World.content:
In a letter to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, European Council President António Costa and Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin, the 22 leaders made direct reference to the need for EU-level cooperation on policies such as Madrid’s migrant regularization scheme.

“We have a duty to effectively deter and relentlessly combat illegal migration, by coordinating our action, strengthening our external borders and addressing all policies that can serve as pull factors, such as the regularization of [a] very large number of irregular migrants,” the leaders wrote.

Madrid has pushed back against the claim that the country’s regularization scheme triggered the crisis in Ceuta, and has pointed out that none of the people who illegally entered the exclave would be eligible to benefit from the measure.

“This process is based on very specific conditions, such as proof of residency in Spain before January 1, 2026, and having resided in Spain for five consecutive months at the time of application,” said a spokesperson for the Spanish foreign ministry. Moreover, the deadline for filing applications for the scheme, which was launched in April, was in June.

But those explanations have not appeared to sway the EU leaders who signed the letter to Costa, Von der Leyen and Martin.

“We cannot allow uncontrolled mass crossings, the instrumentalisation of migration or other hybrid threats to create the perception that illegal entry into the European Union is possible. That a migrant’s illegal entry can turn into legal stay,” they went on.

World.content:

World.title: Labour holds Greater Manchester mayoralty after counting goes to second round
World.content:
Speaking at the Co-Op Live arena to the east of the city, Craig said she stands “ready to serve” her 3 million constituents.

“Every single decision I take as your mayor of Greater Manchester will pass the test of making your life better,” Craig pledged.

The vote was triggered after three-time mayoral contest winner Burnham resigned the job in June to return to Westminster, where he swiftly claimed leadership of the governing Labour Party and became prime minister. There had been concern that Burnham’s move would allow Reform UK — which performed strongly in local elections in England earlier this year — to seize the mayoralty.

Craig will now be have to deal directly with Burnham, who has promised to devolve more powers to England’s mayors as a part of a devolution package. The post currently comes with powers over transport, policing, and housing.

Turnout for the special election was noticeably lower than when Burnham last ran back in 2024, with only 25 per cent of voters heading to the polls this time, compared to 32 per cent at the last vote. POLITICO witnessed some voters on doorsteps Thursday evening learning of the election for the first time.

Counting continued late into the night as the re-instated supplementary voting system took the contest to a second round for the first time ever.

World.title: Almost all of Ceuta migrants have returned to Morocco, Spain says
World.content:
People gather on a hilltop near Bab Sebta on the Morocco-Spain border, near Ceuta and the Moroccan town of Fnideq on July 30, 2026. | Abdelmajid Bziouat/AFP via Getty Images

“Most of the people that came yesterday are now back in Morocco,” an official said.

BRUSSELS — More than 48,300 of the approximately 50,000 people who entered the Spanish exclave of Ceuta from Morocco have returned, a Spanish government official told POLITICO.

“Most of the people that came yesterday are now back in Morocco,” said the official, who was granted anonymity to speak freely, adding that the situation was “on the path back to normality.”

The influx of migrants could be linked to a recent Spanish court ruling that limited the use of the country’s immediate-return procedure for migrants, the official added.

The European Commission said “there are no onward movements towards the European continent or other member states” by the migrants.

World.title: Trump administration slams Spain’s Sánchez for migrant ‘invasion’ of Ceuta
World.content:
“This unacceptable incident is the direct result of the Spanish Government’s deliberate efforts to enable and facilitate mass illegal migration into Europe. We are considering actions to defend Americans at home and abroad from this threat and stand ready to assist other European allies considering similar options,” wrote the department.

Sánchez will hardly be surprised by the scathing American reaction, having emerged as the fiercest Trump critic among EU leaders, slamming U.S. military action in the Middle East and barring U.S. military planes from using Spanish air bases.

“Thank God POTUS was elected and our country’s border no longer looks like this. These images out of Spain are an unfortunate reminder of the consequences of mass migration and the radical left-wing globalist policies that have enabled the Invasion of the West,” wrote U.S. Vice President JD Vance.

The U.S. Department of Homeland Security made the same argument, saying: “If Spain had their own President Trump, this wouldn’t be an issue.”

The U.S. criticism came as the situation in Ceuta escalated into a Europe-wide political flashpoint in little more than a day. Neighboring governments moved to tighten their response on Friday, with France restoring border checks and Italy calling for Spain to be suspended from the Schengen area, exposing divisions over the bloc’s migration policy.

Former Trump adviser and world’s first trillionaire Elon Musk initially shared a video comparing footage from the Ceuta migrant crisis with scenes from the 2013 zombie film “World War Z.” “Wow, the situation in Spain looks crazy!” he posted.

Clarifying the comparison was a joke, he then shared footage from 2023, showing hundreds of Venezuelan migrants attempting to cross into the U.S., captioning it: “This is what America looked like under Biden.”

World.title: Northern Ireland misses a deadline to fix its budget crisis
World.content:
Bryant, a former Anglican priest who’s never held a Cabinet post before, held his first press conference as Northern Ireland secretary shortly before meeting delegations from the region’s two main government parties, Sinn Féin and the Democratic Unionists.

Bryant emphasized that the U.K. government expects Stormont to get more bang for its buck by reforming the delivery of local services, most crucially hospital care, where Northern Ireland suffers the worst waiting lists in the entire National Health Service.

“Look, we need to get to a budget,” Bryant said. “And I understand the financial pressures. I know everybody expects me to come with a checkbook. I’m actually coming with a checklist of things that I want to get sorted.”

Sinn Féin, which holds the key finance and economy ministries, has shied from taking any significant decisions on raising local taxes—not that the DUP wouldn’t immediately veto such moves. Nothing much can happen in Northern Ireland’s system of cross-community government unless the largest parties on each side of the divide can agree.

The two parties blame each other for delivering so little and agree that it’s up to the U.K. Treasury to break the budgetary impasse by providing them much more annually to spend. An independent budgetary watchdog, the Northern Ireland Fiscal Council, recently concluded that the region wasn’t being subsidized by English taxpayers to the same levels as in Scotland and Wales — and if it was, Northern Ireland could gain an extra £1 billion to £3.5 billion annually.

While few expect the Burnham administration to come anywhere close to that, both sides in Belfast do expect Bryant to take charge of key budget decisions — which is what his predecessors did when the Northern Ireland Executive collapsed in 2017 from a Sinn Féin walkout, and again in 2022 from a Democratic Unionist walkout.

World.title: Rumours ignite social media over alleged Cristiano Ronaldo and Georgina Rodríguez wedding
World.content:
In an interview at the end of 2025 with British journalist Piers Morgan, Cristiano Ronaldo confided how he asked Georgina Rodriguez, his partner of ten years, to marry him, and spoke about when that might happen.

 

"I had bought the ring, a friend slipped it into my hand and our daughters saw the moment. They asked me if I was going to ask their mum to marry me and I felt it was the right time to do it," he said.

When it came to the wedding date, Cristiano deftly sidestepped the question, denying a goal to the thousands of curious fans wondering when the long‑awaited ceremony would take place. The captain of the Portuguese national team merely said it would be "after the World Cup, with the champion's trophy". With no trophy, does that mean no wedding?

Once the World Cup was over, with Portugal going no further than the last 16, rumours around the wedding began to grow. It was already known that Georgina wanted it to be "private" and that the weekend of 1 and 2 August was the most likely time for it to take place, since Al-Nassr start their season on 13 September and the star would be heading back to the club to begin pre-season training.

The media then started making their own preparations for the wedding. As Cristiano Ronaldo and his family had been spending a lot of time in the municipality of Cascais, where the player is building a house, rumours surfaced that the wedding might be held at the Quinta da Regaleira in Sintra, a palace west of Lisbon, as reported by Portuguese TV show "V+ Fama" on TVI.

Previously, a local newspaper in Madeira had already claimed the wedding would be on the island. Several reports suggested the island's cathedral had been booked for the occasion, as well as another luxury hotel.

On 28 July, Cristiano Ronaldo posted a photo with his children on their way to his private jet, which fuelled speculation that the wedding would be on a Balearic island or, perhaps, on a private plane hired just for the occasion. It was not. It turned out to be just a holiday trip to Palma de Mallorca.

The journalistic digging by some outlets into the wedding plans went so far that even the schedule of artist Luan Santana, a Brazilian singer Cristiano Ronaldo is very fond of, was scrutinised, and it was concluded there were no concerts booked for that particular weekend. The theory is that the singer would be hired to perform at Cristiano and Georgina's wedding.

However, to cool some of the heated excitement, Elma and Katia Aveiro, Cristiano's sisters, poured cold water on things by saying that the wedding was not going to happen just yet.

"There is no date set. This year I won't be wearing a wedding dress, not for myself and not for him," revealed the younger sister, Katia Aveiro, to Portuguese magazine TV7 Dias, during the launch of a new collection from her brand.

Elma Aveiro, the older sister, said that the wedding had been postponed and that she did not know how her brother and future sister-in-law were planning new dates.

Some still believe these comments were a way of throwing people off the scent and that the wedding could actually be taking place as we write this article. Could it be? If so, it has been the best‑kept secret in history.

From Gucci to the 37‑carat oval diamond

The story of Cristiano Ronaldo and Georgina Rodríguez began in 2016.

The couple met in a Gucci store in Madrid, where Georgina worked as a sales assistant. They later bumped into each other again at other events and began dating discreetly.

At first, they tried to keep the romance out of the public eye, but in January 2017 they went public with their relationship when they appeared together for the first time at the FIFA awards ceremony.

In June 2017, twins Eva and Mateo were born via surrogacy, as had already been the case with Cristiano Jr. A month later, Cristiano Ronaldo and Georgina Rodríguez announced they were expecting their first child together.

In November 2017, Alana Martina was born. Over that period, Georgina also took on a central role in the lives of Cristiano Jr., Eva and Mateo.

In August 2025, the couple announced their engagement, after almost nine years together.

The announcement was made on social media on 11 August, with Georgina posting the striking ring with the caption: "Yes, I do. In this life and in all my lives," she wrote.

The ring also became a focus of attention for the international press, which sought out jewellery experts to estimate its value. The 30‑carat ring is thought to be worth between 2 and 4.5 million euros.

Throughout their relationship, Georgina has followed Ronaldo through his various club moves, from leaving Real Madrid for Juventus in 2018, to his return to Manchester United in 2021, and his transfer to Al Nassr in Saudi Arabia in 2023.

Along the way, the couple also faced defining moments, such as the tax fraud case involving the footballer and the rape allegation he faced.

In October 2021, Cristiano Ronaldo and Georgina Rodríguez revealed that they were expecting twins. Months later, in April 2022, the couple announced that their son had died during childbirth. His twin sister, Bella Esmeralda, was born healthy.

World.title: Italian Navy boards tanker from Russian shadow fleet
World.content:
Italian vessel Thaon di Revel boarded a Russian shadow fleet tanker to inspect it in international waters near Pantelleria, an island located between Sicily and Tunisia.

 

The inspection was carried out by the Italian navy on Sunday morning, 2 August, as part of the Operation EUNAVFOR MED IRINI, the European Union mission in the Mediterranean monitoring arms and oil trafficking.

The tanker Toa Payoh, which is subject to European Union sanctions and belongs to the so-called Russian 'shadow fleet', has undergone nationality verification, which for ships is determined by the flag they are authorised to fly. The Toa Payoh is sailing under the declared flag of Cameroon.

The tanker, which left the port of Cotonou in Benin on 16 July bound for Istanbul, was intercepted west of Pantelleria. According to the ministry's account, the tanker's master initially did not provide the requested cooperation. A team of Italian military personnel then reached the vessel by helicopter from the ship Thaon di Revel and carried out the planned checks.

Operation IRINI: ship Thaon di Revel boards tanker belonging to the Russian 'shadow fleet' Ministero della Difesa italiano

"I would like to congratulate the crew of the ship Thaon di Revel and all the service personnel involved in the operation for the professionalism, preparation and resolve they have shown. This activity too is a concrete demonstration of Italy's contribution to the security of the Mediterranean and to the European Union's action," said Defence Minister Guido Crosetto.

How the operation was carried out

The Ministry of Defence reported that the operation, carried out with the support of a Greek ship and a Polish patrol aircraft, lasted around two hours and was concluded routinely and in complete safety.

Operation IRINI: ship Thaon di Revel boards tanker belonging to the Russian 'shadow fleet' Ministero della Difesa italiano

The operation, conducted in international waters under the European mandate, was carried out, the ministry note says, in full compliance with Article 110 of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), which allows a naval vessel, when the conditions laid down are met, to carry out the necessary checks on the nationality of a merchant ship and the flag it is authorised to fly.

At the moment, the Italian authorities are reviewing the information and documentation obtained during the inspection.

World.title: Spanish teen behind massacre threats and leader of 764 network arrested
World.content:
A joint operation involving the Guardia Civil, the autonomous police forces of the Basque Country and Catalonia (Ertzaintza and Mossos d'Esquadra) has led to the arrest in Guipúzcoa, a region near the northern border with France, of a 17-year-old Spanish national.

 

The three police forces consider him to be the main figure in Spain for the neonazi, paedophile and satanist 764 network. This organisation, which, according to the investigation, has for months been generating public alarm through threats targeting educational centres, town councils, libraries and other public and private entities.

Between January and April this year, the teenager is believed to have sent numerous messages announcing shootings and armed attacks. None were carried out, but they were enough for several institutions to activate exceptional security protocols.

In some of these messages, according to police sources, the author claimed that he would broadcast the attacks live so that other members of the organisation could watch them. Threats against a well-known leisure centre and against several individuals are also being investigated.

Searches were carried out on 16 July at two homes in Guipúzcoa linked to the suspect, once the corresponding judicial authorisations had been obtained. Officers seized electronic devices, storage media and documents which are now being analysed. The detainee has appeared before a judge and is subject to a custodial measure in a specialised centre in Donostia/San Sebastián.

What is the 764 network and how did it operate in Spain

The 764 network emerged in the United States and takes its name from the first three digits of the postcode for Stephenville, Texas, the hometown of its founder.

Over time it evolved from a marginal community on internet forums into a structure with a presence in different countries, linked to offences such as sextortion, the distribution of child sexual abuse material, incitement to self-harm, the dissemination of content showing extreme violence and animal abuse. Canada has classified it as a terrorist entity, and several countries have ongoing investigations into its activities.

In Spain, the investigation has also identified the use of techniques typical of these communities, such as swatting, doxing and identity theft, aimed at falsely pointing to people unconnected with the events in order to trigger police interventions, create dangerous situations and divert investigators' attention. At least two people, one in the Basque Country and another in Catalonia, were subjected to harassment campaigns arising from these practices.

Investigations have also revealed that the detainee took part in digital spaces where psychological manipulation was exerted on children and vulnerable young people, involving dynamics of humiliation, coercion to self-harm and submission to the will of those who recruited the victims. Images and videos obtained in this way were later shared within the community as a means of exerting control over those affected.

Prevention, the main line of defence

Investigators stress that organisations such as the 764 network actively target minors on social media, messaging apps and gaming platforms. The initial contact is usually presented as a friendship or shared interests, and only over time does it turn into manipulation, blackmail and isolating the victim from their environment.

For that reason, the authorities recommend that families and educators remain alert to signs such as requests for private photos, conversations the child hides, proposals involving self-harm or demands to take part in degrading challenges.

Early communication with the family, the school or the security forces remains, according to those responsible for the investigation, the most effective way of preventing a teenager from becoming trapped in this type of network.

World.title: Spanish government received intelligence warnings of Ceuta migrant surge according to a report
World.content:
The leader of the Popular Party, Alberto Núñez Feijoo, had already warned of the situation during his appearance yesterday in Ceuta: the Spanish Government had been aware of it since last Monday.

 

New information from several military and civilian intelligence sources suggests that the Spanish government had advance warning of the risk of a mass arrival of migrants in the North African exclave of Ceuta this week.

Intelligence alerts were issued over several days, including in the hours immediately before tens of thousands of people crossed from Morocco, sources said.

Intelligence services, consulted by The Objective media, had warned that King Mohammed VI was likely to make a "gesture of magnanimity" at the border to coincide with Morocco's Throne Day celebrations. Those initial warnings were followed by reports of migrants swimming across from Fnideq, known as Castillejos in Spanish, and buses carrying people from different parts of Morocco towards the border.

Over the course of around ten days, nearly 1,000 people swam into Ceuta. Intelligence officials reportedly viewed this as a test by Moroccan authorities and passed that assessment on to the government.

In the end, between 60,000 and 75,000 migrants crossed into Ceuta, marking the largest migration crisis in the autonomous city's history. According to Spain's Interior Ministry, about 53,000 people had returned to Morocco in the days that followed.

Border forces overwhelmed

The Civil Guard and National Police stationed at the Tarajal border crossing were unable to stop the influx of migrants and instead focused on assisting the injured, several sources said.

An injured migrant who crossed into Spain returns to Morocco with the assistance of a Spanish soldier from the Spanish enclave of Ceuta, Saturday, Aug. 1, 2026. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved.

The same sources, speaking to The Objective, criticized Madrid for not deploying the army immediately, despite military units in both Ceuta and Melilla being on standby.

"They could have been mobilized without prior meetings, simply following a political decision and an order from the operations command,” they said.

Officers deployed in the area also reported that the Moroccan gendarmerie stood "with their arms folded" while migrants attempted the crossing, both along the breakwater and on the access road to the border crossing, where other people climbed over fences and roofs.

Civil Guard sources added that the current situation differs from that seen in May 2021, when Morocco relaxed its border controls in a diplomatic response to Spain's decision to admit the Polisario Front leader, Brahim Ghali.

This time, they say, the number of people swimming into Ceuta had already been rising for weeks, partly because of a Spanish Supreme Court ruling prohibiting the immediate return of migrants who reach Spanish territory by swimming.

The government's response

The Interior Ministry insisted hours later that cooperation with Morocco was "exemplary, loyal and permanent."

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez described the mass entry as a "violation of Spain's territorial integrity" and blamed the incident on people-smuggling networks, arguing that they had exploited the Supreme Court ruling by encouraging thousands of people to attempt the crossing.

People walk on a beach after attempting to cross from the Moroccan northern town of Fnideq to the Spanish enclave of Ceuta, Friday, July 31, 2026. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved

Sánchez also insisted that Moroccan authorities had cooperated "swiftly and consistently" from the outset, adding that Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska had reinforced border security as arrivals by sea increased.

That reinforcement ultimately resulted in about thirty additional officers and a boat that, a few days later, broke down.

Despite repeated warnings from intelligence agencies, the Ministry of the Interior did not order the deployment of reinforcements until late Thursday, when the army was called in along with additional personnel from the Civil Guard and the National Police.

World.title: Grand designs: Tashkent’s modernist architecture joins UNESCO World Heritage List
World.content:
A group of ten modernist buildings and urban complexes associated with the transformation of Tashkent has been inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List, bringing international recognition to a distinctive period of Central Asian architectural history.

 

Officially titled “Tashkent Modernist Architecture: Modernity and Tradition in Central Asia,” the serial property includes structures built between the 1960s and the early 1990s.

UNESCO describes the ensemble as an example of how international modernist architecture was adapted to local cultural traditions, climatic conditions and the seismic risks facing the Uzbek capital.

State Museum of Arts Euronews

The decision was taken during the 48th session of the UNESCO World Heritage Committee, held in Busan, Republic of Korea, from 19 to 29 July 2026. The property was inscribed under criterion IV, which recognises outstanding examples of architectural or urban development representing a significant period in human history.

A modern city shaped after an earthquake

Tashkent’s modernist transformation had begun before the devastating earthquake of 1966, but the disaster accelerated the reconstruction of the city on a much larger scale.

New avenues, public squares, housing complexes, museums and cultural institutions reshaped the capital. International modernist principles were combined with courtyards, loggias, geometric decoration and monumental artworks drawn from the architectural and craft traditions of Uzbekistan.

Kosmonavtlar Metro Station Euronews

Designs also responded to the region’s practical requirements. Deep façades, screens and shaded spaces were used to address the intense summer heat, while new construction methods reflected the need for greater resistance to earthquakes.

State Museum of History Uzbekistan Art and Culture Development Foundation

The ten component parts are the Zhemchug, or “Pearl”, Residential Building; the State Museum of History; the Central Exhibition Hall of the Academy of Arts; Kosmonavtlar Metro Station; the Big Solar Furnace, also known as the Sun Heliocomplex; the Peoples’ Friendship Palace; the State Museum of Arts; the State Circus; Chorsu Market; and the Alisher Navoi Cinema Palace.

Peoples' Friendship Palace Uzbekistan Art and Culture Development Foundation

Nine of the ten are situated along the main urban axes created during the reconstruction of central Tashkent. The Big Solar Furnace, an experimental scientific complex completed in the late 1980s, stands outside the capital near Parkent.

Alisher Navoi Cinema Palace Uzbekistan Art and Culture Development Foundation

Together, the sites show how modernist architecture was used across a wide range of public and everyday functions — from housing and transport to museums, entertainment, commerce and scientific research.

Central Exhibition Hall of the Academy of Arts Uzbekistan Art and Culture Development Foundation

“This is recognition of the value not only of individual buildings, but of an entire era,” said Saida Mirziyoyeva, Head of Uzbekistan’s Presidential Administration.

For Mirziyoyeva, the architecture created after the earthquake brought together modern design, Central Asian traditions and solutions adapted to the country’s climate.

Preserving a recent layer of cultural history

Many of the buildings remain in active use and continue to shape daily life in Tashkent. Their inscription reflects a broader reassessment of 20th-century architecture, which has often received less protection than older monuments despite its importance to the identity and collective memory of modern cities.

“Pearl” Residential Building Uzbekistan Art and Culture Development Foundation

Gayane Umerova, Chairperson of the Uzbekistan Art and Culture Development Foundation and of the country’s National Commission for UNESCO, said the inscription placed an important part of Uzbekistan’s recent architectural history within the international account of 20th-century heritage and the global modernist movement.

Chorsu Market Uzbekistan Art and Culture Development Foundation

“These buildings record how Tashkent imagined public life, collective identity and the future through architecture,” Mirziyoyeva said.

State Circus Uzbekistan Art and Culture Development Foundation

“UNESCO recognition also carries a long-term responsibility: to conserve these buildings with rigour, keep them part of the life of the city and pass their knowledge to future generations.”

Uzbekistan’s cultural and natural World Heritage sites

The inscription brings the number of Uzbekistan’s cultural properties on the World Heritage List to six. The other five are Itchan Kala in Khiva, the historic centres of Bukhara and Shakhrisyabz, Samarkand – Crossroad of Cultures, and the transnational Silk Roads: Zarafshan-Karakum Corridor.

The country also has two natural properties on the list. The Western Tien-Shan, inscribed in 2016, includes the Maidantal and Bashkizilsay sections of the Chatkal State Biosphere Nature Reserve in Uzbekistan, an area known for its mountain landscapes, forests and rich biodiversity.

The Cold Winter Deserts of Turan, inscribed in 2023, includes five components in western Uzbekistan: Saigachy, Saigachy-Beleuli, Saigachy-Duana, Saigachy-Zhideyli and Southern Ustyurt. Part of a wider transnational property shared with Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan, these areas protect desert ecosystems adapted to extremely dry conditions, cold winters and hot summers.

World.title: Delicious dumplings: The evolution of delicacies enjoyed all along the Silk Road to Spain
World.content:
The story of the metamorphosis of these delicious pastry parcels begins its journey in China – Central Asia – South Caucasus - Europe.

 

Parallel to the Silk Road story runs what might be called the “Dumpling Belt”, where these humble dishes travelled the trade routes, changing names, shapes and cooking methods as they moved westwards.

As we explore the tasty treats, we see the subtle changes as you travel through borders, regions and countries.

Once Upon a Time in China

According to Chinese tradition, their story begins with the legendary physician Zhang Zhongjing, who, during a bitter winter nearly two millennia ago, folded dough around mutton, herbs and warming spices to treat villagers suffering from frostbitten ears, shaping the parcels to resemble the ears themselves.

Archaeological discoveries in Xinjiang’s Turfan region – dumplings preserved for over a thousand years – and early writings such as the 3rd-century poem of scholar Shu Xi describing Mantou suggest that these simple bundles of dough and filling have long been part medicine, part sustenance, and wholly enduring companions of travellers across the ancient routes of Eurasia.

The shapeshifter

From the steaming baskets of China, dumplings then travelled westwards with merchants, nomads and caravans.

They adapted to new landscapes and tastes as they went and as they evolved across Central Asia, they became larger, heartier creations such as manty and Manti, filled more generously with lamb and onion and cooked over rising clouds of steam.

Further along the ancient routes, the dumpling continued to transform and in Uzbekistan the delicate chuchvara and Manti emerged; in Kazakhstan the robust Manti settled, and in the South Caucasus the finely crafted Azerbaijani Düşbərə and Gürzə were created.

Each reflected the ingredients, techniques, and traditions of its home, and these variations revealed how a simple idea—dough wrapped around a savoury filling—became a culinary traveller, reshaped by every culture it encountered along the Dumpling Belt.

In the kitchens of Azerbaijan

In Azerbaijan, the dumpling takes on two particularly distinctive forms: Düşbərə and Gürzə.

At first glance they may seem modest, but both are celebrated for the precision and care they demand. Düşbərə are famously tiny—delicate parcels of dough filled with minced lamb and served in a fragrant broth/soup—so small that tradition says dozens should fit onto a single spoon.

Gürzə, by contrast, is slightly larger and hand-pinched along the top in a braided fold said to resemble a snake, their name echoing the local word for a viper.

Both dishes rely on simple ingredients—fine dough, seasoned meat, herbs and broth—but their true character lies in the technique and patience required to shape them, where the skills are often passed from generation to generation in Azerbaijani kitchens.

Today, chefs continue to honour these traditions while adding their own interpretations, keeping these beloved dumplings at the heart of the country’s culinary identity.

Local Azerbaijani women preparing dumplings euronews

Chef Ilkin Akbarzadeh is President of the Baku Culinary Association and has a substantial following of over 60 000 on instagram. He explained why dumplings are an intrinsic part of Azerbaijani heritage.

“Dumpling, this is part of our traditional cuisine, the heritage cuisine in Azerbaijan.”

“I think probably, many of these dumplings are coming from Asia, from China, and after some kind of transformers for every culture, every people, and all regions,” he says.

All the types are made with flour, Akbarzade notes:

“I mean the dushbarar, kingels and the gurza, and different types of this type of food was cooked from the dough and stuffed with meat.”

He says the consumption of dumplings happens in the colder months: “Usually in our culture, people eat it in winter time. For energy, for the health, for cold weather, you're heating the whole body, and that usually representing this food in the winter, in our culture.”

There are many versions of meat or vegetables wrapped in dough in Azerbaijan, including dushbara, kutabs and gurza. The renowned chef says that the way to eat dusbara, which is used in a broth is “in the one spoon, 13 on the 15 pieces of the small dushbaras.”

The gurzas dumpling, he says are traditionally served with a sprinkling of sumac and/or yogurt/mint/garlic sauce.

Uzbekistan: The home of Manti

Across Central Asia, dumplings take on heartier forms shaped by nomadic traditions and the region’s love of communal cooking.

In Uzbekistan, one of the most iconic is Manti, which are large, steamed dumplings whose recipes are carefully passed down through generations. They are often filled with a mixture of lamb, beef and finely chopped onion. The balance of ingredients is absolutely key.

Local resident Yulduz Rakhmonova explains: “I learned how to make Manti from my grandmother, who patiently taught us, her grandchildren, the craft of Uzbek cuisine. For the filling, we would mix lamb with beef and use an equal amount of onion to the meat, which would form a broth that gives Manti its distinctive flavour.”

She adds that the choice of meat is crucial, insisting that only fresh, high-quality ingredients should be used.

For many families, the techniques of preparing Manti are inherited alongside the recipe itself.

Ezoza Irmatova recalls learning from her mother-in-law:

“The dough for Manti must be very thin, yet strong. For this, you should use premium-quality wheat and room-temperature water. If you do everything correctly, even elderly people will enjoy the dish.”

The careful folding of each dumpling is considered an art, with cooks striving for uniform shapes that are as aesthetically pleasing to the eye as they are to the palate.

Manti is commonly prepared in large quantities at home using stacked steamers known as a Mantyshnitsa, allowing families to cook dozens at once.

The process often becomes a shared activity, with several generations gathering around the table to roll dough, fill and fold the dumplings before they are steamed.

The process of making dumplings euronews

While small regional variations exist in seasoning and shape, the essence of the dish remains the same.

In Uzbekistan, Manti is more than a meal - it is a symbol of hospitality, family tradition and the enduring culture of the dumpling along the ancient trade routes

Crossing the steppe from Uzbekistan to neighbouring Kazakhstan, the dumpling continues its journey, still widely known as Manti, though other variations of the name—such as mantas—also appear across the region. Despite the subtle shifts in language and preparation, the essence remains unchanged: seasoned meat wrapped carefully inside thin dough.

Kazakhstan: Dumplings of the Steppe

In Kazakhstan, Manti occupy an important place in both everyday cooking and festive gatherings.

Traditionally, the dish was prepared for holidays or to welcome honoured guests, though today it is also enjoyed as a comforting meal at home. Compared with another beloved national dish, Beshbarmak, which can take several hours to prepare, Manti is considered relatively convenient, typically taking around one-and-a-half to two hours.

For many families, the recipe is passed down through generations.

Dinara Amangeldina, a resident of Astana, recalls learning the craft from her mother.

“As a child, my mother cooked Manti only for holidays, and every time she invited my brother and me to help her in sculpting,” she says.

“Now, years later, Manti has become an integral part of our cuisine, and we can cook them at will. We will never forget the thrill of anticipating a delicious meal that brings the whole family together.”

The dough itself plays an essential role. Usually made from flour, water and salt—sometimes with the addition of an egg for extra firmness—it is kneaded by hand and rolled thin, around two to three millimetres thick, before being cut into squares and filled.

What gives Kazakh Manti their distinctive juiciness is the filling. While minced meat with onion is the classic combination, cooks often add Kurdyuk, which is rich sheep fat, or vegetables to enhance flavour and texture. The choice of meat—horse, beef or mutton—can subtly change the character of the dish.

Kamilya Anasheva, also from Astana, explains that preparing Manti is as much about family as it is about food.

“We cook Manti when they bring sogym [fresh meat from the butcher] on weekends. The whole family is engaged in its processing—cutting and preparing the minced meat—and then all together we sculpt Manti.”

Kazakh Manti are typically larger than many other dumplings along the Silk Road, with thin dough wrapped around generous fillings. Most are shaped like envelopes, with the edges joined crosswise, though some cooks form them into elegant “roses” or braided shapes.

Ultimately, the significance of the dish lies not only in its ingredients but in the ritual of making it. The shared process of rolling, filling and folding brings families together, giving Kazakh Manti their enduring place in the country’s culinary and cultural life.

Traditional red meat filling of dumplings euronews

The Dumpling Belt reaches Europe

As the Dumpling Belt stretches further west, the familiar idea of dough wrapped around a savoury filling continues its quiet transformation across Europe.

In Italy, the concept evolves into elegant forms such as ravioli, tortellini and agnolotti, where delicate pasta envelopes rich fillings of meat, cheese or vegetables.

Across Eastern Europe, dumplings appear as pierogi in Poland and pelmeni in Russia, while in the United Kingdom, pastry parcels take shape in hearty regional traditions such as pasties and suet dumplings.

Even in France and Spain, echoes of the same culinary idea appear in dishes that combine dough, filling and careful folding, adapted to local tastes and ingredients.

Though the names, shapes, and techniques differ, the principle remains remarkably consistent. From the medicinal dumplings of ancient China to the family kitchens of Central Asia and the refined pasta traditions of Europe, the dumpling’s journey tells a story not just of food, but of movement, exchange and shared human creativity.

Along the old trade routes of the Silk Road, this enduring Dumpling Belt was born out of a simple idea and has travelled thousands of miles.

It proves that sometimes the most universal dishes begin with nothing more than flour, filling, and a pair of patient hands.

World.title: Fears of wheat price surge amid Ukraine-Russia clashes in the Black Sea
World.content:
Intensifying clashes between Ukraine and Russia in the Black Sea are threatening a crucial trade artery responsible for nearly a third of the world's wheat supply, stoking fears of soaring prices and shortages.

Advertising

Earlier in July, a Russian cruise missile struck the grain carrier Golden Leo, claiming ten lives. This marked the deadliest blow yet in a mounting campaign by both Russian and Ukrainian forces targeting cargo ships in the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov.

"This is a new development in recent months," claims shipping analyst Yoruk Isik, who runs the Istanbul-based Bosphorus Observer consultancy. Isik warns that cargo vessels are caught in a deadly tit-for-tat.

"Ukraine has been targeting Russian seaborne bulkers in particular, the ones transporting stolen grain from the occupied territories of Ukraine," explains Isik, "Russia retaliated and hit Ukraine's civilian port infrastructure in Odesa; a mid-sized vessel carrying corn out of Odesa was totally sunk, other vessels were damaged, and sailors died," he adds.

Turkey’s Shipowners’ Association, having logged 136 incidents involving commercial vessels in recent months, is now urging its members to avoid the Black Sea altogether.

Beyond its role as a key channel for Russian oil, the Black Sea is a lifeline for global grain exports, with Russia and Ukraine among the top suppliers.

"It is very important to note that most of Russia's agricultural commodities are exported through the Black Sea, and that almost all of Ukraine's agricultural commodities are shipped via Ukraine's ports," warns Isik.

Bad timing for harvest

Around a third of the world's wheat moves through these waters. The surge in attacks across the Black Sea and the neighbouring Sea of Azov has brought exports to a near standstill.

"No port is officially closed, but almost no shipowner wants to go there, so trade is close to zero," claims Istanbul-based international grain dealer Can Atbasoglu. "Sellers want buyers to handle the vessels, and buyers want sellers to handle the vessels, but shipowners don't want to risk it."

This deadlock arrives at the worst possible moment: harvest time. "Normally, Russian sellers would have sold all their August cargoes by now; I don't know if anybody has any sales on their books at present," says Atbasoglu.

Turkey agrees deal to clear Black Sea of mines that threaten Ukrainian exports

Wheat prices are already reacting. "The price in Romania is, say, 20-25 percent higher – that's the clearest effect we're seeing. But everybody is waiting for some kind of intervention, and soon," adds Atbasoglu.

Turkey now leads a NATO mission, along with Bulgaria and Romania, to safeguard navigation in the Black Sea. However, former Turkish ambassador and navigation rights expert Mithat Rende believes Ankara will be wary of any effort to enforce passage for commercial ships. "It's very important that the Ukrainian war should not be transformed into a regional war," cautions Rende.

"Where would it stop? Would you fire missiles and intercept Russian missiles in the Black Sea? They (Russia) already accuse all of us of fighting Russia as NATO. It's very important to avoid such operations," he adds.

Full impact yet to be felt

Rende argues Ankara’s priority is diplomacy, having played a pivotal role in brokering the 2022 United Nations-backed grain export deal after Russian forces blocked Ukrainian shipments. "Turkey maintained a dialogue with both the Russian and the Ukrainian sides at the same time," says Rende, "But is there political will for a ceasefire now? I don't see it at present."

Grain trader Atbasoglu warns the full impact of the disruption is not yet reflected in prices. "Buyers are still not fully reacting. It's seen more as an August, or at the latest a September issue, and the markets still want to believe both sides will get together and talk," he says.

However, Atbasoglu cautions that time may be running out. "In 2022, Ukraine was completely closed off, and there was a major panic. We saw the effect: wheat prices jumped 50 percent in 2022, and we could expect something similar if this continues," he concludes.

Africa and the Middle East, which are heavily reliant on Black Sea grain, are beginning to seek pricier alternatives. Europe, too, may soon feel the strain, as drought-hit wheat harvests threaten to push global food prices even higher.

World.title: Ukraine hits targets deep inside Russia, killing eight
World.content:
Ukrainian drone strikes inside Russia killed eight people overnight in attacks that targeted military and civilian infrastructure. Russia said Moscow's forces downed 635 drones in the assault.

Ukrainian drones rained down on numerous military, energy and civilian infrastructure sites deep inside Russia on Sunday, killing at least eight people overnight.

Russia's Defense Ministry said its forces downed 635 drones over the course of the attacks.

Two people were killed in the city of Engels on the Volga River when drones hit residential buildings. Another apartment complex in nearby Saratov City was also damaged.

Three people were reported killed and two injured in the Udmurtia region (1,300 kilometers from Ukraine), and another three killed and five injured in Belgorod according to local officials.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Sunday said Kyiv had targeted an oil refinery in Saratov and a military base that is home to Russian long-range bombers in Engels.

Zelenskyy said the attacks were his country's answer to Russian aggression and thanked Ukrainian forces for taking the war "back to where it came from."

Kyiv said fires had damaged both sites and that its forces had also struck an oil depot in the western Kaluga region.

Unverified video uploaded to social media sites purported to show fires burning at the Saratov oil facility.

Why is Ukraine targeting Wildberries warehouses?

Ukraine again targeted the online retailer Wildberries in its attacks, striking a logistics warehouse in Samara — more than 800 kilometers (500 miles) from Ukraine's front-line positions.

Sunday's attacks on Wildberries were just the latest onslaught on the retail giant, which Kyiv says aids Russia's military.

Kyiv has attacked nearly a dozen Wildberries warehouses since July 18.

No casualties were reported at the facility and local management said that a fire at the site had been brought under control.

Although the number of drones that Russia claims to have downed cannot be confirmed, the figure is indicative of the scale of Kyiv's effort to strike Russia deep inside its own territory as it defends itself against an army that launched a full-scale invasion on February 24, 2022.

The Wildberries attacks are seen as an attempt to bring President Vladimir Putin's war home to Russia's citizens, applying pressure to the country's already anaemic economy in hopes of finally ending Moscow's ongoing invasion.

Edited by: Jenipher Camino Gonzalez

World.title: Ceuta: Most who breached border have left, Spain says
World.content:
08/02/2026 August 2, 2026 Far-right politicians call for migrant expulsions, security reinforcement

Abascal called for the border with Morocco to be closed immediately Image: Gabriela Sardá Núñez/Europa Press/IMAGO

The border crisis in Ceuta has sparked debates in Spain and across Europe about the Spanish government's migration policy.

Many governments in Europe have sought to curb immigration, but Spain has pursued a different approach, recently announcing a plan to provide legal status to up to 500,000 undocumented migrants.

Pedro Sanchez and his Socialist government have been heavily criticized this week by politicians from Spain's right and far-right parties.

The leader of the opposition, the conservative People's Party's Alberto Nunez Feijoo, has traveled to the exclave, where he slammed Sanchez for failing to prevent the border rush.

The leader of the far-right Vox party, Santiago Abascal, who was also in Ceuta on Sunday, blamed the Socialist government for the migrant surge, which he described as "an invasion."

He said the surge was an "act of war" and an "attack on the sovereignty and security of Spaniards."

Abascal also said Sanchez was "a danger" to the country, and called for the EU-Morocco agreement, which functions as a partial free trade area, to be scrapped.

Far-right influencer and Member of the European Parliament Alvise Perez called for migrants to be expelled during a confrontation with a crowd of rival protesters in Ceuta. Much of the city's population is of Moroccan descent.

Perez had to shelter in a bar before being escorted away by police.

Sanchez and his government have also been criticized by other right-wing politicians in Europe, most notably Italy's Interior Minister Antonio Tajani.

Italy has suspended free movement with Spain, even though both are part of the Schengen Area.

World.title: Greece: fire brigade helicopters collide as wildfires spread
World.content:
The crew of one of the helicopters is reported to be safe but the search for the second is ongoing. Prime Minister Mitsotakis has warned of "extremely difficult" days ahead while on expert has referred to a "megafire."

Two fire brigade helicopters collided mid-air in Greece on Sunday, as firefighters continued to battle fierce wildfires around the Gulf of Corinth.

The fire service said the two aircraft collided in the Psatha area, just to the west of the capital, Athens, adding that search and rescue teams were "immediately mobilized to locate and assist the crews."

Television footage showed one of the helicopters explode and plunge to the ground in flames after an apparent rotor collision.

Greek public broadcaster ERT reported that the crew of one of the helicopters had been found and were safe. The fate of the crew of the second helicopter initially remained unclear.

Greece wildfires: 'Extremely difficult' days ahead, says PM

The accident came as Greek firefighters continued to battle wildfires on multiple fronts. Three firefighters died in recent days in the line of duty, two in Crete and one in the Peloponnese.

Greek firefighters struggle to save coastal resort To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The fires are being exacerbated and spread by winds of up to 100 kilometers (60 miles) per hour, with Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis warning of "extremely difficult" days ahead.

"When the winds blow with such force, even the dozens of aircraft we have at our disposal cannot operate safely," he wrote on social media.

"There are moments when nature and the intensity of weather phenomena surpass any human planning and any operational capability."

Volunteers battle a wildfire burning near Porto Germeno Image: Costas Baltas/Anadolu Agency/IMAGO

Just to the north of Psatha in the neighboring town of Porto Germeno, nearly 500 firefighters were attempting to keep a blaze from approaching the western outskirts of Athens after it scaled a mountain overnight.

Footage released by Greek police showed officers going door to door on motorcycles in the nearby hilltop village of Agios Nektarios, sounding sirens and shouting "Is anyone there?" as they urged residents to evacuate.

On Friday, firefighters evacuated 254 people by sea – often the last escape route for isolated coastal communities – followed by another 12 on Saturday.

"We could not believe what we were seeing," Nikos Georgopoulos from the laboratory of forest management at the Aristotle University of Thessaloniki, told state TV channel ERT. "The fire spread extremely rapidly."

Greece: man arrested on suspicion of arson

Further west and on the opposite side of the Gulf of Corinth, some 100 firefighters were fighting another blaze in Aigialia in the northern Peloponnese region.

Three firefighters have lost their lives while on duty Image: Michael Varaklas/AP Photo

Meanwhile, a 44-year-old man was arrested on Sunday on suspicion of deliberately starting a new fire which broke out late Saturday on the popular Ionian Sea island of Cephalonia.

The National Observatory's climate tracker meteo.gr said early estimates indicated that over 6,500 hectares (16,000 acres) had been burned in separate fires around the Gulf of Corinth.

Meteorologist Theodore Giannaros said that the fires around Porto Germeno are "likely, if not almost certain … [to] be classified as a megafire."

World.title: Small insects, big damage: The global ant trade is booming
World.content:
Legal or not, the trade in African ants bound for Europe is booming. What do hobbyists find appealing about these insects, and what risks does the trade pose to ecosystems, including power outages?

They are unusual pieces of evidence that regularly appear in Kenyan courtrooms: thousands of ants packed into tiny containers.

Since 2025, such finds have been presented in court several times. Staff from the Kenya Wildlife Service discovered them during baggage inspections. In multiple cases, they identified thousands of specimens of the sought-after Messor Cephalotes species also known as the Giant African Harvester Ant. A single queen can fetch more than €200 ($230) on the market.

The export of wild animals is generally prohibited in Kenya. Due to high levels of poaching — particularly involving elephants and rhinoceroses — many African countries have introduced tough laws against wildlife trafficking.

Kenya has also tightened its legislation. Under these rules, a Chinese national who attempted to export ants was sentenced last April to one year in prison for biopiracy. Given the growing scale of smuggling and its ecological consequences, the judge said the sentence should serve as a deterrent.

It was already the second major ant-smuggling case in 12 months. The previous year, the wildlife service stopped four men who referred to themselves as the "Ant Gang." Among them were two 19-year-old Belgians who were trying to smuggle 5,500 queens to Europe. They were fined around €5,000 each.

The complex organization of ant colonies also fascinates animal keepers in Germany Image: Simone Schlindwein/DW

Whenever such cases arise, authorities often call entomologist Dino Martins to the airport. "I was shocked," he said. "Not only by the sheer number of ants, but also because they were queen ants."

The seized insects were young queens that had been dug up from nests in the ground, according to Martins, who has led several research institutes in Kenya and is regarded as one of Africa's leading ant experts, These queens have wings that allow them to fly away and establish new colonies.

"When you collect queens at this critical moment, you interrupt a key stage in the creation of new colonies," he said, adding that Kenya's ecosystems are also affected because ants transport grass seeds, helping to regenerate the savannah.

A new niche hobby

In Europe, keeping ants as pets has become increasingly popular, particularly among young people. Colonies are housed in glass terrariums where a queen produces offspring and establishes an entirely new population.

One person who keeps ants as a hobby is Michael Meier, who asked not to be identified by his real name. While at university, he wanted a pet that required little attention.

"With ants, it doesn't really matter whether I feed them today or tomorrow," he said.

At one point, Meier kept almost 30 colonies in a room specially set up for them. Today, he has four. He admits that exotic species are considered especially attractive to ant enthusiasts because they do not hibernate.

"That way, you can enjoy the animals all year round," he said.

Thousands of ants were intercepted at the airport in Nairobi in 2025 Image: Monicah Mwangi/REUTERS

On the websites of numerous online shops, ants can be ordered through the mail with just a few clicks. "African ants" is a category commonly used to attract customers. Among the species on sale is the very one repeatedly discovered at Kenyan airports.

Anyone who asks dealers how the ants reach Europe receives few answers. Even sellers who advertise "import permits" have declined to answer media inquiries. The trade operates in a legal gray area.

Under the international wildlife trade agreement monitored by the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES), ants are not considered a threatened species. Their trade is therefore neither prohibited nor regulated globally.

Kenya, meanwhile, bans the export of all wildlife. But unlike ivory, ants can easily be smuggled out of the country in hand luggage or through the mail.

High profits, low risk

The online trade in wildlife has expanded rapidly beyond the ant business, says Russell Gray. Working with an international team, he investigated the issue for the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime.

"The key finding is that this is no longer a marginal problem hidden away on obscure websites," Gray said. "Today, we see it happening on popular platforms such as Facebook."

Last year, Gray's team examined more than 60 online platforms. They found 266,000 s that included prices. The combined value of wildlife listings amounted to around $66 million. Insects were not even included.

"If we looked at the entire online wildlife trade," Gray concludes, "we would probably be talking about a market worth billions."

Chris Shepherd, a biologist at the US-based Center for Biological Diversity, which advocates globally for biodiversity conservation, is deeply concerned.

The Kenyan cases demonstrate that compared with other forms of crime, such as drug trafficking, profits are high while "the risks are significantly lower," he said. Once rare species begin commanding high prices, organized criminal networks become interested in the trade.

Shepherd therefore calls for stricter regulation. In open letters, he has urged CITES to address the ant trade. He is particularly concerned about the consequences for ecosystems.

Ants have no lobby

Those consequences are already making headlines in Germany.

Entire colonies of North African large gland ants regularly cause power and internet outages in southern Germany by nesting inside electrical distribution boxes.

To address the issue, local government representatives from Austria, Switzerland and southern Germany met at an ant conference in the summer of 2025 to exchange experiences.

Climate change, bringing higher temperatures and less frost, has made conditions in Central Europe increasingly suitable for the species.

Shepherd notes that most ants probably arrive in Europe through plant imports rather than the online pet trade. Even so, he argues that the hobby market poses risks as well. No one can guarantee that colonies will never be released into the wild.

Ant keepers such as Meier are familiar with these debates, which frequently take place in online forums. Meier advises owners who lose interest to either pass colonies on to other enthusiasts or euthanize them properly rather than releasing them.

For Shepherd, that is not enough. As long as the international ant trade remains largely unregulated, he says, it will continue to pose a risk.

Translated from German by Silja Fröhlich

World.title: Germany news: DB hampered by 'organized irresponsibility'
World.content:
08/02/2026 August 2, 2026 Deutsche Bahn chief Evelyn Palla blasts 'organized irresponsibility' in the company

Germany's railway operator has been plagued by years of delayed schedules Image: Arne Meyer/dpa/picture alliance

The culture inside Germany's Deutsche Bahn (DB) is already shifting but the current crisis will take years to overcome, the head of the national railway company told Germany's Welt am Sonntag.

CEO Evelyn Palla criticized the old decision-making process in DB, saying that the central management often made big decisions on the operative level.

"The people in the headquarters, who made those decisions, don't have any responsibility for implementing them in the field," Palla said. "They have to be implemented by colleagues who are out there. But they say 'I didn't make this call, and it also doesn't work for me.' Then the headquarters says 'I have no operational responsibility, those people in the field did not implement [the decision] properly.' In the end it was something like organized irresponsibility."

Deutsche Bahn: Reliable no more? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

She told the paper that much has been "reformed" and "slimmed down" since she took the reins of the state-owned firm last October, and that multiple administration levels inside DB had been cut.

"But all of that does not make for a better (Deutsche) Bahn," she added. "Things will only change when the management changes, when decentralized units take responsibility and live with it."

In the interview published on Sunday, she also said that the German railway network was "run into the ground by 25 years of saving money" and that tangible improvements will take time.

She pointed to DB's 200-year anniversary coming in 2035, saying that "this should be the year when the worst is behind us."

World.title: Moscow restaurant blast a 'brutal terror attack,' mayor says
World.content:
The deadly explosion outside an upscale Moscow restaurant at Kudrinskaya Square was a "brutal terror attack," Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said, promising the perpetrators would be punished. But many questions remain.

An explosion at a restaurant in central Moscow killed at least three people, including the suspected bomber on Saturday night, authorities said.

Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin described it as a "brutal terrorist attack."

"Law enforcement agencies are investigating the circumstances of the incident. Those responsible for this crime will certainly be found and face the punishment they deserve," he said in an online post on Sunday.

Russia's Anti-Terrorism Committee said a woman carrying "a homemade explosive device" tried to enter the restaurant on Kudrinskaya Square but was stopped by a security guard.

The device exploded at the entrance, killing the woman, the guard and a restaurant patron.

What do we know about the explosion?

State news agency RIA Novosti reported that at least 21 other people were injured in the blast, which occurred shortly before 8 p.m. local time (5 p.m. UTC).

The restaurant's website said the venue had been closed on Saturday for a private event.

The explosion occurred at an Italian restaurant located in one of ​Moscow's seven Stalin-era skyscrapers Image: Sergei Vedyashkin/Moscow News Agency/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

Heavily armed law enforcement officers sealed off the area and launched an investigation.

Authorities did not immediately identify those they believed to be behind the attack.

Russia has faced several attacks since the start of the war in Ukraine in 2022. They blamed a ‌series of assassinations and attempted killings on Kyiv. Russian officials have yet to comment on any possible Ukrainian involvement into the Kudrinskaya Square blast.

Russian general shot and badly wounded in Moscow To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Ukraine hits targets deep inside Russia overnight

However, Ukraine used drones to attack other parts of Russia on Saturday evening and early on Sunday, including a bombing which targeted an apartment block and killed two in the city Engels, some 900 kilometers (560 miles) southeast of Moscow.

Russia's Defense Ministry also said Kyiv struck a warehouse belonging to Wildberries, a major online retailer in Russia, with the Ukrainian drones hitting a site in the Samara Oblast, deep inside Russian territory. Regional Governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev said it was not immediately clear if there were any casualties.

Russian officials also reported over a 100 Ukrainian strikes in the Belgorod Oblast, which borders Ukraine. They said Kyiv forces used artillery, rocket launchers, and drones, leaving 14 people injured.

Over 200 Ukrainian drones have allegedly been shot down during the wave of attacks.

Overall, Russia claimed 635 downed Ukrainian drones overnight.

Meanwhile, at least one person was killed and seven wounded in the Russian attack on Ukraine's Kherson, with the attack involving artillery fire.

In Dnipro, seven passengers were wounded in a drone strike on a minibus, with the regional military administrator Oleksandr Hanzha describing it as a "deliberate and cynical attack on civilians."

At least nine people were killed and 33 injured in Russian strikes on Kyiv earlier this weekend.

World.title: Indonesia: At least 5 dead in ferry fire
World.content:
Search and rescue officials report some 41 missing after a fire on a ferry near the Indonesia island of Madura. The cause of the blaze remains unclear.

At least five people have died and another 41 are missing after a ferry caught fire in Indonesia on Sunday morning, authorities have confirmed.

The Mutiara Sentosa 2 ferrywas carrying a total of 271 passengers and crew members from Indonesia's second-largest city, Surabaya in East Java, across the Java Sea to Makassar in South Sulawesi.

Search and rescue officials said 225 people had been rescued by Sunday afternoon but that an operation was still ongoing.

Some passengers reportedly jumped overboard and were picked up by a nearby ship. Four other vessels were on standby nearby but could not approach because of the risk posed by flammable material on the ferry, officials said.

What have Indonesian authorities said?

"Based on preliminary reports from the field, passengers are waiting to be evacuated by the vessels in the vicinity of the incident site," said Muhammad Masyhud, a senior official at the Indonesian Ministry of Transportation.

"The safety of passengers and crew is our top priority. We are continuously coordinating with all relevant parties to ensure that the evacuation process can proceed quickly, safely, and effectively," he added.

The fire, the cause of which remains unclear, was reported by the ship's captain who, according to officials, has not been in contact since.

Are shipping accidents common in Indonesia?

Indonesia is an archipelago of more than 17,000 islands where marine accidents are a regular occurrence, due to a combination of unpredictable weather conditions and lax safety standards.

Last month, a ferry transporting more than 70 people sank while sailing near Selayar, a small tropical island south of the much larger Sulawesi.

At least four people were found dead, and 14 others remained missing until the end of the search operation.
