World.title: How Trans-Caspian Cable Fits Kazakhstan’s Evolving Connectivity Strategy
World.content:
ASTANA — For decades, Kazakhstan’s connectivity strategy was measured in highways, railways and pipelines. Today, that vision is expanding. As global competition increasingly depends on the movement of data alongside the movement of goods, the country is investing in a new layer of strategic infrastructure — one designed not to carry cargo, but information.

Among the clearest examples of this shift is the Trans-Caspian fiber-optic cable project. The first-ever underwater telecommunications link across the Caspian Sea will connect Aktau and Sumqayit, creating a new digital corridor between Central Asia, the South Caucasus and Europe.

The project reflects a broader vision articulated by President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, who has increasingly framed Kazakhstan’s connectivity agenda as extending beyond physical transport routes to include cross-border digital infrastructure. In his September 2024 State of the Nation Address, he called for the project to be completed, describing it as essential for “creating a digital infrastructure linked with international corridors and cross-border data flows.”

Several months later, speaking at an informal meeting of the Council of Heads of State of the Organization of Turkic States in Budapest, Tokayev expanded that vision beyond Kazakhstan.

“This project will significantly improve digital communication between our countries and will be a strategic step towards strengthening regional integration. Such initiatives open up opportunities to create a new digital corridor across the Eurasian continent,” he said.

The regional context continues to evolve. As the cable enters its final construction phase, regional leaders are once again gathering, this time in Cholpon-Ata for an informal Consultative Meeting of the Heads of State of Central Asia and Azerbaijan, underscoring how cooperation between the countries increasingly extends across transport, energy and digital connectivity.

Nearly two years after Tokayev first identified the project as a strategic priority, it is entering its most tangible phase. Kazakhstan is now carrying out the final stages of the project, with commercial commissioning expected by the end of 2026. The latest phase has shifted from engineering preparation to offshore construction.

According to the Ministry of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development’s release from July 31, regulatory, customs and organizational procedures have been completed, including the approval of equipment required for the offshore works, allowing construction to proceed without administrative delays.

Preparatory work in 2025 included desktop and offshore engineering surveys, selection of the optimal route avoiding anchorage zones and military training areas, environmental approvals from the Mangystau Region authorities, and the production and factory testing in China of a specially armored submarine cable equipped with ROPA optical amplifiers.

With the planning phase complete, attention has shifted from engineering design to execution at sea. The cable, previously delivered from China to the port of Kuryk together with three cable baskets weighing a combined 600 tons, was transported to Baku aboard a specialized logistics vessel. It has now been transferred into the cable tank of the cable-laying vessel, which has departed Baku and is laying the line toward Aktau.

The operation is being carried out by a cable-laying vessel with a displacement exceeding 20,000 tons and equipped with dynamic positioning technology to ensure precise installation on the seabed. Around 70 crew members are involved, including technical supervisors and representatives of Kazakhtelecom. The project is being implemented by CaspiLink B.V., the joint venture established by Kazakhtelecom and AzerTelecom.

A dedicated jointing room has also been installed onboard to allow engineers to repair or reconnect the cable if required during installation. Both the Kazakh and Azerbaijani cable ends have already undergone testing. Subject to favorable weather conditions, installation of the submarine cable is expected to be completed within the next 15 to 20 days, while the overall commissioning process remains on schedule for completion by the end of 2026.

The significance of the project, however, extends well beyond the technical operation. As economies become more deeply integrated through both physical and digital infrastructure, international corridors are no longer defined solely by the goods they carry. They are increasingly shaped by the data they enable to move across borders. While the cable spans just 380 kilometers across the Caspian seabed, the vision behind it reaches much further. The Trans-Caspian fiber-optic cable reflects Kazakhstan’s ambition to remain an important link in the movement of both goods and data across Eurasia.

World.title: Russian woman faces prison after calling Armenians ‘rat-like’ people
World.content:
Russian calls Armenians ‘rats’

A criminal case has been opened in Armenia against Russian national Nadezhda Pirozhkova. A blogger who has lived in Armenia for the past year and a half, Pirozhkova came under fire after criticising Vardavar, the Armenian tradition of pouring water over one another on the holiday. She described the custom as an act of aggression. In another video, she referred to Armenians as a “rat-like people”.

Armenia’s Investigative Committee has initiated criminal proceedings against Pirozhkova under the article on “public statements aimed at inciting hatred and discrimination through the use of the internet”. Armenia’s Criminal Code provides for a prison sentence of up to four years under this article. If Pirozhkova is found guilty in court, she could therefore face imprisonment.

For now, however, she has been banned from leaving her place of residence as a preventive measure. The blogger may leave Yerevan only with written permission from a prosecutor or a judge.

Vardavar is one of the principal feasts of the Armenian Apostolic Church, celebrating the Transfiguration of Jesus Christ, although its origins date back to pagan times. It is virtually impossible to stay dry on the streets that day, but taking offence is not customary, as drenching someone with water is considered a way of congratulating them on the holiday. The water is believed to bring health, good fortune and purification.

Pirozhkova’s Instagram posts sparked outrage among social media users—not only Armenians, but also fellow Russians.

Many have not only criticised Pirozhkova but have also called on law enforcement authorities to punish her as severely as possible or deport her from the country.

Political commentator Artyom Yerkanian did not rule out the possibility that certain actors interested in damaging Armenia’s image as a tourist destination were behind the spread of such videos. He pointed to the large number of Russian tourists visiting Armenia. In the first half of 2026 alone, Armenia received 1.042 million foreign visitors, around 40% of whom were from Russia.

“It’s interesting, isn’t it? On the one hand, the Russian government imposes trade restrictions [on imports of Armenian products and goods], while on the other, Russians happily travel to Armenia, enjoying its nature, its people and, why not, its traditions,” Yerkanian said.

What else Pirozhkova said

In a video about Vardavar, the Russian blogger said that the holiday made her want to leave Yerevan more than anything else. She described the tradition of pouring water over one another as “the height of tactlessness”. In her view, Armenians do not understand the concept of “personal boundaries” and routinely violate them.

Pirozhkova argued that splashing passers-by with water was disrespectful towards those who did not wish to take part in the celebration.

“If I’m in your country, I’m not obliged to follow your traditions. This is a direct manifestation of aggression.“

Following the video, Pirozhkova has periodically posted about the wave of online abuse directed at her. She has also publicly apologised several times, saying:

“I understand that many people saw it as disrespect towards the Armenian people. And I’m truly sorry. That was never my intention, and it still isn’t.”

At the same time, the blogger has acknowledged that she is using the controversy to promote her Instagram page.

“People recognise me now. Why shouldn’t I make use of something I’ve been through after putting in so much effort? I’ve worked hard for this. Why shouldn’t a person take advantage of circumstances and situations they have rightfully earned? I just want to change my life.“

Foreign nationals are required to respect Armenia’s national customs and traditions

The legal status of foreign nationals in Armenia is governed by the Law on Foreigners. Article 5 of the law states that foreigners in Armenia enjoy the same rights, freedoms and obligations as Armenian citizens. At the same time, it stipulates that “foreigners in the Republic of Armenia are obliged to respect the Constitution and laws of the Republic of Armenia, other legal acts, as well as national customs and traditions.”

The same article also provides that foreign nationals bear the same legal responsibility as Armenian citizens while in Armenia.

Armenia’s Criminal Code provides for penalties for “public statements aimed at inciting or promoting hatred, discrimination, intolerance or hostility against an individual or group of persons on the grounds of race, nationality or ethnicity, as well as the dissemination of materials or objects for that purpose.”

The available penalties include fines, community service, restriction of liberty and imprisonment.

Under Article 329, offences committed “through publicly displayed works, the mass media, or information and communication technologies” are punishable by one to four years’ imprisonment

Commentary

Political commentator Artyom Yerkanian said in an interview with a local television channel::

“After the Russian blogger publicly apologised, this story could have ended there. But some social media users continued calling on the Armenian law enforcement authorities to examine Nadezhda Pirozhkova’s actions and determine whether they amounted to a criminal offence. The authorities decided to respond to those calls.

Perhaps there was no need to be so severe. The court will, of course, take all mitigating circumstances into account.

Perhaps we should not politicise everything. It is obvious that the aim was not to incite ethnic hatred but simply to increase her audience through provocative videos.

In two weeks, the video attracted more than 250,000 views and over 5,000 comments. As a result, the number of followers on her page increased more than fifteen-fold.

In other words, this blogger simply found a ridiculous and foolish way to grow her audience.

Nevertheless, perhaps such cases should be monitored more closely, because this is not an isolated incident.

In recent weeks, there have been several similar cases in which foreign bloggers, particularly Russians, have made remarks discrediting Armenians and damaging Armenia’s reputation as a tourist destination.

There was one case in which a young woman accused an Armenian taxi driver of attempting to rape her. I also recall another similar incident, and there are probably many more. But what is more important?

Notably, these videos are deliberately amplified by non-existent users. An army of fake accounts is spreading this material in pursuit of a specific objective.

It cannot be ruled out that certain forces are behind these fake accounts and are interested in ensuring that Armenia is not perceived as a safe destination for tourists.

Every tourist who enjoys visiting the country indirectly becomes its ‘agent of influence’. Perhaps that is exactly what some people dislike.

I don’t know whether it is a coincidence, but it was precisely during those days that the Russian Foreign Ministry added Armenia to its list of countries where Russians cannot feel safe, citing the possibility that the Armenian authorities could extradite them to third countries. Perhaps it is a coincidence—or perhaps it is not.”

Social media reaction

“If, after a year and a half of living in Armenia, she still allows herself to speak like this, it cannot be dismissed as an accident or naivety.”

“The police should investigate her actions. She’s a planted agent.”

“She should be fined heavily and deported.”

“She should be tried and deported from our country. It’s a matter of the nation’s dignity.”

“If an Armenian had behaved like this in Russia, he would already have disappeared.”

“Foreign visitors are obliged to obey the law, respect the country and its people, and behave like guests.”

World.title: Meet Nitsa, Elvis and Oliver: Pine martens at Tbilisi Zoo. Video
World.content:
Nitsa, Elvis and Oliver are young pine martens and the newest residents of Tbilisi Zoo. A local resident found the orphaned cubs alone in an attic and took them home after discovering they had no mother.



However, pine martens are wild predators with powerful teeth and strong natural instincts. Once the cubs had grown up, releasing them back into the wild was no longer an option. Contact with humans had altered their natural behaviour, leaving them unable to survive on their own. Their rescuer therefore turned to Tbilisi Zoo for help.

Konstantin Pkhakadze, head of the zoo’s exotic animals department, said the pine martens arrived at Tbilisi Zoo about a month ago. He said such cases are quite common. People often assume that young animals found alone have been orphaned and need rescuing, but that is not always the case.

In most instances, the mother is nearby, hunting, searching for food or moving her young to a new location. Pkhakadze said intervening at that stage is the biggest mistake people can make. They should not even approach the cubs, as the mother may detect the scent of humans, see it as a threat and never return to her offspring.

Tbilisi Zoo currently has very limited capacity to take in new animals. Its existing site is overcrowded, while most of its resources are being directed towards the construction of a new zoo.

Nitsa, Elvis and Oliver were initially housed in the zoo’s exotics pavilion. However, the small enclosed space was unsuitable for such active and energetic animals. Zoo staff therefore built a temporary outdoor enclosure, giving the pine martens more space, fresh air and room to move freely.

Tbilisi Zoo‘s history spans nearly a century. It was founded on 10 February 1927 on the basis of the Caucasian Society for the Acclimatisation of Animals, which had been keeping wild animals since the early 20th century, though without official zoo status. The zoo was originally built on 70 hectares in the Vere River gorge. Over the years, the expansion of the capital — and later the devastating flood of 13 June 2015 — significantly reduced the territory of the old zoo. Today, it covers five hectares and is home to around 1,500 animals, each with its own story. In this video series, we will introduce you to the residents of Tbilisi Zoo. We will show how their day unfolds, how they interact with other animals and people, and how their behaviour changes depending on the weather and the season. Get ready to hear many fascinating stories.

Pine martens at Tbilisi Zoo

World.title: Georgia’s opposition launches campaign to restore voting rights for emigrants
World.content:
In Georgia, the opposition alliance Coalition for Change and the Strategy Aghmashenebeli party have launched the Emigrant’s Vote campaign, calling for the restoration of Georgian citizens’ right to vote from abroad in parliamentary and municipal elections.

Under the new Election Code, approved by the ruling Georgian Dream party on 17 December 2025, emigrants are no longer allowed to vote from abroad. Instead, they must travel to Georgia to cast their ballots.

One of Coalition for Change’s members, Tengo Tevzadze, announced the launch of the campaign, saying the initiative would culminate in a constitutional challenge seeking to restore emigrants’ right to take part in elections.

According to Tevzadze, the campaign aims to demonstrate that allowing emigrants to vote is consistent with Georgia’s constitution and that every Georgian citizen, regardless of where they live, should be able to take part in elections.

Tevzadze noted that Georgian Dream won just 13.4% of the overseas vote in the disputed 2024 parliamentary election, which the opposition says was rigged. He argued that this was why the authorities later moved to strip emigrants of their voting rights.

Tevzadze argues that depriving emigrants of the right to vote violates Georgia’s constitution and is unfair to a group of citizens that makes a significant contribution to the country’s economy.

The campaign’s organisers have set out two main demands: restoring emigrants’ right to vote and creating an electoral system that allows Georgian citizens living abroad to cast their ballots.

“We need as many emigrants as possible to sign the petition so that, alongside political efforts, we can also challenge the regime through legal means. Through a constitutional lawsuit, we will clearly demonstrate that emigrants’ participation in elections and their voting rights are protected by the constitution, and that Georgians, both at home and abroad, must be able to take part in free and fair elections,” Tengo Tevzadze said.

Voting rights for Georgian emigrants

World.title: Evening illuminations in South Ossetia: Video
World.content:
Evening illuminations in South Ossetia

Major reconstruction work has been completed in the South Ossetian capital, Tskhinval. The city centre has been renovated, dozens of streets repaired, and new utility networks installed.

The redevelopment of Theatre Square included new lighting, benches and marble planters, while boxwood and juniper shrubs were planted. Several school and college buildings, along with the Kosta Khetagurov State Drama Theatre, have also been restored.

The work was funded through Russia’s investment programme.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Evening illuminations in South Ossetia

World.title: Russian mass strike on Ukraine leaves several dead and dozens injured. Video from Lviv
World.content:
Russian strike on Ukraine: Video from Lviv

Russia launched a mass overnight attack on Ukraine on 30 July, according to Ukrainian authorities, firing a total of 74 missiles and 284 attack drones. Ukraine said its air defences intercepted a significant number of the incoming targets, but some missiles and drones struck their intended targets.

Several regions across Ukraine came under attack, including Lviv, Kyiv and the Dnipropetrovsk region.

In Lviv, one resident was killed. In the village of Radushne, near Kryvyi Rih, a ballistic missile struck the home of a large family. Six people were killed, including three children, while several others were injured.

Lviv Mayor Andriy Sadovyi said the city had suffered direct Russian missile strikes on residential buildings for the first time in a long period.

The heaviest damage was reported on Paton and Vyhovskoho streets, where more than 20 residential buildings, a school, two kindergartens and other civilian infrastructure were damaged.

Rescue workers recovered the body of a man from beneath the rubble.

According to the latest official figures, 34 people, including three children, were injured in the attack on Lviv. Nine people were rescued from damaged buildings. Emergency crews are continuing search and rescue operations and clearing the debris.

Lviv city authorities said some residents whose homes were damaged would be provided with temporary accommodation, while municipal services are assisting those left homeless.

Russian strike on Ukraine: Video from Lviv

World.title: German broadcaster ARD investigates Georgia’s rise as a crypto hub
World.content:
Crypto mining in Georgia

“Crypto war: How Putin is using bitcoin to wage war against us” is the title of a 45-minute investigative documentary by German public broadcaster ARD, which portrays Georgia as a major cryptocurrency mining hub and an alleged transit route used by Russia to circumvent Western sanctions.

The documentary focuses on bitcoin mining and crypto systems which, the journalists argue, have enabled Russia to adapt to international financial restrictions.

Georgia’s favourable conditions for crypto industry

The investigation’s authors say Georgia has developed a particularly favourable legal and tax environment for the cryptocurrency industry over many years. They argue that this was closely linked to political and economic decisions taken during the rule of the Georgian Dream party and its founder, Bidzina Ivanishvili, turning the country into what they describe as one of the world’s cryptocurrency “grey zones”.

The documentary focuses in particular on the free industrial zones in Poti and Rustavi. According to the journalists, Russia can no longer sell natural gas to Europe at pre-sanctions levels, with some of that gas instead being used to generate low-cost electricity. The filmmakers argue that this electricity powers large-scale bitcoin mining infrastructure, the ultimate financial benefits of which serve Russia’s interests.

The German journalists say they travelled to Georgia and visited cryptocurrency mining facilities themselves, including infrastructure in the Rustavi Free Industrial Zone.

Russia said using cryptocurrency to circumvent sanctions

Nino Bakradze, founder of the investigative journalism organisation iFact, says in the documentary that Russia has not been completely cut off from the international financial system and is increasingly using cryptocurrency for cross-border transactions.

Nino Bakradze

She says iFact investigated exports of dual-use goods to Russia by conducting an undercover experiment. The organisation contacted a Russian trading company and asked whether it could ship around 30 drones to Russia. According to Bakradze, the company replied that such a shipment was possible and said it had carried out similar transactions before despite the risks posed by sanctions.

Bakradze says the investigation found that companies involved in such transactions use cryptocurrency to settle payments in order to circumvent sanctions, often without being detected by Western authorities.

‘Bitcoin mining in Georgia is profitable’

The documentary also features local bitcoin miner Nikoloz Museridze, who says the main advantage of mining bitcoin in Georgia is the country’s relatively low electricity prices.

Nikoloz Museridze

Museridze says his mining farm consumes about 2 megawatts of electricity. He estimates that, at this capacity, it takes about a year to mine one bitcoin, while the cost of producing a single bitcoin in Georgia is around $30,000-$40,000.

The miner describes bitcoin as “borderless money” that can be transferred anywhere in the world at any time and which, he claims, cannot be blocked or frozen.

World.title: Nauru withdraws recognition of occupied Abkhazia and South Ossetia
World.content:
The government of the Pacific island nation of Nauru says it has formally withdrawn its recognition of the self-proclaimed republics of Abkhazia and South Ossetia as independent states.

“The Government of the Republic of Nauru declares that it has withdrawn its recognition of the ‘Republic of South Ossetia’ and the ‘Republic of Abkhazia’ as independent states.

Accordingly, the Republic of Nauru has immediately terminated diplomatic relations with South Ossetia and Abkhazia,” the Nauru government said in a statement.

On 29 July, Nauru severed diplomatic relations with the Russian-occupied Georgian regions of Abkhazia and South Ossetia.

Georgia’s foreign ministry described the decision as a sign of respect for the principles of international law and said Tbilisi was ready to establish diplomatic relations with Nauru and strengthen bilateral cooperation on the basis of shared interests.

“The decision once again confirms that respect for and adherence to international law are the foundation of healthy international relations,” the ministry said in a statement.

The self-proclaimed Abkhaz foreign ministry claimed that Nauru had come under “unprecedented pressure” to end diplomatic relations with Abkhazia.

“The development of cooperation between the Republic of Abkhazia and the Republic of Nauru has consistently encountered resistance from Georgia and its Western partners. As joint initiatives turned into practice, a campaign of aggressive external pressure was unleashed against the Republic of Nauru.

For many years, states maintaining diplomatic relations with the Republic of Abkhazia have faced external pressure aimed at abandoning their independently determined foreign policy course. Small states, with limited resources to counter large-scale political, diplomatic, and economic instruments of influence, are particularly vulnerable to such pressure.

Such practice contradicts the fundamental principles of the UN Charter, including the principles of the sovereign equality of states and non-interference in their internal affairs.

The Republic of Abkhazia remains committed to strengthening its international subject status, protecting its national interests, and developing mutually beneficial cooperation with states that share the principles of sovereign equality, mutual respect, and international law,” the statement said.

Nauru recognised the independence of Abkhazia and Georgia’s Tskhinvali region (South Ossetia) in 2009, after Russia declared the two Georgian regions independent states. Nauru was one of only a handful of countries to support the move backed by Moscow.

Nauru is a small Pacific island state in the Micronesia region. It is one of the world’s smallest countries, both by land area and population. Covering about 21 sq km (8 sq miles), it is home to around 12,000-13,000 people.

World.title: Pashinyan: ‘Russia wants either exclusive ties or nothing’
World.content:
Pashinyan rejects exclusive ties with Russia

Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan has once again addressed the current state of relations between Armenia and Russia. He commented in particular on Russia’s restrictions on imports of Armenian goods, an issue that has caused growing concern in Armenia. During a briefing, Pashinyan said the country should view the situation not as a crisis but as an opportunity to diversify its economy.

Journalists asked him to address the political dimension of the issue, arguing that it clearly extends beyond economics. Pashinyan said the problem stems from Armenia’s search for alternatives that it previously did not have.

As an example, he pointed to the signing of strategic partnership agreements with China, the United States, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, France and other countries.

According to Pashinyan, Armenia had never before had — and could not have had — strategic relations with so many partners.

“I cannot speak about Russia’s feelings. I can say that Russia sees this as a problem. There is also an element of exclusivity here. The issue is this: either the relationship is exclusive, or there should be no relationship at all. We do not share that view,” he said.

Pashinyan said Yerevan’s position is “legitimate.” Armenia’s ties with Russia are not exclusive, he said, but the relationship should continue.

“I ask that our position be treated with understanding and respect, especially since its legitimacy is not questioned in practice,” he said.

Pashinyan also stressed that Armenia would continue discussions with Russia over the economic restrictions that Russia and the Eurasian Economic Union have imposed on Armenian goods.

“That would be the worst possible course of action,” he added.

“What was wrong with Armenia? What did Armenia do?”

Journalists asked why Russia places such importance on Armenia’s political orientation and whether Pashinyan had given Moscow any reason to doubt that Armenia remains a reliable partner. In response, the prime minister posed a series of questions:

“What was wrong with Armenia in 2022 that the Collective Security Treaty Organization failed to fulfil its obligations? What did Armenia do wrong? Whom did Armenia harm? What did Armenia do that justified what happened?” he said, referring to Russia’s and the CSTO’s failure to respond after Azerbaijani forces entered Armenia’s internationally recognised territory in 2021–2022, despite the alliance’s obligation to act in the event of an attack on a member state’s territorial integrity.

What was wrong with Armenia that the Russian peacekeepers in Karabakh failed to fulfil their mission? Was the problem October 2022?” he continued, referring to the 6 October 2022 statement signed by Armenia and Azerbaijan in Prague, in which the two countries recognised each other’s territorial integrity. “But there were incidents even before that. What was wrong with Armenia? And why is it always assumed that we are the bad partner?”

“We are showing who needs Armenia”

Continuing on the issue, Pashinyan referred to Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko’s remark, “Who needs Armenia?”

“Has Armenia harmed anyone? Has it harmed Belarus? How can anyone speak about a sovereign state like that?” he said.

Pashinyan argued that the Belarusian president had asked the question but failed to find an answer. Now, he said, Armenia is showing exactly who values relations with it.

“Armenia matters to China, the United States, the European Union and Iran. And Armenia needs all of those partners as well. Georgia needs Armenia, and Armenia needs Georgia. Armenia matters to France, Germany, Poland and the United Kingdom. That’s the whole story.”

“The alternative is not yet in place” for a referendum

In recent months, Moscow has repeatedly urged Armenia to choose between the Eurasian Economic Union and the European Union. Russian officials have insisted that Armenia should hold a referendum on the issue as soon as possible. At the end of May, the leaders of four EAEU member states issued a joint statement calling for such a vote.

“I respect the fact that, on 29 May, the leaders of four EAEU countries issued a statement supporting the idea of a referendum on EU membership. But there is still nothing to vote on,” Pashinyan said.

He reiterated that it would make sense to hold a referendum only after Armenia obtains EU candidate status or once the issue formally appears on the agenda.

According to the prime minister, Moscow does not challenge Yerevan’s right to pursue alternatives. Instead, it is telling Armenia: “Decide today which alternative you choose.”

“But the alternative is not yet in place. The process of creating it has only just begun. It would be dishonest to ask people now whether they support an alternative that does not yet exist. They would ask many questions that we simply cannot answer today,” he said.

Pashinyan said the government would continue working to answer those questions before asking the public to make a choice.

Pashinyan rejects exclusive ties with Russia

World.title: A 13-year-old boy asked me a question no child should
World.content:
In the tiny community of Baniyala in East Arnhem Land, I sat next to a 13-year-old boy on the porch of a donga that served as a community centre for the day.

The taps in the kitchen have been running constantly because there is no hardware store or tradesman there to fix them.

The boy was funny, charismatic, and deeply proud of his home.

He was carrying around a sea rights flag, designed after his elders took their case to the High Court to establish the first native title claim over the coastline of north-east Arnhem Land.

He told us confidently about how it is his flag to fly.

He told me how he has brothers and sisters who he loves to tease, including one who had passed away just a few years ago.

And then he asked me to guess what colour his coffin was going to be.

It was as casual as if he had asked me to guess what footy team he supports, but it pulled me up short.

On the one hand, this young boy knows and lives his culture with confidence.

On the other, he has seen death so often he has his coffin colour picked out.

Closing the gap in health, wealth, and life expectancy has been the subject of many conversations at Garma Festival over the past three days. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

Righting the wrongs of the past

Death has brought me to Baniyala — at a remote burial ground, nine Yolŋu ancestors who were taken from the Northern Territory by an anthropologist almost a century ago were laid to rest in a repatriation ceremony aimed at helping to heal the "wrongs of the past".

Yolŋu remains repatriated in Arnhem Land Decades after being taken by a University of Melbourne anthropologist, the remains of nine Aboriginal ancestors have been returned to their sacred home in Arnhem Land.

Before the Garma Festival began, I travelled almost 200 kilometres to the homeland the way that most people get there, via small charter plane — to drive from Nhulunbuy takes more than three hours, mostly on dirt roads.

Baniyala is home to around 150 people, mostly members of the Maḏarrpa clan, almost all of whom attended the ceremony I was there to observe.

While the community is strong and their country is beautiful, their lives are tough.

It is not new that those living in remote communities do without so much that we in the cities take for granted — like a hospital, major supermarket, or even phone service.

As a visitor, I could see that they are resilient and adaptive in ways most Australians do not have to be, and do not really understand.

'Killing our people and our future'

From Gulkula in north-east Arnhem Land, the beauty of the land and the pride of Yolŋu people is everywhere.

They are strong in their culture and identity, which sits at the centre of life here in the territory.

But their lives — and the lives of so many Indigenous Australians — are harder, shorter, and poorer.

Yolŋu elder Yingiya Guyula lays the blame at the feet of governments. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

Leaders like independent territory MP Yolŋu elder Yingiya Guyula lay the blame for so much of the struggle here at the feet of governments who he says do not listen to communities.

"Even though I have been sent by my people to be their voice and fix these problems, each time the [Country Liberal Party] passes these laws, they take part in a slow genocide of our people," Guyula told the Garma Festival.

"Each law is another step on the path to killing our people and culture."

Loading

The gaps that have not closed

Closing the gap in health, wealth, and life expectancy has long been the ambition of state, territory and federal governments, and it has been the subject of many conversations at Garma Festival over the past three days.

But despite an overhaul to the agreement in 2020, the gap persists, and there is now renewed focus on how to make the national agreement work for Indigenous people.

Like many discussions in this space, opinions are divided.

Palawa activist Michael Mansell believes the agreement is "corrupt".

"I think it's time for Closing the Gap, as the main focus of Aboriginal policy, to be dumped. Get rid of it. Forget about it," Mansell said.

Others, like National Children's Commissioner Sue-Anne Hunter, believe accountability for the failure to meet targets is key.

"Who's accountable for these targets? Who answers for these targets not being met? When it doesn't, whose heads roll? At this point it doesn't seem that anybody is accountable for those targets," she told me.

Sue-Anne Hunter believes accountability for the failure to meet targets is key. (ABC News: Billy Cooper )

Others fall somewhere in the middle, like Shadow Indigenous Affairs and Education Minister Julian Leeser, who wants to change the focus of governments around the targets.

"If we are going to shift the dial, we have to understand whether federally funded interventions are achieving their intended outcomes and if they are not, why not. Unfortunately, the Closing the Gap data does not tell us that story," he told the Garma Festival on Friday.

But the common ground between these varied viewpoints is clear: the clock is fast running out to meet targets by 2031, and something needs to change soon.

Because we can all recognise it is not normal for kids, like that young boy I met in Baniyala, to be thinking about the colours of their coffins.

He told me his coffin will be white, and his little sister's will be green.

World.title: Two firefighting helicopters collide midair fighting blazes in Greece
World.content:
Two Greek firefighting helicopters have collided in midair while battling a wind-driven wildfire west of Athens, with footage showing one aircraft crashing to the ground.

Local fire officials said two firefighters aboard one of the helicopters died in the crash, while the crew on the second helicopter survived.

The collision laid bare the danger at the most volatile front of Europe's wildfire emergency.

Strong winds drove flames deeper into the region of the Greek capital and forced fresh evacuations, France guarded a still-burning scar four times the size of Paris, while Spain's major fires stopped advancing.

The aircraft were Bell helicopters operating over the Psatha area west of Athens, each with a two-person crew. Two of those aboard were Greek and two were foreign nationals, but authorities did not identify their countries.

Flames spread rapidly through western Attica, threatening communities and an industrial district outside Megara as violent gusts prevented firefighting aircraft from collecting water from the sea.

The advance carried grim resonance in a region where the 2018 Mati wildfire killed 104 people, Europe's deadliest blaze this century.

The blazes burning in Greece are the latest in a string of bushfire emergencies across Europe this summer. (AP: Michael Varaklas)

Farther west, containment brought no end to the emergency.

France's largest wildfire remained held within its perimeter after forcing 224,000 people to flee in what may have been the country's largest civilian peacetime evacuation.

Hot spots still burned within a 420-square-kilometre scar, thousands remained unable to return home, and nearly 3,000 firefighters were deployed against the Gironde megafire and a second, still-uncontained blaze in Provence.

Together, fires in France and Spain have driven roughly a third of a million people from homes and vacation sites, emptied communities at the height of the European summer and stretched emergency services across simultaneous disasters.

Europe's growing wildfire threat

The mass evacuations in France and Spain are the latest measure of a wildfire threat growing across Europe.

Climate scientist caught up in Europe's 'dystopian' summer Stefan Rahmstorf was holidaying in southern France when he came face to face with the climate future he has tried to fight.

The continent entered 2026 after its worst fire year on record, with more than 10,000 square kilometres burned in 2025.

Over the past four decades, wildfires have been linked to nearly 800 deaths across much of Europe, according to the European Environment Agency.

Europe is the world's fastest-warming continent. It has warmed more than twice the global average since the 1980s, according to the European Union's Copernicus Climate Change Service.

Human-caused climate change made the extreme fire weather conditions behind this year's French blazes at least twice as likely, scientists at World Weather Attribution found in a rapid analysis conducted while the fires were still burning.

Gale-force winds fan flames near Athens

Nearly 500 firefighters and 23 aircraft were deployed, but gale-force winds drove flames through dry forest and crippled the response, preventing some aircraft from reaching the sea to collect water.

Authorities ordered the evacuation of the communities of Kandili, Agia Skepi and Toutouli as smoke rose over the mountains.

Crews were particularly concerned about Porto Germeno, a seaside community on the Gulf of Corinth. Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis was briefed on the operation.

The fire began on Friday near Agios Vasileios before sweeping toward Porto Germeno and into the forested mountains west of Athens.

Firefighters evacuated 254 people by sea on Friday and another 12 Saturday — often the last escape route when fire and smoke cut the few roads from coastal communities.

Tinder-dry conditions and record-breaking heat across Europe are exacerbating the fire threat. (AP: Michael Varaklas)

Wildfire meteorologist Theodore Giannaros estimated the blaze had affected 40 to 50 square kilometres, though authorities had issued no official figure.

Elsewhere in Greece, flames threatened homes on Kefalonia, forcing evacuations from inland communities as aircraft made water drops over the Ionian island. Firefighters battled another blaze near Nea Tenedos in Halkidiki.

Last week, two firefighters died fighting a fire on Crete, while a third was killed in the Peloponnese.

"A pristine forest, a paradise, was surrendered to the hands of the fire," local farmer Minas Tzortzanis said Saturday.

" There are no words to explain what has happened. Destruction. Total destruction. "

France, Spain on alert

In south-western France, the Gironde megafire remained held within its perimeter Sunday but continued to burn after scorching 420 square kilometres of forest in 10 days.

"The fire is now fixed, which does not mean that the fire is extinguished," the Gironde prefecture said, using the French firefighting term for a blaze whose advance has been stopped.

The region remained under France's highest red forest-fire alert. Dry conditions, soaring temperatures around Bordeaux and afternoon winds threatened to rekindle the flames.

In south-eastern France, nearly 1,500 firefighters battled a separate blaze in the Var department that tore through about 18 square kilometres in little more than a day.

Spain's major fires — part of a season that has killed at least 13 people, produced the country's largest recorded wildfire and prompted a national emergency — were no longer advancing on Sunday.

In Zamora province near the Portuguese border, more than 20 ground and aerial units guarded the perimeter of the Fermoselle fire against flare-ups in the rugged Arribes del Duero landscape. Most evacuees had returned home, according to local media.

Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has called for a national pact to confront wildfires, warning that climate change is making them increasingly destructive.

AP/Reuters

World.title: The South Korean drama that has global investors fixated
World.content:
On the Korean peninsula, balance is a fundamental principle of everyday life.

As a cultural belief, yin and yang — eum and yang in Korean — are so ingrained in the national psyche that they are incorporated into South Korea's national flag.

The balancing blue and red flows within a circle — the balance between positive and negative cosmic forces — explain the natural order and the cycle of life.

On the streets of Seoul and across the country, however, there is little sense of balance right now.

Fear and angst have gripped a population in the throes of the worst stock market crash in the nation's history.

In the past five weeks, the market has collapsed, shedding almost 40 per cent, and threatening the livelihood of millions of South Koreans.

"I couldn't breathe," Lee Seung-ho, a 24-year-old university student, told Yahoo Finance as he watched his future disintegrate.

China throws spanner into tech boom Elon Musk's latest venture sent global stock markets to dizzying heights, but its performance since does not augur well for the company or the future of the AI boom.

After borrowing heavily from a trading platform, Lee's stock plunge had delivered a 15-fold increase in his savings over the previous year before his fortune evaporated in just four weeks.

The shockwaves are spreading across the globe as investors fret the meltdown on one of the world's most technology-intensive markets may be an omen of things to come.

Concerns are mounting globally about the stupendous, some say stupid, level of spending by the world's leading technology firms that has begun to rattle Wall Street.

Once considered an exotic financial sideline, the South Korean Kospi has become one of the most acutely observed markets in the world; many view it as a possible harbinger for the end of a four-year boom in technology stocks.

A debt-fuelled boom

More than a million South Koreans are underwater as a result of the crash, and several hundred thousand have lost everything, and then some.

They borrowed to the hilt to take part in a frenzied splurge on technology stocks, particularly memory chip makers, in a market now experiencing a savage reversal.

Nothing, not even the stellar earnings of the country's two biggest chip makers, has been able to stem the panic, primarily because the debt that fuelled the stock market boom is now accentuating the crash.

Many South Koreans have borrowed money to invest in tech stocks, particularly memory chip makers. (Reuters: Max A Cherney )

Repeated attempts by Seoul's market authorities to put a handbrake on the losses by suspending trading have only made the problem worse.

The collapse, which began last month, follows an astonishing rise on the country's market index, the Kospi, over the past 12 months.

At its peak, it had surged more than three-fold in just a little over a year.

That was the yang. Now comes the eum.

For the KOSPI, what went up is coming down. (Source: Trading Economics)

A political leg up

It began with a constitutional crisis and an attempted coup.

To divert attention in the aftermath of last year's political upheaval, new President Lee Jae Myung encouraged citizens to invest in the local stock market in a series of fiery nationalistic speeches about South Korea's global standing.

It was time, he said, for the "Korea Discount" to be erased and replaced, perhaps, by a "Korea Premium" and for the nation to rely less on property speculation.

"The Republic of Korea as a market remains undervalued," he said.

As part of the program, rules around using debt to invest were loosened and debt-infused investment products — known as single stock leveraged Exchange Traded Funds — spurred South Koreans to plunge everything, and more, into the market.

The timing was both impeccable and tragic.

Chip makers were in hot demand as the big American tech firms, having spent trillions of dollars in the race for AI dominance, began the next phase of the boom: rolling out AI to the world.

China's tightening grip on industry Can America wrest back control of global manufacturing? President Donald Trump thinks so.

An obscure American chip maker, Nvidia, had already shot to prominence when it was discovered that its gaming chips were ideal for developing AI platforms, and it suddenly took the mantle of the world's most valuable corporation.

But when Silicon Valley's tech giants — Amazon, Microsoft, Meta, Alphabet, Oracle, Apple and Tesla — began a rush to build data centres, they created an extreme shortage of ordinary memory chips, the kind used in mobile phones and laptops.

A mere handful of companies dominate this area. One is Samsung Electronics, and another is SK Hynix.

How South Korea plans to cash in its AI chips South Korea is doubling down on its bid to lead in AI, unveiling plans last month to spend hundreds of billions on developing its chip manufacturing.

Both are South Korean giants and, three years ago, made up about a quarter of the Korean stock market.

By last month, as their earnings soared on an acute global chip shortage and their stock prices multiplied, they comprised 60 per cent of the Kospi's total value.

As late as April, regulators, in an ill-fated move, approved further new trading methods to allow investors greater use of debt when investing in individual stocks.

On Wednesday, South Korea's Finance Minister Koo Yun-cheol was forced to apologise after several politicians accused the government of turning the stock exchange into a casino.

When red becomes the new black

The extent of the losses is still unclear. But the damage is huge.

According to KB Financial Group, South Korean retail investors have made net purchases of around 14 trillion won ($US9.7 billion) in single-stock leveraged ETFs since their launch, with foreigners tipping in roughly 2 trillion won ($US1.4 billion).

South Korean leaders are scrambling as the worsening situation threatens further instability, with the main opposition, the People Power Party's Lee Jongwook, going on the attack.

"When I think about it now, these products should never have been allowed on to the market. I consider this a policy failure," Mr Lee said.

Loading

According to data from Goldman Sachs, as of a fortnight ago, more than 1.2 million retail investors who had borrowed cash to take part in the frenzy had received what is known as "margin calls".

With losses overwhelming their collateral, they have been told to stump up extra cash to maintain their position. Of those, around 360,000 accounts have been forcefully liquidated.

South Korean media reports indicate that more than 60 per cent of liquidated investors are under 30 and have not just lost everything, but are now in debt.

By Friday, the market was roaring back after a volatile week on Wall Street saw technology giants whipsawing by the day.

Microsoft shares surged 9 per cent, Mark Zuckerberg's Meta slumped 8 per cent and Elon Musk's SpaceX eked out a 2 per cent gain after having shed half its post-float peak value in the few weeks it has been listed.

But a growing sense of unease surrounds the tech giants and the excesses that have accompanied the AI boom.

Volatility usually is the precursor for when red becomes the new black.

World.title: Child workers are the chocolate industry's 'dirty secret'
World.content:
It is early morning and children as young as 10 are already at work.

The boys wield large machetes, clearing weeds and undergrowth on a cocoa farm in Ghana's east. They should be getting ready for school.

Loading...

The children will spend the next few weeks working long days on the cocoa farm, paid as little as two or three Ghanaian cedis ($0.37) an hour, enough to buy a banana, but not enough for a loaf of bread.

Their families have no other choice. It's a matter of survival.

The cocoa these children are helping to produce could end up in chocolate bars with sustainability claims on the wrapper.

For more than two decades, some of the world's biggest chocolate companies have pledged to eradicate child labour from their supply chains.

Certification schemes such as Rainforest Alliance, reassure customers they're making an ethical choice. ( )

Logos on chocolate bars from certification schemes, such as Rainforest Alliance or Cocoa Life, reassure customers that they are making an ethical choice.

But as Four Corners discovered in Ghana, the promises of the multi-billion-dollar global chocolate industry don't always match the reality on the ground.

The child workers

Leaving Ghana's vibrant but chaotic capital, Accra, we travelled deep into the country's remote cocoa-growing regions, spending days on dirt roads, passing through villages with makeshift roadside shops before reaching isolated farms and communities.

Ghana's capital Accra. ( )

A woman carries goods in a box. ( )

A roadside stall. ( )

As we drew closer to the border with Côte d'Ivoire, police checkpoints became increasingly frequent, stopping cars to search for smuggled guns and cocoa.

Ghana is one of the world's biggest cocoa producers and, alongside Côte d'Ivoire, sits at the centre of a child labour crisis.

Four Corners travelled more than 2,000km into Ghana's cocoa-growing heartland. ( )

There are estimated to be more than 800,000 cocoa farms in Ghana, most owned by families living below the poverty line.

We obtained videos and photos of children doing back-breaking work on cocoa farms during school hours. It is fresh evidence that child labour persists, despite decades of industry promises to eliminate it.

Child labour is not simply children helping their families. It is work that keeps them out of school or exposes them to dangerous tasks, like using machetes or spraying chemicals. In Ghana, it is illegal for children to work on cocoa farms during school hours or carry out hazardous tasks.

Boys with machetes on a cocoa farm during school hours. ( )

The boys filmed slashing weeds at the base of cocoa trees live in a community identified at its entrance as participating in Cocoa Life, the flagship sustainability program of Cadbury owner Mondelēz.

The Cocoa Life program promises to support cocoa farming communities and help tackle child labour. Four Corners has not established whether the farm itself supplied cocoa to Mondelēz.

Footage from a nearby cocoa farm shows more children from the community undertaking hazardous work during school hours.

In one video, a nine-year-old boy and his older siblings balance heavy containers of water on their heads as they weave their way along an uneven forest path. They deliver it to a teenage boy spraying chemicals without protective gear. They will wait until the containers are empty, then go back and fetch some more.

Loading...

A teenager sprays pesticide. ( )

"That kicks it into the worst forms of child labour," Fuzz Kitto from the not-for-profit organisation Be Slavery Free, says.

"It's hazardous child labour … Imagine what that's doing to his brain and to his body … Imagine what that's doing to the waterways."

Another video shows young boys collecting cocoa pods, putting them into containers and balancing the heavy loads on their heads.

Loading...

The videos were filmed by an insider, who wanted to expose to the world the truth that child labour is still going on in Ghana, despite the denials.

The man, who asked for his identity to be protected for his safety, said he was a victim of child labour himself.

Boys lift a basket full of cocoa pods in a photo taken last year. ( )

Young children carrying logs. ( )

He says this is what poverty looks like.

"Missing school because harvest season needs hands," he says.

"Stomachs that go without breakfast … None of this happens because parents don't love their children. It happens because survival of a smallholder farm rarely leaves room for anything else," he says.

Cocoa is essential to Ghana's economy. ( )

Nathaniel, whose surname Four Corners is withholding to protect him, is one of many farmers we meet in Ghana who say they are Rainforest Alliance certified.

He says growing cocoa still does not provide enough to support his family.

"Financially, I'm not good at all," he says. "I'm struggling a lot."

Nathaniel says he's struggling financially. ( )

He lives in a community in Ghana's eastern region, near Bibiani, with open drains, no running water and makeshift homes.

His kitchen is a room with buckets of water and little else.

Mondelēz said it was deeply concerned about evidence of child labour and said it was prohibited in its supply chain.

It said it planned to invest $US1.4 billion in its Cocoa Life program by 2030.

'Dirty, rotten little secret'

Child labour and farmer poverty have existed for decades.

Their prevalence in the chocolate industry attracted global attention around 25 years ago with media stories that exposed the use of child labour on West African cocoa farms.

Public outcry over the revelations placed the world's biggest chocolate companies under intense scrutiny, prompting the United States to consider new laws that would have required chocolate sold in America to carry a "slave-free" label.

Cocoa pods growing on a tree. ( )

A farm worker harvests the pods. ( )

Cocoa beans are the key ingredient in chocolate. ( )

The chocolate industry negotiated a voluntary agreement, avoiding regulation. ( )

Instead, the industry negotiated a voluntary agreement promising to eliminate the worst forms. Deadlines came and went in 2005, 2008 and 2010, before the industry shifted to a new target of reducing the worst forms of child labour by 70 per cent by 2020. That target was also missed.

More than two decades after the industry's first major commitment, child labour and severe farmer poverty remain widespread in cocoa-growing regions of Ghana and Côte d'Ivoire.

General Secretary of the Ghana Cooperative Cocoa Farmers and Marketing Association, Issifu Issaka, represents more than 400,000 farmers.

He says 95 per cent of farmers are not earning a living income.

Issifu Issaka says many cocoa farmers live in poverty. ( )

"If you're in a community, you don't have water to drink, you don't have healthcare and other things, how are you going to survive?" he says.

He says certification bodies, including Rainforest Alliance, should work directly with farmer cooperatives instead of relying on companies and intermediaries further up the supply chain.

Several major brands source cocoa through the Rainforest Alliance system. ( )

Mondelez's brands use the Cocoa Life certification scheme. ( )

For Carolyn Kitto, co-director of Be Slavery Free, that's the problem.

"They're marketing labels. They're about making more money for the chocolate companies," she says. "They're about tricking you into buying their product because you feel that it's okay."

Most certification schemes, including Rainforest Alliance, use a system called "mass balance". It means certified cocoa can be mixed with uncertified beans.

Under mass balance, companies can use a certification logo on products that may contain non-certified cocoa, as long as they purchase an equivalent amount of certified cocoa.

Do you know more? Contact Adele Ferguson using ferguson.adele@abc.net.au

If you require more secure communication, please choose an option on the confidential tips page

Human rights lawyer Etelle Higonnet, who has spent years investigating child labour and deforestation in West Africa's cocoa industry, says consumers are being sold a lie.

"In mass balance, you can take clean, sustainable, ethical cocoa and mix it with dirty cocoa that has slavery, kids, human trafficking, deforestation, all these ethical, sustainable problems," she says.

Ms Higonnet says certification is a promise to consumers.

"It's a contract between the consumer and the company that says you will pay more for this product and I will give you a sustainable product … if the consumer pays more but the sustainability is not there, you've just broken that contract. It's a betrayal."

"The public is being duped. They have no idea of this dirty, rotten little secret," she says.

The community of Asempaneye has open drains and no running water. ( )

Locals told us this is a Mondelēz community. ( )

Rainforest Alliance says certification alone can't solve complex challenges, but it helps measure progress.

It says all major sustainability initiatives use mass balance.

What change would cost

As we drive further west, close to the border of Côte d'Ivoire, we visit another community with similar hardship.

They have no running water, just a bore water tank, open drains and farmers stricken by poverty.

Farmers here sell to some of the world's biggest cocoa traders, supplying multi-billion-dollar chocolate companies.

Loading...

Four Corners asked Be Slavery Free to break down where the money from an $8 block of Cadbury Dairy Milk sold at supermarkets ends up. Their modelling estimates the farmer who grew the cocoa receives just 72 cents. Most of the value is captured further up the supply chain by Cadbury and the supermarkets.

"Not only are they the poorest in the supply chain, but they also have the least power in the supply chain. They're the ones that are least able to bargain for price," Fuzz Kitto says.

Be Slavery Free estimates just 20 cents more per block would lift many farmers from poverty to a living income.

Mondelēz, which owns Cadbury, earned more than $50 billion in revenue last year, with almost $20 billion from its chocolate division.

For Carolyn Kitto, the solution starts with paying farmers enough to earn a living. She says it would cost the biggest chocolate companies little.

"That money could easily be absorbed. In some companies it's a rounding error, she says.

Etelle Higonnet has spent years investigating child labour in West Africa's cocoa industry. ( )

But Ms Higonnet says real change will come only if companies face sustained pressure from consumers who understand what is happening.

"All these problems are driven by greed and ignorance," she says.

"Greed of the companies that are making money off of this system and ignorance of consumers who need to be able to see and understand what's happening in order for them to be able to speak out and demand something better," she says.

Ghanaian girl collecting yellow cocoa pod. ( )

Ms Higonnet says consumers rarely see the human cost behind a block of chocolate.

"Behind that delightful treat is all this human suffering. People without running water, kids without school, women without land titles, people whose future is being ruined just so that we can have this taste of chocolate," she says.

Additional reporting by Dylan Welch

Photography by Rob Hill. Additional photography by Jack Fisher

Watch Four Corners' full investigation, Duped: Food Exposed — Part Two, tonight from 8:30 on ABC TV and ABC iview.

World.title: Iranians say the regime is at war 'with its own people'
World.content:
In the city of Isfahan, south of the Iranian capital Tehran, the once-bustling bazaar is much quieter than usual.

Shoppers still wander the streets and laneways, but the upheaval the country has experienced over the last five months is weighing heavily.

"Some days, I sit in my shop, and there are no customers," Vahid, whose name has been changed by the ABC to protect his identity, said in a voice note.

"No-one even asks for the prices. People are completely devastated.

"They don't know whether to save their money, spend it on food or buy something else.

"People are genuinely desperate, and don't know how to move forward."

Inside Tehran's small stores, shopkeepers are suffering from economic uncertainty. (Reuters: Majid Asgaripour/WANA)

Iran was facing significant economic pressures before the war, which was launched by the United States and Israel on February 28.

Surging inflation and the devaluation of the local currency, the Iranian Rial, had been two of the drivers of large-scale protests against the hardline Islamic regime in January — dissent that was met by a brutal, deadly crackdown by Iranian security forces.

Leila, whose name has also been changed by the ABC to protect her identity, said the strict security environment in Iran had only tightened further since the war began.

"The Islamic Republic is not only at war with other countries, sending them messages of death, but it is also at war with its own people," she said.

She said when people step outside their homes for just a few minutes, they are "confronted with checkpoints and a constant atmosphere of security and surveillance".

'The regime has grown much harsher': How the war changed Iran After a wave of assassinations targeting top Iranian officials and a supreme leader who has not been seen in public since the war began, a key question has emerged: who is really running Iran?

"Simply passing by them fills us with fear and anxiety," she said.

"In other countries where people see the police, they feel safe — but in our country, sadly, it's the opposite.

"The moment we see them, our whole body starts shaking, even when we haven't done anything wrong."

The ABC has been inside Iran twice since the war began, but access is tightly controlled. It is rare, if not impossible, to get Iranians to speak critically about the country's situation in person, due to fears of recriminations.

Yet three Iranians have been able to share their insights on life under the regime, as the war passes its fifth month and US President Donald Trump threatens a return to all-out fighting if no long-term peace deal can be struck.

"Right now it's like two stray dogs tearing each other apart, and we're waiting to see what happens," Shadi, whose name has been changed, told the ABC from Tehran.

"We're the ones caught in the middle, the sacrificial victims.

"You know how a sheep gets slaughtered, whether it's for a funeral or a wedding? That's us. Or like florists, they sell flowers for both weddings and funerals.

"We're being sacrificed in this war."

Inside Tehran's brutal crackdown

Before the war began on February 28, attention on Iran had been focused on the bloody crackdown on thousands of protesters who had rallied against the regime.

Mr Trump had even encouraged Iranians to take to the streets, and claimed: "Help is on its way."

Iranian security forces have brutally cracked down on dissent. (Reuters: Majid Asgaripour/WANA)

But for many people inside Iran, that specific assistance never came, and the war that followed drew attention from the human rights concerns.

Trials and sentences, including executions, for dissidents have continued at an alarming pace.

"From the beginning of this year, more than 400 executions happened in Iran," said Arina Moradi, a member of the Hengaw Organisation for Human Rights, an independent Kurdish group monitoring human rights violations in Iran.

"From this number, 57 were political prisoners or prisoners of conscience, and among them are a high number [of] people who were detained during the January protests.

"So the consequences of this repression is still going on, and it's very serious and critical from what we are witnessing."

The organisation monitors social media feeds that are a seemingly endless list of daily, if not hourly, updates of arrests, sentences and executions.

On Tuesday, Hengaw announced the public execution in Isfahan of two men involved in the January protests — Abolfazl Sepahi Badjani, 23, and Amirhossein Safari Hosseinabadi, 29.

"It's still going on, and it's even easier for the regime to use this lack of international attention, because the international attention shifted to the regional conflict," Ms Moradi said.

" It's much easier for the regime to conduct all these unlawful arrests and executions and the trials that are not fair, that are locked, [without] due process. "

Iran's regime 'frightened from its own population'

The surge in executions in Iran is no surprise to Rana Dadpour, founder of diaspora advocacy group AUSIRAN.

Dr Dadpour, who is also a research fellow at James Cook University, said the Iranian government uses this lever as a tactic to send a message to the population and scare people into silence.

Iran was facing significant economic pressures before the war. (Reuters: Majid Asgaripour/WANA)

"Every single time that the regime feels like an existential threat to itself, whether due to attacks by other countries or national uprisings, demonstrations, and protests, it always doubles down on executions," she said.

Despite facing threats from attacks by Israel and the US, Dr Dadpour said the regime was "more frightened from its own population".

"It is scared that … there might be a national uprising as well to double up the pressure on the regime, and that's why there's a surge in executions.

"It does everything it can to basically scare them and send the message that there shouldn't be any uprising. If [people] rise up, there will be more killings."

While dissent and festering anger against the regime is obvious, there are still significant numbers backing the hard-line theocracy — as seen by the crowds that swamped the casket of former ayatollah Ali Khamenei in recent weeks, and who have pledged their lives to support the regime.

Crowds gather in Iran to farewell body of assassinated supreme leader Millions of Iranians have gathered in Tehran as the country begins a week of funeral ceremonies for former supreme leader, ayatollah Ali Khamenei.

It was a similar case when the ABC was given rare access to the country in May on the condition that we remained in Tehran and worked with a translator from a pre-approved local media company.

At a pro-regime rally at Tehran's Enqelab Square, the ABC saw many women dressed in the traditional chador who vowed to fight and die for leaders accused of brutalising them.

Just how rusted on those elements of the Iranian community will be, if the war continues for much longer, is unclear, especially as parts of the country experience blackouts and financial uncertainty.

Energy grid and finances under strain

In the height of summer, with temperatures regularly approaching 50 degrees Celsius in some locations, daily rolling power cuts have been ordered by the regime to ensure the energy grid does not collapse.

There is support for the regime among parts of the Iranian population. (Reuters: Alkis Konstantinidis)

Vahid said the electricity was often cut for around two hours a day, during peak business hours.

"Take a fish seller who needs to keep fish cold, or a butcher whose refrigerators stop working for two hours — they can't keep opening the fridge doors; they have to keep them shut to preserve the temperature," he told the ABC.

"On top of that, the shops are dark because there's no electricity, and they can't serve customers or sell goods — the same goes for clothing shops.

"Businesses across the board are suffering financial losses because of the power blackouts. They can't earn enough to pay their rent, and if they do pay the rent, what's left to put food on the table for their families?"

In recent days, video shared on social media has shown massive queues at Iranian petrol stations across the country, as fuel shortages cause major disruption for the population of more than 90 million.

"I can see this worry on everyone's face," Vahid said.

"Today at work, I noticed that the little bit of cheerfulness people still had last week has completely disappeared.

" People are genuinely crushed, and I don't see a positive future ahead. "

Where to from here?

Shadi questioned how much longer the situation can last.

"If everything were really fine, why are armed patrols still roaming the streets until 1am?" she said.

"Even 12-year-old kids are carrying rifles. There's complete chaos in this country."

The regime says Israel and the US want to destroy their country, while it oversees the mass execution of Iranians. (Reuters: Majid Asgaripour/WANA)

For Leila, the source of that chaos is from within.

"We may blame America and Israel for starting the war, but this [is] the fate of a country that, for 40 years, has woken up every day to chants of 'Death to America' and 'Death to other countries' from morning until night."

Vahid said it was his opinion that this war could lead to several possible outcomes.

"First, military pressure becomes so overwhelming that the Islamic Republic and the decision makers surrender completely, accept all US demands, and perhaps even formally recognise Israel," he said.

"A second possibility is that the military campaign destroys [the] regime's entire power structure, creating a golden opportunity for the people to deliver the final blow to the rotten foundations of this regime.

"If that happens, however, I think there could also be serious clashes between the regime's supporters and general public.

"In any case, people have become deeply hopeless. But their anger has not disappeared. Their hope has faded, but their anger remains."

World.title: Ex-ASIO agent reapplies for visa to testify at Bondi royal commission
World.content:
A former ASIO agent has made a new bid to return to Australia to give evidence to the Bondi royal commission, after his previous visa application was rejected.

The former agent, known as Marcus, has also been contacted by NSW Police about assisting their inquiries into last December's Bondi terror attack.

Marcus has said he wanted to return to Australia to give evidence to the royal commission in person, and the royal commission has previously said it was "eager" to hear from him.

Ex-ASIO source denied visa to give evidence at Bondi royal commission The man who previously warned ASIO about the Bondi gunmen will not be able to give sensitive and classified evidence at the Royal Commission into Antisemitism and Social Cohesion.

He spent years working undercover for ASIO within Sydney's ISIS networks, and has said he warned ASIO about the Bondi gunmen years before the terror attack took place.

ASIO has previously described him as "unreliable and disgruntled", which Marcus rejects.

Marcus has been living abroad for a number of years, and has significant concerns about his personal security.

His previous visa application was rejected by Australian immigration authorities on the grounds they were "not satisfied the applicant has a genuine intention to stay temporarily in Australia".

He has previously sought assistance from Australia for protection and resettlement.

Marcus has now re-submitted his application.

Police reach out following Four Corners program

Earlier this year, the former agent was contacted by NSW Police about the possibility of speaking with them about their ongoing investigation into December's attack.

In emails seen by the ABC, a police officer reached out to Marcus following his appearance on the ABC's Four Corners program.

"You have recently featured in media publications within Australia which has led us to understand that you are likely to hold information that is relevant to our investigations here," the email reads.

" I can assure you — we are open-minded and want to speak with you and take any information you have. "

Solicitors for Marcus have told the ABC that his preference would be to assist police in person in Australia, due to security concerns, the sensitivity of the information he intends to provide, and the need for legal protections.

Royal commission considers antisemitism education The Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion is continuing in Sydney, with witnesses to give evidence about ways to improve education and training to prevent hate.

NSW Police reached out to Marcus about speaking with them again last month.

Marcus's bid to return to Australia has previously attracted support from a number of federal political MPs, while the opposition has said the government should find a way to facilitate his evidence.

The office of Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke declined to comment.

Legal concerns about giving evidence abroad

Marcus's solicitors have previously told the ABC that his evidence would need to be given in an appropriately secure environment, either within Australia or at an embassy abroad.

Marcus is currently living abroad, and his solicitors have said he would not be able to get to an Australian embassy.

Witnesses to royal commissions are afforded a range of legal protections, including around the use of information provided to royal commissions in future criminal or civil proceedings.

Prominent lawyer Geoffrey Watson SC said for Marcus, giving evidence while abroad could expose him to legal risk.

"Depending upon where Marcus is, it could well be a breach of local laws, in which event he is exposing himself up to a real risk," he said.

"In respect of obtaining the ordinary protection which would apply to a witness before a royal commission who gave their evidence in Australia, it's an open question as to whether or not those sorts of privileges would apply to a person who's on foreign soil when they are giving the evidence, the answers to the questions.

"You could look at it as though, perhaps, by giving that evidence they are subject to Australian law, in which event the legal protections apply.

"But if the Australian law doesn't apply in the place where Marcus is giving the evidence, then he could be at risk. It's a difficult question."

David Shoebridge says the easiest legal solution is to allow Marcus to come to Australia. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Greens senator David Shoebridge said the simplest solution to the legal issues arising from giving evidence abroad is to allow Marcus to do so onshore.

"The basic rule is that Australian laws only apply in Australia and the Royal Commission Act is no exception," he said.

"The protections witnesses have under the Royal Commission Act, from injury, fraud and self-incrimination, don't work overseas. This places Marcus in a very vulnerable position.

"Even where the Act contemplates evidence given in a third country, it's all designed for a pre-internet world, and doesn't apply to evidence given by zoom or teams."
