World.title: I discovered an overlooked part of Bali most visitors dream of
World.content:
InspirationBali I discovered an overlooked part of Bali most visitors dream of Nina Karnikowski August 3, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Two weeks before leaving for Ubud, I was already hyperventilating about Bali’s crowds. As someone who spends much of their life chasing quietude, just the thought of the over-development and the Instagrammable chaos made me twitch. Cottages at Kul Kul Farm. Nina Karnikowski So when a friend told me about Sibang – describing it as Ubud’s calmer cousin and the way it might have been 30 years ago – I was in. Now, waiting for said friend on a dirt road corner with just an ancient temple to my left and jungle to my right, I’m glad I’ve come. That Sibang (which actually encompasses two villages, Sibang Kaja and Sibang Gede) has stayed under the radar is no accident. “Locals have told us about a curse that was placed on the village many years ago, by an angry giant who threatened that it would one day be swallowed by ants,” my friend says. “It’s said the villagers fled because of this, and the jungle took over.” The story lingered for decades, leaving Sibang quiet and largely overlooked – until Canadian John Hardy arrived to build Green School Bali.



Green School’s bamboo campus, which offers eco-focused education to about 500 local and international students from kindergarten to year 12, put the village on the map when it opened in 2008. My friend, who’s living in Sibang, so her son can attend the school, walks me down the street flanking the campus. Aside from local homes and a couple of sleepy cafes, a sustainability-focused concept store named Muka, and a slick year-old villa stay called Mahajiva, there is, happily, not much here. 



Each April, Kul Kul runs a 10-day bamboo-building course, teaching about a material that restores land, grows rapidly, and sequesters carbon. Student-built curving structures, five of which are newly open to guests, are dotted between beds of lettuce, tomato, chilli and eggplant. Much of this produce lands on plates at Taani, Kul Kul’s new restaurant where I slurp the best soto (a warming turmeric-spiced soup) I’ve ever had in Indonesia. Inside a cottage at Kul Kul Farm. Next afternoon I walk to Astungkara Way, a regenerative rice-farming collective. Twenty minutes from Kul Kul Farm, the road dissolves into paddies alive with birdsong and the loamy scent of turned earth. Here, travellers learn how rice is grown the natural way. This means ducks instead of pesticides, compost instead of chemicals, and respect for the Subak system, a co-operative irrigation network that has sustained Bali’s farmers for centuries. “Look around,” says manager Oka Dewanti, spreading her arms wide to the rice paddies rolling out around us. “This is what Ubud or Canggu was 30 years ago.” She speaks of the heartbreak of watching development swallow farmland, the urgency of bringing youth back to agriculture, and how travellers can support the kind of Bali they want to see. To that end, alongside hands-on farming courses, Astungkara Way leads multi-day walking journeys that begin in the thick of traffic and development, and slowly carry travellers back to the Bali that once was. Strolling back to Kul Kul in the indigo evening light, past boys fishing in irrigation canals and women carrying baskets of offerings towards local temples, I worry about what Sibang might lose as more travellers arrive. Change is already gathering at its edges. But if places like Kul Kul Farm and Astungkara Way set the tone for what’s to come, maybe this village has a fighting chance to remain the kind of Bali travellers dream about, rather than the kind we flee.

World.title: Lockdowns are looming for Perth’s roaming cats. Here’s what you need to know
World.content:
NationalWALocal government Lockdowns are looming for Perth’s roaming cats. Here’s what you need to know Hannah Murphy August 3, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

West Australian councils could soon get the green light to force roaming cats indoors — but right now, a pet’s freedom depends entirely on which council it lives in. Local Government Minister Hannah Beazley announced plans to change the law to allow local councils to introduce cat containment laws in February. WA’s cats could soon be forced to stay on their own properties. Nick Moir Under the current law, councils need to get permission from a parliamentary committee to introduce changes to their local regulations. More than 20 councils have tried to make their own laws about keeping cats inside in the past, but only three have been successful - all in regional WA.



As a result, the cat laws in each local government differ greatly. Ahead of the planned law change, we asked every Perth metropolitan council what their state of play is when it comes to outdoor cats. Here’s what they told us: The Town of Claremont was the only local council who refused to comment on their current cat laws, and whether it had ever tried to get them changed previously.



Councils said cats were currently banned from upwards of 300 Perth reserves, parks and protected bushland area across the metropolitan area. Nearly all councils have limits on the number of cats people can own, and a select few have trapping programs conducted by rangers for “nuisance” cats. The changes to the 2011 Cat Act are only partway through the parliamentary process, but under its powers, local councils could order owners to: restrict cats to their owners’ premises;

prohibit cats from all public areas;

place conditions on when a cat may be permitted in a public area;

introduce cat curfews; and

require cats to be under the effective control of their owners or contained if leaving their owners’ property. However, Cat Haven chief executive Roz Robinson said it would be interesting to see how any changes would actually worked in practice. “It is interesting times with the review of the cat act coming up and it is interesting to note that whilst many councils are talking about cat containment being part of the cat laws, so many local governments do not enforce the current act,” she said.



“For example, I have it in writing from one western suburbs’ council, when faced with an enquiry from one of their residences about a stray cat, they simply refer them onto us.” Roz Robinson is the chief executive officer of Perth’s Cat Haven. Robinson said the not-for-profit organisation was extremely supportive of cat containment laws, saying it not only improves cat welfare but would ease pressure on the service. “With over 50 per cent of our intake coming in as strays, if we had proper containment laws, it would result in a reduction in these numbers,” she said. However, Robinson also argued any change with the Cat Act needed to focus heavily on the benefits of de-sexing household cats.



“Over 80 per cent of these strays – most friendly re-homable cats – are un-desexed. Un-desexed cats wander – they become strays in their need to mate. “You don’t have to be a mathematician to work out cats are prolific breeders and what numbers would look like without de-sexing. Related Article Exclusive

Biodiversity The staggering death toll of roaming pet cats finally revealed “For years we have been trying to de-sex our way out of the cat problem, but with little appetite from others to assist, we are literally fighting a losing battle.” She said there had to be continual state government funding towards spaying cats, as well as supporting the Cat Haven to deal with stray animals. Currently, she said the government provides just less than two per cent of the charity’s operating costs.



“What changes do we see after the review? It really depends if all stakeholders are serious about improving cat welfare or is it just another review being ticked off,” Robinson said. “Our intake numbers are increasing annually – 8 per cent while the population is only growing two per cent – our site is not fit for purpose, and can only be described as dilapidated. There is no funding forthcoming to improve the site. “We are an open admission shelter, we never say no to any cat and truly believe every cat does matter and want to give them all a second chance. But something has to give.”

World.title: Easy ways to eat more fibre every day without even trying
World.content:
Tips & adviceDietitian’s guide Easy ways to eat more fibre every day without even trying Remember these simple tips and ingredients when grocery shopping and meal-prepping and boost your dietary fibre intake without overthinking it. Susie Burrell August 3, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Health trends may come and go faster than you can say “TikTok made me do it”, but current darling, dietary fibre, is the real deal. From a renewed focus on supporting digestive health and immune function with gut health superfoods, to fibremaxxing, there is plenty of noise that all comes back to one simple concept: eat more fibre. Here are some easy ways to do that every day without even trying. Use multgrain bread for your sandwiches like Neil Perry’s tuna number. William Meppem Upgrade your carbs Whether it’s cereal for breakfast, or a sandwich or wrap for lunch, the key to optimising your daily intake of dietary fibre is to ensure your daily staples have a wholegrain or wholemeal base. Often, we find ourselves picking up foods on the go, and in most cases, the carbs on offer are white, and as such not offering nearly as much fibre as we need. Bread and wraps



Swap white, sourdough, or plain wraps for high-fibre wholemeal, multigrain, rye, or seed-packed options. As a reference, your daily bread or wraps should be adding at least 3-5g of dietary fibre per serve and while sourdough may sound healthier, generally the options at cafes and bakeries are made with white flour. The best recipes from Australia's leading chefs straight to your inbox. Sign up Breakfast staples Choose multigrain or high-bran cereals over refined varieties, and toss oats or bran straight into smoothies. When checking breakfast cereal or granola packets, keep in mind that the higher percentage of wholegrains the breakfast cereal offers, the higher the natural dietary fibre content will be. Natural sources of dietary fibre from wholegrains, seeds, fruits and nuts are better options nutritionally than more processed dietary fibre like chicory root and insulin which are often added to bars, cereals and breads to increase the fibre content. Opt for brown rice over white, like in Katrina Meynink’s chickpea, brown rice and greens salad. Katrina Meynink



Pasta and rice There is a growing range of wholemeal, wholegrain and legume pasta options which are all significantly higher in fibre than regular white pasta. In the case of rice, seek out brown or black varieties where possible, or one of the growing ranges of mixed grain and rice quick-cook options that can offer as much as 5-8g of dietary fibre per serve, compared to less than 1g for regular white rice. Can you guess the hidden veg in Jill Dupleix’s spaghetti bolognese? Sneak vegies into every meal With fewer than one in 10 Aussies getting the recommended five serves of vegetables a day, and even less the 7-10 serves to support the goal of optimal health and longevity, there are plenty of reasons including boosting our intake of dietary fibre that come from increasing veggie intake across all of our meals.



Grate and blend Adding a mix of grated zucchini and carrots, or spinach or silverbeet, into scrambled eggs, pasta sauce bases like bolognese, porridge, or smoothies not only significantly increases nutrient intake, but fibre intake as well. Frozen spinach and kale can also be cost-effective options that slip easily into a number of meals without negatively impacting the flavour. Keep the skins on Whether you are mashing vegetables, adding them to smoothies or grating them into dishes, you get extra dietary fibre from vegetables when you leave the skin on. The same goes for fruits, and if you are especially keen, the skins on nutrient-packed kiwifruit and bananas are edible, too. Related Article Canned, pouched and fresh: A dietitian’s guide to the best (and worst) supermarket chicken soups



Know the easy add-ins Budget-friendly and fibre-rich frozen peas can be added to a wide range of mixed dishes including pasta, risotto and stir-fries. Baby cucumbers and carrots are an easy side to enjoy with your favourite sandwich or wrap, while a starter of pre-made vegetable-rich soups add extra nutrients and dietary fibre to any main meal. Make your own baked beans, like Adam Liaw’s, and get a big fibre boose. William Meppem Learn to love legumes If there is one food Aussies should be eating more of, if only for the cost-effective nature of such a nutrient-rich food, it is legumes. There are so many varieties that can easily be worked into many meals, whilst adding loads of protein and dietary fibre.



Swap in with mince Whether you are making spaghetti bolognese, chilli con carne or a sang choy bao, throw in a can of your favourite beans to make any amount of mince go a lot further. Embrace baked beans Ever-versatile baked beans can be added to any hot breakfast, enjoyed with crackers or even as a light meal, adding a massive 6-8 grams of dietary fibre per serve. If you prefer lower sugar options, it is also easy to make your own using a cannellini or white beans. Eat more edamame



Soy beans are especially nutrient rich, and an easy addition to all of your favourite Asian dishes whether they are enjoyed as a side dish with sushi, added to salads or even as a dried, protein-packed snack. Sprinkle chia seeds and nuts onto your cereal. iStock Sprinkle in seeds and nuts Not only are seeds and nuts extremely nutrient rich — offering nutrients including zinc, selenium, magnesium and plant-based omega-3s — but they are also rich in dietary fibre. Breakfast boosters



Stir a tablespoon of chia, flaxseed or pepitas into any mix of cereal, oats, yoghurt or smoothies for a protein, fibre and good fat hit. Or opt for one of the growing ranges of breakfast toppers or nut spreads which offer a mix of nuts and seeds, and as such a mix of nutrients. Related Article Sprinkle these tiny seeds on just about anything for a mighty nutrition punch Your favourite salads A little crunch goes a long way in a salad, and a few roasted nuts or a sprinkle of seeds adds texture and flavour to any salad. Even better, try roasting your favourite nuts or seeds with a little honey or maple syrup for an even tastier salad topper. A go-to snack

World.title: People think my suburb is just the shopping centre. For better or worse, we do orbit it
World.content:
NationalQueenslandLife in the ’burbs Opinion People think my suburb is just the shopping centre. For better or worse, we do orbit it Chris Burke Contributor August 3, 2026 — 5:00am

August 3, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Before I moved here, I thought “Carindale” was the shopping centre. These days, I know it as a family-friendly suburb with more buses than you can count, and a distinct lack of local coffee shops. In my defence, the shopping centre called Carindale existed before the suburb did (opening in 1979). To this day, the mall, now Westfield Carindale, still has an indelible impact on the time and space of this place. It’s a black hole, and we orbit for better or worse. I’ve seen Christopher Nolan’s Interstellar, so I know that when you get close to a black hole, time slows down. It can even appear to stop. That rings true for Carindale. For much of the past decade, the suburb has felt stuck. When we moved here over a decade ago, Carindale seemed full of possibility. The Greendale Way shopping centre development is local folklore and still shared by real estate agents as “the next big thing” since the planning application was first approved nearly 20 years ago. Some are eager for an alternative to the Westfield whirling dervish, while others wonder why anyone would develop anything so close to a black hole.



That appears to be the recurring theme, and likely the reason for our lack of flat whites that don’t involve a hunt for a Westfield parking space. As Westfield continues to expand, it consumes the attention, investment and daylight, while other opportunities struggle to escape its shadow. The Eastern Busway was coming. Now the Metro. And we’re still waiting for that bus. As Westfield continues to expand, it consumes the attention, investment and daylight, while other opportunities struggle to escape its shadow. The decrepit aged care building on Creek Road was demolished to make way for a new retirement village. For now, we’re just watching the grass grow at the site. Then there was the proposed Taco Bell drive-through, where progress remains firmly at naught.



While the suburb feels stuck, our lives here have been anything but. My adulthood started here. It is where we brought our children home from hospital, and where we have built our family life. My wife and I bought our first home in Carindale because of the location: it was close to the Gateway and not too far from the city. We had lived in Carina for a time, but it felt older, with timber weatherboard cottages belonging to another era. Carindale’s larger blocks and brick-and-tile houses felt more practical for the family life we imagined for ourselves. In the early 2000s, teenage boys in adidas tracksuits congregated around the Carindale bus interchange. That era has long passed, but the black hole still has its pull. Those teenage boys are now adults taking their own children to Rhyme Time at Carindale Library.



It’s a neighbourhood built for children. There are parks, walking and cycling tracks and, of course, the flying disc golf course at Cadogan Street Park. Kids play in the street, there are plenty of trees to climb, and the Home Ice Cream truck rings its bell every second Sunday afternoon. Carindale is full of green space. The prolific gum trees mean we routinely see koalas on the drive home from school. Within walking distance from our front door to the south are places that could be mistaken for Springbrook National Park rainforest. And to the north there’s koala and swamp wallaby habitat. The shopping centre may dominate the landscape but Carindale is also full of green space. Markus Ravik It really is a place of opposites. On a map, Carindale is split down the middle by Bulimba Creek. This is contrasted by our eastern border and the constant hum of the Gateway Motorway, occasionally pierced by the sound of rifles from the Belmont shooting range.



There are giant mansions overlooking the golf course, alongside small townhouses and tired older homes. We’ve noticed recently that the knockdown-rebuild revolution has certainly started. Related Article Opinion

Life in the ’burbs My suburb’s most popular residents have fluffy ears and, like me, they love an elevated position Stephanie Felesina Contributor Carindale did not exist as a suburb until 1980. The original housing estate, developed during the 1970s, was part of Belmont. The former cow paddocks around the northern end of Meadowlands Road were developed by builders such as G.J. Gardner Homes. In the 1990s came the Pacific Golf Course and the large brick homes surrounding it. Many of the residents who bought during those early decades are now empty nesters (or trying to be), while new families competing to find their way in are struggling with a median house price of a bonkers $1.8 million. The Mansfield school catchments have a noticeable impact on the southern side of the suburb, pushing property prices ever higher.



Carindale is also a convenient transport boundary of sorts. It feels like the final point in Brisbane’s geographical middle-east, where multiple bus routes begin and end. Once you cross the Gateway, everything becomes either “too far” or “bayside”. The trade-off is traffic. We are boxed in by the Gateway Motorway and Creek Road, all swirling around the Westfield black hole. The rat runs are well established, with a very clear backstreet peak hour at 4pm on the dot. Recent signals suggest Carindale may finally be about to come off pause. Brisbane City Council is (again) exploring an Eastern Metro route from the CBD to Capalaba. The Greendale Way site has changed hands, renewing (yet again) this never-ending urban legend, and proposed planning changes around Westfield could allow buildings of up to 30 storeys. For better or worse, perhaps Carindale is on the cusp of launching. Whether these projects can escape the gravitational pull of the black hole remains to be seen. In the meantime, we’re happy spotting koalas. But I’d still just like a flat white, please.

World.title: Thousands of NSW children are being abused. Police say it has become an epidemic
World.content:
Exclusive NationalNSWChild abuse Thousands of NSW children are being abused. Police say it has become an epidemic Riley Walter August 3, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Warning: Graphic content More than 300 incidents involving children, including serious sexual and physical assaults, are reported to authorities weekly, as police warn laws designed to protect children are inadvertently shielding offenders. In the past 12 months, almost 16,000 reports were made to the state’s Joint Referral Unit, a multi-agency triage centre that assesses child protection reports, while online offending involving children has also skyrocketed in what senior police say has become an epidemic. Detectives receive on average 10 to 15 reports each weekend of child abuse. Matt Willis “This is thousands and thousands and thousands of children who are being abused,” NSW Police Assistant Commissioner Scott Cook told this masthead.



Cook, who oversees NSW Police’s child abuse and sex crimes squads, said detectives receive on average 10 to 15 reports each weekend of child abuse, ranging from sexual assault to physical assaults “bordering on death”, most of which is offending occurring within families. “Child exploitation and neglect and child abuse occurs, quite often, in the family home. It quite often involves a relative, a person in power,” Cook said. NSW Police Assistant Commissioner Scott Cook. James Brickwood While in-person offending has remained steady over several years, there had been an “explosion” of online child abuse in NSW and across the country, Cook said. The number of reports made to the Australian Centre to Counter Child Exploitation, which is led by the Australian Federal Police and refers matters to state police forces for investigation, is expected to exceed 100,000 this year.



“That is an epidemic of online child abuse,” Cook said. “The number of victims that are now being identified is enormous. Online exploitation is enormous.” Cook said highlighting the levels of child abuse across the state – a topic senior police rarely broach publicly – was crucial ahead of a concerted push to raise awareness of the issue during National Child Protection Week in early September. “It’s important for the prevention of this occurring, to have people aware of what’s going on – whether that’s child grooming, inappropriate touching, whether that’s inappropriate comments and conduct, bystanders need to call this stuff out. We all need to call this stuff out before it escalates, before a child becomes a victim,” Cook said. Talking publicly about what child abuse has long been viewed as a taboo issue, and overcoming that could help police and members of the public detect and prevent offending, he said.



Related Article Exclusive

Crime Revealed: Accused Sydney day care paedophile who ‘abused more than 150 children’ Raising awareness about the levels of abuse is made difficult by laws protecting the identities of child abuse victims in NSW that often prevent police and media outlets from exposing predators. “Non-publication laws relating to the protection of young victims and witnesses are really important, and I don’t want to diminish that or understate that, but an unintended consequence of how we do that, is that this crime type, these abhorrent offences against children, often doesn’t get the attention it should,” Cook said. “In terms of the law, really, I don’t know that any jurisdiction has struck the right balance between protecting a child and inadvertently protecting an offender at the same time. The offenders shouldn’t have protection. They should be unmasked.” Recent cases, including that of Sydney daycare worker Hamish Tait, highlighted the challenges in exposing alleged abusers facing both police and media outlets.



Tait’s identity and the scale of his alleged offending was revealed after a year-long fight by the Herald to lift a suppression order prohibiting his identification. Accused daycare paedophile Hamish Tait’s alleged offending was revealed after the Herald fought a year-long suppression order over his identity. “I don’t think community or people want to confront that this type of offending even occurs,” Cook said. “That puts us in a difficult position to even talk about this publicly. We risk breaching the law, and we risk alienating communities and people because of the subject matter, but when you drill this down, it’s all about children. It’s about their safety, and about their protection.” So voluminous is their workload, both the child abuse and sex crimes squads’ resources are constantly bolstered by detectives from other areas.



In some instances, detectives seize electronic devices containing hundreds of thousands of images of children. In the past year, child abuse squad detectives charged more than 550 people across NSW with 3349 separate offences against children, including almost 900 charges of sexual assault, more than 330 of assault, and almost 1200 of touching, including indecent assault. “The child abuse squad and the sex crimes squad are under immense pressure due to the sheer volume of the level of crime,” Cook said. eSafety Commissioner Julie Inman Grant told this masthead the online regulator received more than 18,000 reports of illegal and restricted content allegedly involving child abuse material in the past financial year, representing a 17 per cent increase compared with the previous year; the number of reports increased 58 per cent the year before. “Child sexual abuse and exploitation is an abhorrent crime that causes profound and lifelong harm to victims and survivors,” Inman Grant said.



Child abuse squad detectives are expected in the coming months to charge notorious Queensland paedophile Ashley Paul Griffith with almost 200 offences related to the time the former childcare worker spent working in NSW. Queensland Attorney-General Deb Frecklington in June confirmed the process to extradite Griffith was in its final stages. Dozens of NSW children have been identified among Griffith’s further alleged victims. Notorious paedophile Ashley Paul Griffith will be extradited to NSW to face almost 200 charges. Nine “He needs to face the allegations that are to be put on behalf of the victims in NSW. That’s why he needs to come back,” Cook said. The assistant commissioner said combatting child abuse would remain a top priority for authorities, but police could not arrest their way out of the growing issue.



“Every police force in Australia is committed to this, and every police force in Australia works on this,” Cook said. “But it is an epidemic, and we shouldn’t pretend that it’s not.” Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732). Anyone affected by sexual, domestic or family violence can also access 24/7, free and confidential trauma-specialist counselling through Full Stop Australia (1800 385 578). World.title: Not many significant monuments let people climb them. This is a corker
World.content:
InspirationIndia Not many significant monuments let people climb them. This is a corker Brian Johnston August 3, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

I don’t rank the squish of pigeon poop beneath my shoeless feet as an agreeable travel experience. Nor is squeezing up a staircase in a space so tight I have to engage in sweaty tangos with those descending. The cause is worth it, though. What traveller can resist a commanding view, or the lure of the unusual? Not me, anyway. So when I see a battered sign that says I can ascend one of the minarets of Delhi’s Jama Masjid, or Friday Mosque, I don’t let pesky pigeons put me off. Jama Masjid in Delhi is framed by its two minarets. iStock In mosques, only a muezzin climbs the minaret to proclaim the call to prayer and even then, not often in this modern age when the mosque relies on loudspeakers. This is something almost unique, and Friday Mosque couldn’t be a better mosque to do it in. Not many places let you clamber onto the roofs of significant monuments either, and this monument, completed in 1656 under Shah Jahan at the peak of the Mughal Empire, is a corker. One of India’s largest and most important mosques, it fuses Persian and Hindu architectural influences and houses relics of the prophet Muhammad.



I pick my way past a sea of temporarily abandoned shoes at its ornamental gateway and enter a vast courtyard, in which, at festival times, 25,000 people assemble to pray. Locals sit on patterned Kashmir carpets under its colonnades, cracking peanuts and gazing towards the Red Fort. 



Just being elevated to roof level provides a different take on this mosque. Three white domes trimmed with black stripes bulge like tethered hot-air balloons. I have to tip back my neck to admire the minarets, which seem to lean against Delhi’s heavy grey skies. I tiptoe over the pigeon poop and into the minaret’s narrow doorway. Corkscrewing steps have a rough red surface like an old hide. Walls are behind-the-scenes rough. There’s no longer any space for handrails. The entrance to the mosque, which was built by the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan between 1644 and 1656. iStock About halfway up in the sweltering humidity, as I push against people coming down in ways that are far too intimate, I begin to think this is a mistake, but plod on. The staircase emerges onto a narrow platform that has barely a toehold. A sign in several scripts I can’t decipher appears to be a warning. Certainly, if anyone stepped incautiously backwards, they would fall down the spiral staircase like a stunt actor. We are, though, protected from falling outwards by the pavilion’s scalloped arches and metal screens.



Related Article India Ten things I learnt on my first visit to India From 40 metres up, Friday Mosque is laid out like an architect’s plan. Vertigo sufferers won’t be happy. The flocks of pigeons now swoop below. Beyond is the Red Fort in one direction and the jumble of Old Delhi in the other. Old Delhi’s crush and crowd – porters hauling boxes and scrums of cycle-rickshaws that are so alarming at street level – seem almost balletic from this height. There’s no escaping the ceaseless splutter of motorbikes and honking of horns, however. They seem to mimic my heart, set thumping by the climb and height and thrill of the view. THE DETAILS Fly

Malaysia Airlines flies to Delhi via Kuala Lumpur. See malaysiaairlines.com



Tour

Luxury Gold’s 18-day Imperial Rajasthan tour spends two days in Delhi and includes a visit to Jama Masjid. It has regular departures between September 2026 and March 2027. From $11,749 a person, twin share. See luxurygold.com See

Jama Masjid is open to non-Muslim visitors daily from 8am to sunset. Arms and legs must be covered and shoes removed. Entry INR400 ($6), minaret ascent INR100. See delhitourism.gov.in More

World.title: Five strength training exercises you need to improve your posture
World.content:
LifestyleHealth & wellnessHealth Five strength training exercises you need to improve your posture Caroline Idiens August 3, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

One of the most common questions I get from clients as a personal trainer is: “What can I do to improve my posture?” It’s a concern I hear repeatedly: people noticing that their shoulders are rounding forwards, they have pain in their necks or lower back, or both, their head is drifting towards their screen, or they simply don’t feel as tall and upright as they once did. In our increasingly digital world, where many of us spend hours each day looking down at devices or sitting for prolonged periods, it’s easy to blame the rise of “tech neck” and rounded shoulders entirely on modern life. It’s easy to blame the rise of “tech neck” and rounded shoulders entirely on modern life. iStock But the story is more complicated than that. While our daily habits certainly play a role, one of the biggest reasons our posture changes as we get older is that we gradually lose the muscle strength needed to support our spine and hold ourselves upright. As we age, muscle mass declines, bones become less dense, spinal discs lose height and connective tissues become stiffer. The result can be familiar: rounded shoulders, a more curved upper back, a forward head position and a tendency to stoop as we walk.



The good news is that this isn’t simply an unavoidable consequence of getting older. Posture is not just about age, it is also about strength. Building the muscles that support your body, will help you stand taller, move more easily in daily life and reduce the risk of injuries due to misalignment. Why does our posture change as we get older? Related Article Ageing Muscle loss is more common than diabetes in old age. Here’s how to avoid it From around the age of 30, we begin to gradually lose muscle mass, a process known as sarcopenia. Unless we actively work to maintain it, this loss can accelerate as we get older. The muscles of the upper back, shoulders, spine and core all play an important role in keeping us upright, acting almost like a natural support system for the skeleton. With poor posture, the muscles at the front of the chest, particularly the pectoral muscles, can become tight and less flexible. At the same time, the muscles of the upper back that help pull the shoulders back and stabilise the shoulder blades can become weaker and less active.



And this is when problems occur and we see rounded shoulders, increased curvature through the upper back and a tendency to lean forwards as we walk. Does poor posture cause back pain? There isn’t one simple answer here. Yes, slouching and forward head posture will place uneven stress on spinal joints, overwork muscles, and compress discs. It is this repetitive mechanical strain that causes stiffness, muscle fatigue and tension that can eventually lead to chronic discomfort. However, poor posture alone does not automatically cause back pain. Plenty of people have rounded shoulders or a less-than-perfect sitting position and experience no discomfort, while others with excellent posture can still develop back problems. It is staying in this position for long periods of time that can contribute to this pain – the spine requires movement to stay healthy. And this is where exercise comes in. A bent over row strengthens the upper back muscles that help pull the shoulders back and support the spine. Getty Images Why strength training is one of the best tools for posture



If there is one intervention backed by strong evidence, it is strength training. Related Article Exclusive

Wellbeing Still working at 80? The future is grim or thrilling, depending on who you ask A 2024 systematic review published in Sports Medicine Open, which analysed 23 studies, found that strengthening exercises led to significant improvements in posture, particularly in the upper back and neck, whereas stretching alone had little measurable effect. In other words, standing taller isn’t simply about remembering to pull your shoulders back and down; it is about building the strength to hold yourself there. Resistance training also has benefits far beyond posture. It helps preserve muscle mass, supports bone health, improves balance and helps maintain independence as we age.



The good news is that you don’t need hours in the gym. A small number of specific exercises, performed consistently, can target the muscles that help us maintain an upright posture. I incorporate the following five movements into all of my full-body workouts and try to do these three or four times per week. I do 10 reps of each and three sets. You can start with just bodyweight and build up to using dumbbells. I recommend anyone starting out to begin with a set of 2-kilogram dumbbells and increase the weights gradually. The last couple of reps should feel like a challenge. Five exercises to help improve your posture 1. Bent over row



Hinge forwards from the hips, keeping your back straight and your core engaged. Holding a dumbbell in each hand, draw the weights towards your lower ribs by squeezing your shoulder blades together. Pause briefly at the top before slowly lowering the weights under control. Why it works: This strengthens the upper back muscles that help pull the shoulders back and support the spine. 2. Prone ‘T’ raise Lie face down with your gaze towards the floor. Keeping your body relaxed, lift your arms slightly away from the mat to form a “T” shape, squeezing the muscles between your shoulder blades before slowly lowering. Start with bodyweight only and progress to holding light weights as you become stronger.



Why it works: This targets the smaller stabilising muscles around the shoulder blades that are often weakened by prolonged sitting and rounded posture. 3. Reverse fly Hinge forwards at the hips and raise your arms out to the side, keeping a soft bend in your elbows. Start with light weights, pause briefly at the top of the movement and gently lower with control. Avoid using momentum – the movement should come from the muscles of your upper back. Why it works: This strengthens the rear shoulders and upper back, helping to counter the forward-rounded position many of us adopt.



4. Single-arm row Hold a weight in one hand and rest your opposite hand on your knee or a chair for support. Using the full range of movement, draw the weight back towards your hip while keeping your elbow close to your body. Slowly lower before repeating on the other side. Why it works: Working one side at a time challenges the upper back while also encouraging the core muscles to stabilise the spine. 5. Weighted dead bug Lie on your back and, with or without weights, slowly extend the opposite arm and opposite leg away from your body. Keep your lower back gently pressed down throughout the movement and return slowly to the starting position before changing sides.



Why it works: A strong core is essential for supporting the spine. This exercise teaches the deep abdominal muscles to stabilise the body while the limbs move. To conclude Related Article Health ‘Strength training for your brain’: This skill may keep you sharp as you age Getting older does not mean we have to accept becoming smaller, weaker or more stooped. While we cannot stop the natural changes that come with ageing, we can influence how our bodies adapt. Building strength helps us maintain the muscles that support our spine, protect our bones and allow us to move with confidence in all of our everyday activities.



Good posture is not about standing rigidly or trying to hold yourself perfectly all day. It is about having a body strong enough to support you, so you can continue to stand tall, whatever your age. World.title: I was excited to be a ‘boy mum’. Then I picked up my phone
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsParenting Opinion I was excited to be a ‘boy mum’. Then I picked up my phone Hannah Vanderheide Contributor August 3, 2026 — 5:00am

August 3, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Just months away from becoming the mum of two boys, I’m excited for many things. A glass of champagne, naturally, but mostly watching the light of my life step into his new role as big brother and meeting this precious tiny person who will complete our family. My social media feed, however, seems intent on preparing me for something else. Being a “boy mum” is about more than just having sons. iStock Once the almighty algorithm learnt I was pregnant with a second boy, it unlocked a vault of something I wasn’t prepared for: “boy mum” content. It started with stereotypical portrayals of a boy mum v girl mum house, serene calm pit against utter chaos. But it quickly escalated to depictions of actual violence, like one reel set on an escalator contrasting a pristine “girl mum” with a despondent and noticeably injured “boy mum”, black eye and all.





Naturally some of it is satire, stoking outrage to maximise engagement. After all, the internet thrives on extremes and virality rewards exaggeration. But according to Dr Joanne Orlando, expert in digital wellbeing, and author of Generation Connected, this content can still have a negative impact on both parents and their kids. “I think it does put preconceived ideas about what your role as a parent should be, rather than just nurturing your beautiful baby.” In part, she believes the trend taps into growing anxiety about raising boys in the age of Andrew Tate’s “manosphere”. According to these corners of the internet, boys are either feral, violent agents of domestic destruction or the great love of your life. “The default message is that there’s something wrong with boys, and that we need to fix them,” she explains. “It’s really a damaging message.” Essentially, new mothers already carrying the enormous responsibility of raising a child are also being told that he’s a future problem to be fixed.



Orlando says it’s especially concerning for new mums who don’t have a lot of experience with raising boys. “I think they can go into this like, ‘What? I didn’t know I should be worried about having a son’.” I can relate. Before my second pregnancy, I had never thought of raising my son as participation in a particular maternal subculture. He was just my beautiful child. “Boy mum” content twists the mother-son bond to get more interactions. iStock Dr Justin Coulson, co-host of Channel Nine’s Parental Guidance and founder of Happy Families, says some sex differences highlighted in these reels are a biological reality.



“Boys use their bodies more, girls use their words more,” he explains, citing the work of evolutionary psychologist Steve Stewart-Williams and a much-cited 1987 study in which preschoolers had to cooperate to operate a toy viewfinder. The study found preschool boys and girls co-operated equally well on a shared task, but got there differently, with girls using verbal skills, and boys working it out physically. But Coulson says sex differences don’t mean parents of boys should anticipate or excuse violence: “Just because something is normal and natural, if you want to take an evolutionary psychology point of view, that doesn’t mean that it’s good, healthy, or to be encouraged.” Related Article Parenting Pints, ponytails and papas: The latest dad trend is all about daughters That’s the message in some memes depicting violence as inevitable or labelling it “typical boy behaviour”. In one viral TikTok, creator Anna Saccone calls herself a “toxic boy mum” expressing favouritism toward her male child explaining, “he hits his sisters. He punches them. And I’m like ‘maybe he’s having a hard day’.” In his latest book, Boys, Coulson unpacks the importance of parents teaching and modelling healthy masculinity. “As parents, we have an obligation to socialise our kids. For boys, that means we need to teach them how to use their energy and their additional size and power in healthy pro-social ways.”



But when it comes to the viral content that implies an intimate or sexualised relationship between mother and son, Coulson labels it “disgusting”, explaining there’s a larger clickbait element at play. “Social media platforms push us towards edges and boundaries and create a belief that what is edgy and on the boundary is mainstream. But it’s not.” The reality is that many of us find community and belonging online. And many new parents are using AI and social media for parenting advice and reassurance, leaving us vulnerable to increasingly provocative clickbait – the more extreme, absurd or infuriating, the more likely we are to see it. Orlando also points out that new parents can be particularly vulnerable to content that plays on parental guilt or the idea we’re not doing enough. “It’s what social media does best, and it’s really doing a disservice to parents.”



As for me, in a few months, I’ll become the mum of two boys, something I couldn’t be more excited about. Being a #BoyMum? I think I’ll leave that in the algorithm where it belongs. World.title: I discovered an overlooked part of Bali most visitors dream of
World.content:
InspirationBali I discovered an overlooked part of Bali most visitors dream of Nina Karnikowski August 3, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Two weeks before leaving for Ubud, I was already hyperventilating about Bali’s crowds. As someone who spends much of their life chasing quietude, just the thought of the over-development and the Instagrammable chaos made me twitch. Cottages at Kul Kul Farm. Nina Karnikowski So when a friend told me about Sibang – describing it as Ubud’s calmer cousin and the way it might have been 30 years ago – I was in. Now, waiting for said friend on a dirt road corner with just an ancient temple to my left and jungle to my right, I’m glad I’ve come. That Sibang (which actually encompasses two villages, Sibang Kaja and Sibang Gede) has stayed under the radar is no accident. “Locals have told us about a curse that was placed on the village many years ago, by an angry giant who threatened that it would one day be swallowed by ants,” my friend says. “It’s said the villagers fled because of this, and the jungle took over.” The story lingered for decades, leaving Sibang quiet and largely overlooked – until Canadian John Hardy arrived to build Green School Bali.



Green School’s bamboo campus, which offers eco-focused education to about 500 local and international students from kindergarten to year 12, put the village on the map when it opened in 2008. My friend, who’s living in Sibang, so her son can attend the school, walks me down the street flanking the campus. Aside from local homes and a couple of sleepy cafes, a sustainability-focused concept store named Muka, and a slick year-old villa stay called Mahajiva, there is, happily, not much here. 



Each April, Kul Kul runs a 10-day bamboo-building course, teaching about a material that restores land, grows rapidly, and sequesters carbon. Student-built curving structures, five of which are newly open to guests, are dotted between beds of lettuce, tomato, chilli and eggplant. Much of this produce lands on plates at Taani, Kul Kul’s new restaurant where I slurp the best soto (a warming turmeric-spiced soup) I’ve ever had in Indonesia. Inside a cottage at Kul Kul Farm. Next afternoon I walk to Astungkara Way, a regenerative rice-farming collective. Twenty minutes from Kul Kul Farm, the road dissolves into paddies alive with birdsong and the loamy scent of turned earth. Here, travellers learn how rice is grown the natural way. This means ducks instead of pesticides, compost instead of chemicals, and respect for the Subak system, a co-operative irrigation network that has sustained Bali’s farmers for centuries. “Look around,” says manager Oka Dewanti, spreading her arms wide to the rice paddies rolling out around us. “This is what Ubud or Canggu was 30 years ago.” She speaks of the heartbreak of watching development swallow farmland, the urgency of bringing youth back to agriculture, and how travellers can support the kind of Bali they want to see. To that end, alongside hands-on farming courses, Astungkara Way leads multi-day walking journeys that begin in the thick of traffic and development, and slowly carry travellers back to the Bali that once was. Strolling back to Kul Kul in the indigo evening light, past boys fishing in irrigation canals and women carrying baskets of offerings towards local temples, I worry about what Sibang might lose as more travellers arrive. Change is already gathering at its edges. But if places like Kul Kul Farm and Astungkara Way set the tone for what’s to come, maybe this village has a fighting chance to remain the kind of Bali travellers dream about, rather than the kind we flee.

World.title: Lockdowns are looming for Perth’s roaming cats. Here’s what you need to know
World.content:
NationalWALocal government Lockdowns are looming for Perth’s roaming cats. Here’s what you need to know Hannah Murphy August 3, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

West Australian councils could soon get the green light to force roaming cats indoors — but right now, a pet’s freedom depends entirely on which council it lives in. Local Government Minister Hannah Beazley announced plans to change the law to allow local councils to introduce cat containment laws in February. WA’s cats could soon be forced to stay on their own properties. Nick Moir Under the current law, councils need to get permission from a parliamentary committee to introduce changes to their local regulations. More than 20 councils have tried to make their own laws about keeping cats inside in the past, but only three have been successful - all in regional WA.



As a result, the cat laws in each local government differ greatly. Ahead of the planned law change, we asked every Perth metropolitan council what their state of play is when it comes to outdoor cats. Here’s what they told us: The Town of Claremont was the only local council who refused to comment on their current cat laws, and whether it had ever tried to get them changed previously.



Councils said cats were currently banned from upwards of 300 Perth reserves, parks and protected bushland area across the metropolitan area. Nearly all councils have limits on the number of cats people can own, and a select few have trapping programs conducted by rangers for “nuisance” cats. The changes to the 2011 Cat Act are only partway through the parliamentary process, but under its powers, local councils could order owners to: restrict cats to their owners’ premises;

prohibit cats from all public areas;

place conditions on when a cat may be permitted in a public area;

introduce cat curfews; and

require cats to be under the effective control of their owners or contained if leaving their owners’ property. However, Cat Haven chief executive Roz Robinson said it would be interesting to see how any changes would actually worked in practice. “It is interesting times with the review of the cat act coming up and it is interesting to note that whilst many councils are talking about cat containment being part of the cat laws, so many local governments do not enforce the current act,” she said.



“For example, I have it in writing from one western suburbs’ council, when faced with an enquiry from one of their residences about a stray cat, they simply refer them onto us.” Roz Robinson is the chief executive officer of Perth’s Cat Haven. Robinson said the not-for-profit organisation was extremely supportive of cat containment laws, saying it not only improves cat welfare but would ease pressure on the service. “With over 50 per cent of our intake coming in as strays, if we had proper containment laws, it would result in a reduction in these numbers,” she said. However, Robinson also argued any change with the Cat Act needed to focus heavily on the benefits of de-sexing household cats.



“Over 80 per cent of these strays – most friendly re-homable cats – are un-desexed. Un-desexed cats wander – they become strays in their need to mate. “You don’t have to be a mathematician to work out cats are prolific breeders and what numbers would look like without de-sexing. Related Article Exclusive

Biodiversity The staggering death toll of roaming pet cats finally revealed “For years we have been trying to de-sex our way out of the cat problem, but with little appetite from others to assist, we are literally fighting a losing battle.” She said there had to be continual state government funding towards spaying cats, as well as supporting the Cat Haven to deal with stray animals. Currently, she said the government provides just less than two per cent of the charity’s operating costs.



“What changes do we see after the review? It really depends if all stakeholders are serious about improving cat welfare or is it just another review being ticked off,” Robinson said. “Our intake numbers are increasing annually – 8 per cent while the population is only growing two per cent – our site is not fit for purpose, and can only be described as dilapidated. There is no funding forthcoming to improve the site. “We are an open admission shelter, we never say no to any cat and truly believe every cat does matter and want to give them all a second chance. But something has to give.”

World.title: Easy ways to eat more fibre every day without even trying
World.content:
Tips & adviceDietitian’s guide Easy ways to eat more fibre every day without even trying Remember these simple tips and ingredients when grocery shopping and meal-prepping and boost your dietary fibre intake without overthinking it. Susie Burrell August 3, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Health trends may come and go faster than you can say “TikTok made me do it”, but current darling, dietary fibre, is the real deal. From a renewed focus on supporting digestive health and immune function with gut health superfoods, to fibremaxxing, there is plenty of noise that all comes back to one simple concept: eat more fibre. Here are some easy ways to do that every day without even trying. Use multgrain bread for your sandwiches like Neil Perry’s tuna number. William Meppem Upgrade your carbs Whether it’s cereal for breakfast, or a sandwich or wrap for lunch, the key to optimising your daily intake of dietary fibre is to ensure your daily staples have a wholegrain or wholemeal base. Often, we find ourselves picking up foods on the go, and in most cases, the carbs on offer are white, and as such not offering nearly as much fibre as we need. Bread and wraps



Swap white, sourdough, or plain wraps for high-fibre wholemeal, multigrain, rye, or seed-packed options. As a reference, your daily bread or wraps should be adding at least 3-5g of dietary fibre per serve and while sourdough may sound healthier, generally the options at cafes and bakeries are made with white flour. The best recipes from Australia's leading chefs straight to your inbox. Sign up Breakfast staples Choose multigrain or high-bran cereals over refined varieties, and toss oats or bran straight into smoothies. When checking breakfast cereal or granola packets, keep in mind that the higher percentage of wholegrains the breakfast cereal offers, the higher the natural dietary fibre content will be. Natural sources of dietary fibre from wholegrains, seeds, fruits and nuts are better options nutritionally than more processed dietary fibre like chicory root and insulin which are often added to bars, cereals and breads to increase the fibre content. Opt for brown rice over white, like in Katrina Meynink’s chickpea, brown rice and greens salad. Katrina Meynink



Pasta and rice There is a growing range of wholemeal, wholegrain and legume pasta options which are all significantly higher in fibre than regular white pasta. In the case of rice, seek out brown or black varieties where possible, or one of the growing ranges of mixed grain and rice quick-cook options that can offer as much as 5-8g of dietary fibre per serve, compared to less than 1g for regular white rice. Can you guess the hidden veg in Jill Dupleix’s spaghetti bolognese? Sneak vegies into every meal With fewer than one in 10 Aussies getting the recommended five serves of vegetables a day, and even less the 7-10 serves to support the goal of optimal health and longevity, there are plenty of reasons including boosting our intake of dietary fibre that come from increasing veggie intake across all of our meals.



Grate and blend Adding a mix of grated zucchini and carrots, or spinach or silverbeet, into scrambled eggs, pasta sauce bases like bolognese, porridge, or smoothies not only significantly increases nutrient intake, but fibre intake as well. Frozen spinach and kale can also be cost-effective options that slip easily into a number of meals without negatively impacting the flavour. Keep the skins on Whether you are mashing vegetables, adding them to smoothies or grating them into dishes, you get extra dietary fibre from vegetables when you leave the skin on. The same goes for fruits, and if you are especially keen, the skins on nutrient-packed kiwifruit and bananas are edible, too. Related Article Canned, pouched and fresh: A dietitian’s guide to the best (and worst) supermarket chicken soups



Know the easy add-ins Budget-friendly and fibre-rich frozen peas can be added to a wide range of mixed dishes including pasta, risotto and stir-fries. Baby cucumbers and carrots are an easy side to enjoy with your favourite sandwich or wrap, while a starter of pre-made vegetable-rich soups add extra nutrients and dietary fibre to any main meal. Make your own baked beans, like Adam Liaw’s, and get a big fibre boose. William Meppem Learn to love legumes If there is one food Aussies should be eating more of, if only for the cost-effective nature of such a nutrient-rich food, it is legumes. There are so many varieties that can easily be worked into many meals, whilst adding loads of protein and dietary fibre.



Swap in with mince Whether you are making spaghetti bolognese, chilli con carne or a sang choy bao, throw in a can of your favourite beans to make any amount of mince go a lot further. Embrace baked beans Ever-versatile baked beans can be added to any hot breakfast, enjoyed with crackers or even as a light meal, adding a massive 6-8 grams of dietary fibre per serve. If you prefer lower sugar options, it is also easy to make your own using a cannellini or white beans. Eat more edamame



Soy beans are especially nutrient rich, and an easy addition to all of your favourite Asian dishes whether they are enjoyed as a side dish with sushi, added to salads or even as a dried, protein-packed snack. Sprinkle chia seeds and nuts onto your cereal. iStock Sprinkle in seeds and nuts Not only are seeds and nuts extremely nutrient rich — offering nutrients including zinc, selenium, magnesium and plant-based omega-3s — but they are also rich in dietary fibre. Breakfast boosters



Stir a tablespoon of chia, flaxseed or pepitas into any mix of cereal, oats, yoghurt or smoothies for a protein, fibre and good fat hit. Or opt for one of the growing ranges of breakfast toppers or nut spreads which offer a mix of nuts and seeds, and as such a mix of nutrients. Related Article Sprinkle these tiny seeds on just about anything for a mighty nutrition punch Your favourite salads A little crunch goes a long way in a salad, and a few roasted nuts or a sprinkle of seeds adds texture and flavour to any salad. Even better, try roasting your favourite nuts or seeds with a little honey or maple syrup for an even tastier salad topper. A go-to snack

World.title: People think my suburb is just the shopping centre. For better or worse, we do orbit it
World.content:
NationalQueenslandLife in the ’burbs Opinion People think my suburb is just the shopping centre. For better or worse, we do orbit it Chris Burke Contributor August 3, 2026 — 5:00am

August 3, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Before I moved here, I thought “Carindale” was the shopping centre. These days, I know it as a family-friendly suburb with more buses than you can count, and a distinct lack of local coffee shops. In my defence, the shopping centre called Carindale existed before the suburb did (opening in 1979). To this day, the mall, now Westfield Carindale, still has an indelible impact on the time and space of this place. It’s a black hole, and we orbit for better or worse. I’ve seen Christopher Nolan’s Interstellar, so I know that when you get close to a black hole, time slows down. It can even appear to stop. That rings true for Carindale. For much of the past decade, the suburb has felt stuck. When we moved here over a decade ago, Carindale seemed full of possibility. The Greendale Way shopping centre development is local folklore and still shared by real estate agents as “the next big thing” since the planning application was first approved nearly 20 years ago. Some are eager for an alternative to the Westfield whirling dervish, while others wonder why anyone would develop anything so close to a black hole.



That appears to be the recurring theme, and likely the reason for our lack of flat whites that don’t involve a hunt for a Westfield parking space. As Westfield continues to expand, it consumes the attention, investment and daylight, while other opportunities struggle to escape its shadow. The Eastern Busway was coming. Now the Metro. And we’re still waiting for that bus. As Westfield continues to expand, it consumes the attention, investment and daylight, while other opportunities struggle to escape its shadow. The decrepit aged care building on Creek Road was demolished to make way for a new retirement village. For now, we’re just watching the grass grow at the site. Then there was the proposed Taco Bell drive-through, where progress remains firmly at naught.



While the suburb feels stuck, our lives here have been anything but. My adulthood started here. It is where we brought our children home from hospital, and where we have built our family life. My wife and I bought our first home in Carindale because of the location: it was close to the Gateway and not too far from the city. We had lived in Carina for a time, but it felt older, with timber weatherboard cottages belonging to another era. Carindale’s larger blocks and brick-and-tile houses felt more practical for the family life we imagined for ourselves. In the early 2000s, teenage boys in adidas tracksuits congregated around the Carindale bus interchange. That era has long passed, but the black hole still has its pull. Those teenage boys are now adults taking their own children to Rhyme Time at Carindale Library.



It’s a neighbourhood built for children. There are parks, walking and cycling tracks and, of course, the flying disc golf course at Cadogan Street Park. Kids play in the street, there are plenty of trees to climb, and the Home Ice Cream truck rings its bell every second Sunday afternoon. Carindale is full of green space. The prolific gum trees mean we routinely see koalas on the drive home from school. Within walking distance from our front door to the south are places that could be mistaken for Springbrook National Park rainforest. And to the north there’s koala and swamp wallaby habitat. The shopping centre may dominate the landscape but Carindale is also full of green space. Markus Ravik It really is a place of opposites. On a map, Carindale is split down the middle by Bulimba Creek. This is contrasted by our eastern border and the constant hum of the Gateway Motorway, occasionally pierced by the sound of rifles from the Belmont shooting range.



There are giant mansions overlooking the golf course, alongside small townhouses and tired older homes. We’ve noticed recently that the knockdown-rebuild revolution has certainly started. Related Article Opinion

Life in the ’burbs My suburb’s most popular residents have fluffy ears and, like me, they love an elevated position Stephanie Felesina Contributor Carindale did not exist as a suburb until 1980. The original housing estate, developed during the 1970s, was part of Belmont. The former cow paddocks around the northern end of Meadowlands Road were developed by builders such as G.J. Gardner Homes. In the 1990s came the Pacific Golf Course and the large brick homes surrounding it. Many of the residents who bought during those early decades are now empty nesters (or trying to be), while new families competing to find their way in are struggling with a median house price of a bonkers $1.8 million. The Mansfield school catchments have a noticeable impact on the southern side of the suburb, pushing property prices ever higher.



Carindale is also a convenient transport boundary of sorts. It feels like the final point in Brisbane’s geographical middle-east, where multiple bus routes begin and end. Once you cross the Gateway, everything becomes either “too far” or “bayside”. The trade-off is traffic. We are boxed in by the Gateway Motorway and Creek Road, all swirling around the Westfield black hole. The rat runs are well established, with a very clear backstreet peak hour at 4pm on the dot. Recent signals suggest Carindale may finally be about to come off pause. Brisbane City Council is (again) exploring an Eastern Metro route from the CBD to Capalaba. The Greendale Way site has changed hands, renewing (yet again) this never-ending urban legend, and proposed planning changes around Westfield could allow buildings of up to 30 storeys. For better or worse, perhaps Carindale is on the cusp of launching. Whether these projects can escape the gravitational pull of the black hole remains to be seen. In the meantime, we’re happy spotting koalas. But I’d still just like a flat white, please.

World.title: Thousands of NSW children are being abused. Police say it has become an epidemic
World.content:
Exclusive NationalNSWChild abuse Thousands of NSW children are being abused. Police say it has become an epidemic Riley Walter August 3, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Warning: Graphic content More than 300 incidents involving children, including serious sexual and physical assaults, are reported to authorities weekly, as police warn laws designed to protect children are inadvertently shielding offenders. In the past 12 months, almost 16,000 reports were made to the state’s Joint Referral Unit, a multi-agency triage centre that assesses child protection reports, while online offending involving children has also skyrocketed in what senior police say has become an epidemic. Detectives receive on average 10 to 15 reports each weekend of child abuse. Matt Willis “This is thousands and thousands and thousands of children who are being abused,” NSW Police Assistant Commissioner Scott Cook told this masthead.



Cook, who oversees NSW Police’s child abuse and sex crimes squads, said detectives receive on average 10 to 15 reports each weekend of child abuse, ranging from sexual assault to physical assaults “bordering on death”, most of which is offending occurring within families. “Child exploitation and neglect and child abuse occurs, quite often, in the family home. It quite often involves a relative, a person in power,” Cook said. NSW Police Assistant Commissioner Scott Cook. James Brickwood While in-person offending has remained steady over several years, there had been an “explosion” of online child abuse in NSW and across the country, Cook said. The number of reports made to the Australian Centre to Counter Child Exploitation, which is led by the Australian Federal Police and refers matters to state police forces for investigation, is expected to exceed 100,000 this year.



“That is an epidemic of online child abuse,” Cook said. “The number of victims that are now being identified is enormous. Online exploitation is enormous.” Cook said highlighting the levels of child abuse across the state – a topic senior police rarely broach publicly – was crucial ahead of a concerted push to raise awareness of the issue during National Child Protection Week in early September. “It’s important for the prevention of this occurring, to have people aware of what’s going on – whether that’s child grooming, inappropriate touching, whether that’s inappropriate comments and conduct, bystanders need to call this stuff out. We all need to call this stuff out before it escalates, before a child becomes a victim,” Cook said. Talking publicly about what child abuse has long been viewed as a taboo issue, and overcoming that could help police and members of the public detect and prevent offending, he said.



Related Article Exclusive

Crime Revealed: Accused Sydney day care paedophile who ‘abused more than 150 children’ Raising awareness about the levels of abuse is made difficult by laws protecting the identities of child abuse victims in NSW that often prevent police and media outlets from exposing predators. “Non-publication laws relating to the protection of young victims and witnesses are really important, and I don’t want to diminish that or understate that, but an unintended consequence of how we do that, is that this crime type, these abhorrent offences against children, often doesn’t get the attention it should,” Cook said. “In terms of the law, really, I don’t know that any jurisdiction has struck the right balance between protecting a child and inadvertently protecting an offender at the same time. The offenders shouldn’t have protection. They should be unmasked.” Recent cases, including that of Sydney daycare worker Hamish Tait, highlighted the challenges in exposing alleged abusers facing both police and media outlets.



Tait’s identity and the scale of his alleged offending was revealed after a year-long fight by the Herald to lift a suppression order prohibiting his identification. Accused daycare paedophile Hamish Tait’s alleged offending was revealed after the Herald fought a year-long suppression order over his identity. “I don’t think community or people want to confront that this type of offending even occurs,” Cook said. “That puts us in a difficult position to even talk about this publicly. We risk breaching the law, and we risk alienating communities and people because of the subject matter, but when you drill this down, it’s all about children. It’s about their safety, and about their protection.” So voluminous is their workload, both the child abuse and sex crimes squads’ resources are constantly bolstered by detectives from other areas.



In some instances, detectives seize electronic devices containing hundreds of thousands of images of children. In the past year, child abuse squad detectives charged more than 550 people across NSW with 3349 separate offences against children, including almost 900 charges of sexual assault, more than 330 of assault, and almost 1200 of touching, including indecent assault. “The child abuse squad and the sex crimes squad are under immense pressure due to the sheer volume of the level of crime,” Cook said. eSafety Commissioner Julie Inman Grant told this masthead the online regulator received more than 18,000 reports of illegal and restricted content allegedly involving child abuse material in the past financial year, representing a 17 per cent increase compared with the previous year; the number of reports increased 58 per cent the year before. “Child sexual abuse and exploitation is an abhorrent crime that causes profound and lifelong harm to victims and survivors,” Inman Grant said.



Child abuse squad detectives are expected in the coming months to charge notorious Queensland paedophile Ashley Paul Griffith with almost 200 offences related to the time the former childcare worker spent working in NSW. Queensland Attorney-General Deb Frecklington in June confirmed the process to extradite Griffith was in its final stages. Dozens of NSW children have been identified among Griffith’s further alleged victims. Notorious paedophile Ashley Paul Griffith will be extradited to NSW to face almost 200 charges. Nine “He needs to face the allegations that are to be put on behalf of the victims in NSW. That’s why he needs to come back,” Cook said. The assistant commissioner said combatting child abuse would remain a top priority for authorities, but police could not arrest their way out of the growing issue.



“Every police force in Australia is committed to this, and every police force in Australia works on this,” Cook said. “But it is an epidemic, and we shouldn’t pretend that it’s not.” Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732). Anyone affected by sexual, domestic or family violence can also access 24/7, free and confidential trauma-specialist counselling through Full Stop Australia (1800 385 578). World.title: Not many significant monuments let people climb them. This is a corker
World.content:
InspirationIndia Not many significant monuments let people climb them. This is a corker Brian Johnston August 3, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

I don’t rank the squish of pigeon poop beneath my shoeless feet as an agreeable travel experience. Nor is squeezing up a staircase in a space so tight I have to engage in sweaty tangos with those descending. The cause is worth it, though. What traveller can resist a commanding view, or the lure of the unusual? Not me, anyway. So when I see a battered sign that says I can ascend one of the minarets of Delhi’s Jama Masjid, or Friday Mosque, I don’t let pesky pigeons put me off. Jama Masjid in Delhi is framed by its two minarets. iStock In mosques, only a muezzin climbs the minaret to proclaim the call to prayer and even then, not often in this modern age when the mosque relies on loudspeakers. This is something almost unique, and Friday Mosque couldn’t be a better mosque to do it in. Not many places let you clamber onto the roofs of significant monuments either, and this monument, completed in 1656 under Shah Jahan at the peak of the Mughal Empire, is a corker. One of India’s largest and most important mosques, it fuses Persian and Hindu architectural influences and houses relics of the prophet Muhammad.



I pick my way past a sea of temporarily abandoned shoes at its ornamental gateway and enter a vast courtyard, in which, at festival times, 25,000 people assemble to pray. Locals sit on patterned Kashmir carpets under its colonnades, cracking peanuts and gazing towards the Red Fort. 



Just being elevated to roof level provides a different take on this mosque. Three white domes trimmed with black stripes bulge like tethered hot-air balloons. I have to tip back my neck to admire the minarets, which seem to lean against Delhi’s heavy grey skies. I tiptoe over the pigeon poop and into the minaret’s narrow doorway. Corkscrewing steps have a rough red surface like an old hide. Walls are behind-the-scenes rough. There’s no longer any space for handrails. The entrance to the mosque, which was built by the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan between 1644 and 1656. iStock About halfway up in the sweltering humidity, as I push against people coming down in ways that are far too intimate, I begin to think this is a mistake, but plod on. The staircase emerges onto a narrow platform that has barely a toehold. A sign in several scripts I can’t decipher appears to be a warning. Certainly, if anyone stepped incautiously backwards, they would fall down the spiral staircase like a stunt actor. We are, though, protected from falling outwards by the pavilion’s scalloped arches and metal screens.



Related Article India Ten things I learnt on my first visit to India From 40 metres up, Friday Mosque is laid out like an architect’s plan. Vertigo sufferers won’t be happy. The flocks of pigeons now swoop below. Beyond is the Red Fort in one direction and the jumble of Old Delhi in the other. Old Delhi’s crush and crowd – porters hauling boxes and scrums of cycle-rickshaws that are so alarming at street level – seem almost balletic from this height. There’s no escaping the ceaseless splutter of motorbikes and honking of horns, however. They seem to mimic my heart, set thumping by the climb and height and thrill of the view. THE DETAILS Fly

Malaysia Airlines flies to Delhi via Kuala Lumpur. See malaysiaairlines.com

Jama Masjid is open to non-Muslim visitors daily from 8am to sunset. Arms and legs must be covered and shoes removed. Entry INR400 ($6), minaret ascent INR100. See delhitourism.gov.in More
