World.title: Five strength training exercises you need to improve your posture
World.content:
LifestyleHealth & wellnessHealth Five strength training exercises you need to improve your posture Caroline Idiens August 3, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

One of the most common questions I get from clients as a personal trainer is: “What can I do to improve my posture?” It’s a concern I hear repeatedly: people noticing that their shoulders are rounding forwards, they have pain in their necks or lower back, or both, their head is drifting towards their screen, or they simply don’t feel as tall and upright as they once did. In our increasingly digital world, where many of us spend hours each day looking down at devices or sitting for prolonged periods, it’s easy to blame the rise of “tech neck” and rounded shoulders entirely on modern life. It’s easy to blame the rise of “tech neck” and rounded shoulders entirely on modern life. iStock But the story is more complicated than that. While our daily habits certainly play a role, one of the biggest reasons our posture changes as we get older is that we gradually lose the muscle strength needed to support our spine and hold ourselves upright. As we age, muscle mass declines, bones become less dense, spinal discs lose height and connective tissues become stiffer. The result can be familiar: rounded shoulders, a more curved upper back, a forward head position and a tendency to stoop as we walk.



The good news is that this isn’t simply an unavoidable consequence of getting older. Posture is not just about age, it is also about strength. Building the muscles that support your body, will help you stand taller, move more easily in daily life and reduce the risk of injuries due to misalignment. Why does our posture change as we get older? Related Article Ageing Muscle loss is more common than diabetes in old age. Here’s how to avoid it From around the age of 30, we begin to gradually lose muscle mass, a process known as sarcopenia. Unless we actively work to maintain it, this loss can accelerate as we get older. The muscles of the upper back, shoulders, spine and core all play an important role in keeping us upright, acting almost like a natural support system for the skeleton. With poor posture, the muscles at the front of the chest, particularly the pectoral muscles, can become tight and less flexible. At the same time, the muscles of the upper back that help pull the shoulders back and stabilise the shoulder blades can become weaker and less active.



And this is when problems occur and we see rounded shoulders, increased curvature through the upper back and a tendency to lean forwards as we walk. Does poor posture cause back pain? There isn’t one simple answer here. Yes, slouching and forward head posture will place uneven stress on spinal joints, overwork muscles, and compress discs. It is this repetitive mechanical strain that causes stiffness, muscle fatigue and tension that can eventually lead to chronic discomfort. However, poor posture alone does not automatically cause back pain. Plenty of people have rounded shoulders or a less-than-perfect sitting position and experience no discomfort, while others with excellent posture can still develop back problems. It is staying in this position for long periods of time that can contribute to this pain – the spine requires movement to stay healthy. And this is where exercise comes in. A bent over row strengthens the upper back muscles that help pull the shoulders back and support the spine. Getty Images Why strength training is one of the best tools for posture



If there is one intervention backed by strong evidence, it is strength training. Related Article Exclusive

Wellbeing Still working at 80? The future is grim or thrilling, depending on who you ask A 2024 systematic review published in Sports Medicine Open, which analysed 23 studies, found that strengthening exercises led to significant improvements in posture, particularly in the upper back and neck, whereas stretching alone had little measurable effect. In other words, standing taller isn’t simply about remembering to pull your shoulders back and down; it is about building the strength to hold yourself there. Resistance training also has benefits far beyond posture. It helps preserve muscle mass, supports bone health, improves balance and helps maintain independence as we age.



The good news is that you don’t need hours in the gym. A small number of specific exercises, performed consistently, can target the muscles that help us maintain an upright posture. I incorporate the following five movements into all of my full-body workouts and try to do these three or four times per week. I do 10 reps of each and three sets. You can start with just bodyweight and build up to using dumbbells. I recommend anyone starting out to begin with a set of 2-kilogram dumbbells and increase the weights gradually. The last couple of reps should feel like a challenge. Five exercises to help improve your posture 1. Bent over row



Hinge forwards from the hips, keeping your back straight and your core engaged. Holding a dumbbell in each hand, draw the weights towards your lower ribs by squeezing your shoulder blades together. Pause briefly at the top before slowly lowering the weights under control. Why it works: This strengthens the upper back muscles that help pull the shoulders back and support the spine. 2. Prone ‘T’ raise Lie face down with your gaze towards the floor. Keeping your body relaxed, lift your arms slightly away from the mat to form a “T” shape, squeezing the muscles between your shoulder blades before slowly lowering. Start with bodyweight only and progress to holding light weights as you become stronger.



Why it works: This targets the smaller stabilising muscles around the shoulder blades that are often weakened by prolonged sitting and rounded posture. 3. Reverse fly Hinge forwards at the hips and raise your arms out to the side, keeping a soft bend in your elbows. Start with light weights, pause briefly at the top of the movement and gently lower with control. Avoid using momentum – the movement should come from the muscles of your upper back. Why it works: This strengthens the rear shoulders and upper back, helping to counter the forward-rounded position many of us adopt.



4. Single-arm row Hold a weight in one hand and rest your opposite hand on your knee or a chair for support. Using the full range of movement, draw the weight back towards your hip while keeping your elbow close to your body. Slowly lower before repeating on the other side. Why it works: Working one side at a time challenges the upper back while also encouraging the core muscles to stabilise the spine. 5. Weighted dead bug Lie on your back and, with or without weights, slowly extend the opposite arm and opposite leg away from your body. Keep your lower back gently pressed down throughout the movement and return slowly to the starting position before changing sides.



Why it works: A strong core is essential for supporting the spine. This exercise teaches the deep abdominal muscles to stabilise the body while the limbs move. To conclude Related Article Health ‘Strength training for your brain’: This skill may keep you sharp as you age Getting older does not mean we have to accept becoming smaller, weaker or more stooped. While we cannot stop the natural changes that come with ageing, we can influence how our bodies adapt. Building strength helps us maintain the muscles that support our spine, protect our bones and allow us to move with confidence in all of our everyday activities.



Good posture is not about standing rigidly or trying to hold yourself perfectly all day. It is about having a body strong enough to support you, so you can continue to stand tall, whatever your age. World.title: I was excited to be a ‘boy mum’. Then I picked up my phone
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsParenting Opinion I was excited to be a ‘boy mum’. Then I picked up my phone Hannah Vanderheide Contributor August 3, 2026 — 5:00am

August 3, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Just months away from becoming the mum of two boys, I’m excited for many things. A glass of champagne, naturally, but mostly watching the light of my life step into his new role as big brother and meeting this precious tiny person who will complete our family. My social media feed, however, seems intent on preparing me for something else. Being a “boy mum” is about more than just having sons. iStock Once the almighty algorithm learnt I was pregnant with a second boy, it unlocked a vault of something I wasn’t prepared for: “boy mum” content. It started with stereotypical portrayals of a boy mum v girl mum house, serene calm pit against utter chaos. But it quickly escalated to depictions of actual violence, like one reel set on an escalator contrasting a pristine “girl mum” with a despondent and noticeably injured “boy mum”, black eye and all.





Naturally some of it is satire, stoking outrage to maximise engagement. After all, the internet thrives on extremes and virality rewards exaggeration. But according to Dr Joanne Orlando, expert in digital wellbeing, and author of Generation Connected, this content can still have a negative impact on both parents and their kids. “I think it does put preconceived ideas about what your role as a parent should be, rather than just nurturing your beautiful baby.” In part, she believes the trend taps into growing anxiety about raising boys in the age of Andrew Tate’s “manosphere”. According to these corners of the internet, boys are either feral, violent agents of domestic destruction or the great love of your life. “The default message is that there’s something wrong with boys, and that we need to fix them,” she explains. “It’s really a damaging message.” Essentially, new mothers already carrying the enormous responsibility of raising a child are also being told that he’s a future problem to be fixed.



Orlando says it’s especially concerning for new mums who don’t have a lot of experience with raising boys. “I think they can go into this like, ‘What? I didn’t know I should be worried about having a son’.” I can relate. Before my second pregnancy, I had never thought of raising my son as participation in a particular maternal subculture. He was just my beautiful child. “Boy mum” content twists the mother-son bond to get more interactions. iStock Dr Justin Coulson, co-host of Channel Nine’s Parental Guidance and founder of Happy Families, says some sex differences highlighted in these reels are a biological reality.



“Boys use their bodies more, girls use their words more,” he explains, citing the work of evolutionary psychologist Steve Stewart-Williams and a much-cited 1987 study in which preschoolers had to cooperate to operate a toy viewfinder. The study found preschool boys and girls co-operated equally well on a shared task, but got there differently, with girls using verbal skills, and boys working it out physically. But Coulson says sex differences don’t mean parents of boys should anticipate or excuse violence: “Just because something is normal and natural, if you want to take an evolutionary psychology point of view, that doesn’t mean that it’s good, healthy, or to be encouraged.” Related Article Parenting Pints, ponytails and papas: The latest dad trend is all about daughters That’s the message in some memes depicting violence as inevitable or labelling it “typical boy behaviour”. In one viral TikTok, creator Anna Saccone calls herself a “toxic boy mum” expressing favouritism toward her male child explaining, “he hits his sisters. He punches them. And I’m like ‘maybe he’s having a hard day’.” In his latest book, Boys, Coulson unpacks the importance of parents teaching and modelling healthy masculinity. “As parents, we have an obligation to socialise our kids. For boys, that means we need to teach them how to use their energy and their additional size and power in healthy pro-social ways.”



But when it comes to the viral content that implies an intimate or sexualised relationship between mother and son, Coulson labels it “disgusting”, explaining there’s a larger clickbait element at play. “Social media platforms push us towards edges and boundaries and create a belief that what is edgy and on the boundary is mainstream. But it’s not.” The reality is that many of us find community and belonging online. And many new parents are using AI and social media for parenting advice and reassurance, leaving us vulnerable to increasingly provocative clickbait – the more extreme, absurd or infuriating, the more likely we are to see it. Orlando also points out that new parents can be particularly vulnerable to content that plays on parental guilt or the idea we’re not doing enough. “It’s what social media does best, and it’s really doing a disservice to parents.”



As for me, in a few months, I’ll become the mum of two boys, something I couldn’t be more excited about. Being a #BoyMum? I think I’ll leave that in the algorithm where it belongs. World.title: Power restoration gathers pace on Rota after Super Typhoon Bavi
World.content:
The US Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) says it has completed more than half of the requested temporary generator installations on Rota, as crews work to restore essential services following the devastation caused by Super Typhoon Bavi last month.

The USACE Temporary Power Team has been installing generators at critical facilities, including shelters, the Rota Health Center, telecommunications sites, water wells, police and fire stations, the judicial center, hotels housing emergency responders, a bottled water plant, an ice production facility and a diesel service station.

USACE said additional personnel and equipment had been pre-positioned before Bavi struck because crews were already deployed in the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands (CNMI) following Super Typhoon Sinlaku in April.

While Sinlaku caused extensive damage on Saipan and Tinian, Bavi knocked out Rota's power system.

The agency said a generator was also installed at Rota's power plant to power heaters drying out storm-soaked engines, helping speed the restoration of the island's electricity network.

USACE Recovery Field Office commander Lt Col Lamar Cantelou said restoring electricity remained the top priority.

"Restoring power is the critical first step in helping the people of Rota rebuild their lives after these devastating storms."

Cantelou added that each generator installed at key facilities moves the island closer to recovery.

Mission leader Major Blake Ritchey said restoring electricity to healthcare facilities was among the team's highest priorities.

"Bringing power to hospitals and health centers is always a priority on a temp power mission because it reduces the potential for loss of life and is a symbol to the communities devastated by the storm that they are not alone."

USACE said its crews have been averaging about two generator installations each day while working extended shifts.

Nearly 2000 people live on Rota, where officials said many residents were left without electricity and water after Bavi struck on 6 July, causing widespread damage to homes, vegetation and infrastructure.

President Donald Trump approved an emergency declaration for the CNMI on 3 July, allowing the Federal Emergency Management Agency and USACE to coordinate the federal disaster response.

World.title: Explainer: What is a data centre and why is everyone freaking out now?
World.content:
Explainer - Data centres have existed for decades, so what's the big deal now?

The politics of big data officially became part of New Zealand's election campaign last week, after the Green Party launched a policy calling for a one-year pause on new AI data centres.

It mirrors a moratorium imposed by New York state earlier in July, until the state government can finalise standards governing how massive data centres are built and run.

But before we ban them or welcome them, how did we even get here?

What is a data centre, anyway?

At its most basic level, a data centre is a large, cooled building that houses racks of servers and other IT hardware.

"You've got really compact computers in there that have air-conditioning units in them, obviously the chips for processing data and then you would have storage as well," technology writer Peter Griffin says.

The crucial bit is the air conditioning, he says - the intensity of the processing heats everything up. "That's the big battle in data, is keeping everything cool."

They're also incredibly loud places. "You have to put on ear muffs [inside] because of the collective roar of not only the fans in the servers, but the air-conditioning units all around those."

Some data centres are deliberately built in cooler locations, to limit the amount of artificial cooling that has to be done.

How long have they been around?

Despite the surge of debate and interest in data centres, they are not a new concept. Griffin says data centres have existed in some form here in New Zealand since the 1980s, with the advent of early forms of cloud computing (basically, storing files, data and other computing services on someone else's server and accessing them over a network or internet connection).

He says Telecom (now Spark) was among the first companies to set up its own data centres, followed by other large companies and services, including New Zealand Post, The Warehouse, and various government departments.

These 'on-premises' data centres are still being built - an all-of-government data centre that hosts the country's most sensitive public data opened at Whenuapai airbase last year.

But as demand for cloud-computing grew, third-party companies like Datacom built larger data centres - managing the infrastructure and leasing space to companies which needed it. "As a company, you might pay to put some racks of server hardware in someone's data centre, and you would run your applications," Griffin says. That could include billing systems, event ticketing - anything that requires sufficiently large processing power.

Most recently, the likes of Microsoft and Amazon Web Services (AWS) have been building or renting 'hyperscale' data centres, which provide cloud computing services to anyone who wants to pay for them. Griffin says there's a "latency" benefit from having these locally based data centres - previously, anyone in New Zealand using AWS or a similar service was accessing their data from servers hosted in Sydney or even further afield.

So if they've existed for decades, why is everyone freaking out now?

The crucial differences between any of these examples, and what is being opposed in New Zealand and globally, are scale and purpose.

The new data centres being proposed and constructed are AI data centres - to train and run proprietary AI models. Datagrid - the large-scale data centre that's been given permission to go ahead in Southland - is the first of these 'AI factories' to be constructed in New Zealand. "They're a different sort of data centre, very much more power-hungry, water-hungry," Griffin told RNZ Nights recently.

The difference in scale to what has been built to date is enormous. The Datagrid facility will use 280 megawatts of power, which will make it the country's second-biggest user of electricity behind Tīwai aluminium smelter. It also has consents to draw up to 600,000 litres of groundwater a day - similar to what a town the size of Kaikōura would use - though the company says it expects to mostly use rainwater.

Construction of the Datagrid centre in Makarewa is expected to start in the next month. Supplied / Datagrid

While processing is getting increasingly efficient, the rapid uptake of AI across business and society means its overall global energy use is growing.

Both the International Energy Agency and a United Nations research group recently published reports estimating that data centre energy use will double by 2030.

The other difference is purpose. Data centres in New Zealand have previously either been locally owned and run, or provided ongoing data-hosting and other services to local users. A data centre that exists purely to train an AI model doesn't do that.

"That will mainly serve an international audience," Griffin says. "It won't serve New Zealand companies and New Zealand consumers… The government has seen that as basically a digital export."

What's the backlash been?

Globally, opposition to the construction of AI data centres is heating up, and is especially strong in the US.

Data Center Watch - a research project run by AI company 10a Labs - reported that in the first three months of 2026 alone, local opposition blocked or delayed 75 projects worth US$130 billion in the states. Protesters there staged more than 140 demonstrations across 42 states earlier this month during a coordinated day of action.

Most of the opposition clusters around concerns about resource allocation and environmental effects. Energy use is a particular "bone of contention", Peter Griffin says. "These companies are so desperate to fast track development of these data centres that they're actually scooping up electricity and are competing with communities, and that's a really bad outcome."

Similarly, data centres have faced criticism over of the vast quantities of water needed for cooling. As well as the pressure this might place on supply, there have also been reports that data centres have made water supplies undrinkable. This is not because of the discharged cooling water from data centres - but because of contaminated run-off from construction and sediment build-up in water supplies disrupted by data centres' off-take.

Griffin believes the opposition in the US is particularly acute because of existing pressure on water resources, and communities' prior experiences with fracking and the environmental issues that created. The lower proportion of renewable energy available means many centres in the US are powered using gas - augmenting carbon emissions.

There have also been complaints about noise, the consenting or permitting process, and a lack of transparency from data centre companies.

Should New Zealanders be worried about this, too?

Griffin says the issues US communities have faced don't exist to the same extent in New Zealand - yet.

The most pressing issue is around the allocation and use of resources - particularly energy. "We've had years now of feeling the pinch, particularly in dry winters when the spot price of electricity goes up."

Datagrid has arranged a 140MW agreement with gentailers, but it's not clear how the company will generate its remaining energy requirements. "We need to be really clear if we're going to have these big data centres, these AI factories in New Zealand, that they're not going to compete with our existing industry," Griffin says. "How much water are they going to use? Will they use renewable energy? Are they doing a deal to ensure that they're not going to compete with others for that energy?"

At the moment there's no detail around any of that, or any particular rules requiring data centres to invest in their own generation, for instance.

Are there any upsides?

Yes, Griffin says, and one of them is the technology itself. "If we don't embrace it, we are going to be less competitive than other countries."

Invest New Zealand, an agency set up to attract foreign investment to New Zealand, "is targeting something like $25 to $35 billion in data centre investment in the next five years".

Southland's mayor Rob Scott says he got over his initial concerns due to the economic opportunity and jobs the construction of Datagrid's facility will create.

But once the centres are built, the financial benefits to New Zealand are "murky", Griffin says. The country might "clip the ticket" on the initial investment, but because the companies involved are mostly American or European, there's no guarantee that profits stay - or even get taxed - here.

The energy requirements of massive data centres may have an upside, though, with gentailers saying the long-term, high-volume contracts involved will give them greater certainty to commit to major new renewable projects.

There might also be benefits available to universities, research agencies and other organisations with major data processing and modelling requirements, Griffin suggests. "If you're building all of this high-capacity computing, can our own businesses and our researchers, our scientists, have access to some of it, even if it's two or three percent of it, so that we can have breakthroughs in science and climate change and health?"

Ok, so if there are some benefits, then what are the solutions?

The Greens are campaigning on a one-year moratorium on new data centres while the country figures the answers to some of these questions out.

Neither Labour nor National support that, but Prime Minister Christopher Luxon said last week that the country did need some "commonsense rules".

Australia announced last month it would set up an AI office, and Griffin says New Zealand should be collaborating with its neighbour on what sensible regulations could look like.

That could include 'closed loop' cooling, which recirculates water, treats it, and returns it; instead of the more common evaporative cooling where most of the water taken is lost during the cooling process. Some countries were also requiring data centres to only use grey water, rather than drawing from groundwater resources. Here, tech expert Dr Karaitiana Taiuru has suggested that seawater could also be used.

New Zealand could also mimic the Australian requirement for large-scale data centres to underwrite their own power supply, or require the energy used to be renewable, Griffin says.

"You can't just draw from the existing grid without adding capacity … and you have to pay the full share of grid connection cost - that can't just be carried on to existing customers."

Rather than putting off companies, having a clear framework and rules could provide the certainty they need to invest here, he says.

He believes New Zealand should learn from the cautionary tale of social media before unquestioningly embracing either AI, or the data centres that power it. "The utility of being on these platforms seems so beneficial to us that we didn't really see the downsides til it was too late, and we were let down by regulators and watchdogs - they didn't see what was happening either."

World.title: Live: Glasgow Commonwealth Games, closing ceremony
World.content:
All the medals have been handed out and the Glasgow Commonwealth Games draws to a close with the ceremony at OVO Hydro.

Traditionally, this has been a chance for athletes to let their hair down and party, after the tension of competition, but this has been anything but a traditional Games.

World.title: Commonwealth Games: Silver Ferns break 16-year gold-medal drought at Glasgow
World.content:
RNZ national

New Zealand have won their first Commonwealth Games gold medal in 16 years, after beating Jamaica 56-48 in Glasgow in a stunning show of resilience.

Victory was a huge statement from the Silver Ferns, against the backdrop of an incredibly difficult period for the sport in New Zealand.

The game plan was executed brilliantly by Silver Ferns, who managed to nullify the world-class Jamaican defenders for the second time at the Games.

They were playing in their first Commonwealth Games gold medal match since 2014, after beating England in their semi-final.

In a gruelling schedule, the Silver Ferns managed to win seven games in nine days.

They were reduced to 11 players, when defender Catherine Hall was ruled out of the Games, after rupturing the anterior cruciate ligament in her knee against Wales on Thursday.

Coach Dame Noeline Taurua stuck with the same starting seven that beat England in the semi-finals.

Despite the Silver Ferns barely going to the bench in the semi, the players showed no signs of fatigue and committed very few turnovers.

The first break of the game came when Jamaican shooter Romelda Aiken-George missed, and New Zealand snaffled the rebound and scored quickly.

Goal attack Georgia Heffernan brought out all her tools, including two off-the-post passes to herself, and continued to act as the perfect foil to strike shooter Grace Nweke.

The Silver Ferns looked more energised than Jamaica, who had knocked Australia out in the semi-finals 24 hours earlier, in a massive boilover.

Kelly Jackson and Grace Nweke (right) embrace. Jayne Russell / Photosport

New Zealand led by four, before Jamaican goal keep Shamera Sterling-Humphrey sparked up with her first intercept, which was converted just on the buzzer.

The Silver Ferns led by 16-13 after the first quarter in front of crowd that largely supported a Jamaican win.

Jamaica got within one early in the second quarter, before New Zealand broke back to take a three-goal lead again and maintained that margin into half time (28-25).

One change came after the break, when Kimiora Poi replaced Maddy Gordon at wing attack.

Jodi-Ann Ward intercepted a bounce pass and Jamaica levelled the score, which pleased the crowd at the Hydro.

Nweke copped a second offensive contact, but goal keep Kelly Jackson had two intercepts in quick succession to help New Zealand push out to a five-goal lead.

Poi's connection with Nweke built nicely across the quarter and the Silver Ferns led 41-36 heading into the final period

Silver Ferns crowned Commonwealth Games champions. www.photosport.nz

Gordon replaced Kate Heffernan at centre with nine minutes left, before the vice-captain returned for the last few minutes to replace Mila Reuelu-Buchanan.

The Silver Ferns were able to enjoy the final moments, knowing they had the game in the bag.

Jackson and Karin Burger were dogged again in the defensive circle, with wing defence Reuelu-Buchanan constantly nagging her opposite.

Until this tournament, Reuelu-Buchanan had only ever played in the centre or wing attack bib for New Zealand, but became a key part of the line-up.

Nweke was a tremendous target under the post and finished the game with 48 goals. Kate Heffernan again underlined her status as one of the best players in world netball.

Grace Nweke had a tight battle with defender Shamera Sterling-Humphrey. Jayne Russell / Photosport

The Silver Ferns last won Commonwealth Games gold at the 2010 Delhi Games.

The Glasgow result was remarkable, given the potential demise of the ANZ Premiership is playing out in the background, with no guarantees of an elite domestic competition next year.

The other storyline underpinning this campaign was that, when Taurua sat on the coaching bench for the Silver Ferns' opening match against Scotland, it was her first time in charge since October 2024.

Last September, Taurua was suspended due to concerns raised from players about the high performance environment, which dominated headlines for weeks.

Taurua was eventually re-instated, but only got her hands on the team three weeks before the start of the Commonwealth Games, when they came together for a camp.

Jackson told Sky Sport the gold medal would take a while to sink in.

"We've been through hell and back, but I think that's really galvanised this team, we came out this week and really showed what we're made of," she said.

"I think we were probably under-estimated by a lot of people, but man, it just feels so good. We've got so much pride in this dress and to give some positivity to the sport that's in a pretty tough place at the moment it's pretty cool."

Silver Ferns coach Dame Noeline Taurua. Simon Stacpoole / Photosport

Taurua said she didn't consider the gold medal a vindication.

"Not a vindication," she said. "When I came in being very professional about what my role is and my contribution to the team, it's sweet is what I would say..

"It's lovely to be able to put that performance out there, they were sublime."

The Silver Ferns last won a pinnacle event at the 2019 Netball World Cup, when Taurua was also in charge. Captain Burger is the only current Fern left from that campaign.

Burger, who moved to New Zealand from South Africa when she was 18, told Sky Sport the result was surreal.

"We've been through so much, but to be able to stand up there, knowing what we're capable of and actually showing the rest of the world is pretty awesome," she said.

Australia did not feature in the Commonwealth Games gold medal match for the first time. The Diamonds, who came in as reigning champions, won the bronze medal, after beating England 68-50.

World.title: 'We just can't handle any more': Queenstown congestion concerns keep building
World.content:
Locals say Queenstown tourism reputation at risk Morning Report Download MP3 3m

Some Queenstown residents and authorities say the town's roads are not coping as international arrivals hit a new high - more than two-thirds above pre-pandemic levels.

The Regional Tourism Organisation is calling for immediate changes to protect the town's reputation, while Queenstown's mayor is setting up an anti-traffic congestion taskforce.

Data from Queenstown Airport shows 247,820 international arrivals in the first six months of 2026 - nearly 100,000 more people than in the same period in 2019.

The number of domestic arrivals also rose, with an extra 14,000 people compared to the first six months of 2019, including locals taking trips away and then returning.

The town's permanent population has grown more than twice as fast as the rest of the country since 2018, topping 35,000 last year.

Destination Queenstown & Lake Wānaka Tourism chief executive Mat Woods said although there was enough physical room for visitors, transport had become a major problem at peak times.

"The last long weekend we had, Queenstown was gridlock - and no one comes on holiday to go to gridlock. As residents and visitors alike, that was really unpleasant. You definitely heard people unhappy about that," he said.

Last year a report to councillors warned the resort town could become the next Barcelona, as local sentiment towards tourism deteriorated.

Woods said the town's reputation would suffer if it stopped delivering a quality experience.

"We actually have to do something immediately, because I think we are seeing that point, with infrastructure, where the residential growth and visitation - we just can't handle any more," he said.

"I think we all have concerns that Queenstown is the real draw card for New Zealand tourism, and grows New Zealand tourism. And if we aren't delivering a great experience for the people that live here, as well as the people that visit, we actually do run the risk of killing the golden goose."

Residents told RNZ that hour-long traffic delays on an eight-kilometre stretch of Frankton Road - heading into central Queenstown - were not uncommon.

Callum Fisher said the town felt like a far cry from the place he first moved to 25 years ago.

"It's just exploded really. It's always been busy... but it seems worse than it probably ever was," he said.

"The town can't keep up - the hospital... the roads - there are numerous things you could look at which are undersize for the amount of people that are here."

Daniel Wren - who worked at a local holiday park - said he was among those in the town who relied on visitors for a job, but the summer rush was turning some daily errands into a logistical battle.

"I feel like the town's been outgrown by the number of people that are coming here. Even getting home - just simple things - are becoming quite a hassle. Getting to work, going to the supermarket - everything is so busy. The town is not really keeping up," he said.

Ben Hollins, who was visiting from Australia, said the volume of fellow tourists came as a surprise.

"It is a lot more busy than I thought it would be. Especially last night when we were coming back home... it was like 30 minutes just to get through the city. Walking around it feels within capacity, but the transport situation I think is a bit overloaded," he said.

However, another Australian visitor Natasha Jones said the popularity of the town was a positive for her - in part because it felt safe at night.

"I was quite surprised how many people are still wandering around when it's dark... I feel safer walking around," she said.

New taskforce to tackle traffic woes

On Friday, Queenstown Lakes District Mayor John Glover announced he would be setting up a mayoral taskforce to tackle traffic congestion, bringing together councils, government agencies, mana whenua and transport experts to find solutions over the next three to six months.

Modelling showed Queenstown's transport would fail "even if every currently identified intervention is delivered", he said.

"Continuing to plan within the existing framework is therefore not enough... we must act now, implement faster and think differently," he said.

"Our community expects us to show leadership rather than wait for someone to do something, and we are responding to that."

World.title: Auckland axe attacker quietly deported to China
World.content:
A man who launched a frenzied attack on guests at three Auckland restaurants has been deported.

Government briefings show how the man was allowed to leave New Zealand's specialist mental health clinic, a year after a judge ruled he should be detained there.

Fanrong Meng wielded a wood-chopping axe and metal pole when he attacked customers at neighbouring eateries in Albany in June 2023, three months after he arrived in Auckland.

The courts ruled the 25-year-old was insane at the time of the offending - suffering hallucinations and delusions - and was not criminally liable for his actions.

Three people were hospitalised, and one needed emergency surgery to his skull. The attacks only ended when his sixth victim managed to overpower him - despite being hit so hard his head hit the bowl of food he was eating. He managed to hold onto the axe and Meng until police arrived.

His victims and restaurant staff told RNZ how they had been left traumatised by the late-night rampage.

A psychiatric report in court said Meng had a lengthy history of mental illness, and had been previously diagnosed with obsessive compulsive disorder and schizophrenia in China.

His detention as a 'special patient' under mental health laws at the Mason Clinic initially prevented him from being deported.

In the 'no surprises' notes to ministers, released to RNZ, officials set out the steps needed to have him deported.

They show a Special Patient Review Panel decided to downgrade Meng's 'special patient' status in September 2024, paving the way for his deportation.

In February last year, government agencies met to discuss the case, officials noting that 'due to the number of unresolved issues, the individual's deportation will not be imminent.'

They included a health minister needing to sign off on Meng's new patient status, MFAT confirming that the treatment of people with mental illness in China met human rights standards and the logistics of holding him in custody after he left the clinic while awaiting deportation.

But after the agency meeting it took less than six weeks to deport him, and officials say he was met off the plane in China by health officials in March last year.

"Immigration Compliance worked on this complex case for 12 months with the Ministry of Health and other agencies," said officials in the final ministerial notes. "As arranged, the Chinese government health officials met the client on his arrival in Shanghai."

Under the judge's original ruling, Meng could have been detained for seven years in a secure psychiatric facility, half the length of the maximum sentence for the most serious charge he faced of wounding with intent to cause grievous bodily harm.

His lawyer Michael Kan said the young man should not be subject to a special patient order, so that he could return to China, live with his parents and receive treatment. https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/chinese/514610/albany-restaurant-axe-attack-fanrong-meng-to-be-detained-as-special-patient-in-mason-clinic

But the judge agreed with prosecutors that Meng posed a significant and ongoing risk to others.

'Degree of trust' in visa application

Meng, a carpenter assistant, reportedly said the cost of medication prompted him to stop taking anti-psychotics before moving to New Zealand.

He arrived in Auckland in March 2023 on an accredited employer visa, but lost his job only weeks before the June attack because his employer did not have enough work available.

He had been suffering from delusional beliefs about being attacked himself.

His victims and staff at the affected restaurants questioned how Meng came to be granted a three-year work visa, given his health condition.

RNZ asked Immigration New Zealand (INZ) what medical tests visa applicants underwent, and whether INZ assessors would have seen medicals documents from Meng's own doctors.

In a statement, INZ acting deputy chief operating officer Peter Elms said it empathised with Meng's victims.

"The case of Fanrong Meng has been deeply traumatic for everyone involved," he said. "As Mr Meng applied for a temporary work visa that was valid for more than 12 months, he was required to undergo an immigration medical examination and provide a chest X-ray as part of his visa application. Applicants in these circumstances cannot simply self-certify that they are healthy."

Medical examinations are completed by INZ-approved 'panel' physicians based in New Zealand and overseas.

"The immigration medical examination includes questions about an applicant's medical history, along with a physical examination and blood and urine tests," he said.

"Mr Meng underwent the required immigration medical examination in November 2022. Based on the information available through that process, INZ's Health Assessment Team assessed him as having an acceptable standard of health. The medical assessment did not identify any pre-existing psychiatric condition."

Elms said INZ medical assessors do not see applicants in person, instead reviewing information they receive. "This includes the assessment completed by panel physicians, as well as any specialist reports or test results provided with an application. INZ did not receive any medical documentation from Mr Meng's doctors in China."

Applicants were warned if they provide false or misleading health information they can face a visa decline or deportation.

"There is a degree of trust involved in the immigration system, and while not every piece of information supplied by every applicant can be independently verified, all applicants are required to declare that the information they provide is true, complete and correct.

"It is also important to note that psychiatric conditions can be difficult to identify through a general immigration medical examination. Where an applicant does not disclose a pre-existing psychiatric condition, a panel physician may have no basis to identify that condition through the standard assessment process.

INZ said requiring specialist psychiatric assessments for all visa applicants would add significant cost and administrative burden, as serious undisclosed psychiatric conditions would only occur in a 'very small proportion' of applications.

World.title: More laws rushed through Parliament under urgency than any term since 2008
World.content:
Andrew Geddis discusses government’s use of urgency Morning Report Download MP3 6m

The coalition government has passed more legislation in one go under urgency than any other Parliament since at least 2008, raising concerns that public scrutiny of proposed laws is diminishing.

Parliamentary Library data provided to RNZ showed 17.4 percent of all bills sent for Royal Assent in the first 940 days of this Parliament - to 2 July this year - passed through all stages of lawmaking all at once, skipping the select committee stage and its public feedback process.

This is part of an increasing trend over multiple parliaments. Over the same period, the Labour government passed 15.5 percent of bills in this way.

Former Labour Prime Minister and Attorney-General Sir Geoffrey Palmer said the coalition government's use of urgency wasn't about coping with large volumes of legislation.

He said it was more about "avoid[ing] the scrutiny of select committees" - something the government rejected.

Parliamentary Library data showed that while the total number of bill stages passed under urgency jumped in the first 940 days of this Parliament, the number of bills passed into law remained steady at just under 200 over the past few terms.

The previous Labour government passed several laws in this way, including the bill enabling the Covid-19 traffic light system and workforce vaccination mandates.

Palmer said governments of all stripes had used urgency, but not on this scale.

"Its use has been normalised by degrees until it has become an instrument of convenience rather than of necessity," he said.

"I do think the desire to get things done quickly is driving some of this.

"Impatience is a very bad thing for lawmaking, because you'll get it wrong, and it has to be done in a solemn and serious way."

Palmer said overworked and under-resourced select committees were a related issue. For example, the government received hundreds of thousands of submissions for the Treaty Principles Bill.

"They only give you about five minutes, but try to hear most people. It's become overwhelming."

Chris Finlayson, who was Attorney-General in the John Key government, said the data pointed to a need for Parliament to consider extending House sitting hours, given the complexity and volume of legislation.

"I don't necessarily see it as a sort of a partisan issue against this government, but perhaps a wider question.

"The real area of concern is if legislation goes through all its stages without some kind of committee work being done, because that enables the public to have their say about the bill.

"Often, and I think for example… the New Zealand Law Society invariably makes very valuable comments on legislation."

Government: Urgency used when necessary

Shadow Leader of the House Kieran McAnulty said National criticised Labour's use of urgency during the pandemic, but then quickly surpassed those figures once in government.

"They [the government] have used urgency to pass laws that will negatively impact many people. In many cases, these Bills are passed in the dead of night, with no consultation with the public," he said.

"Labour's use of urgency to get through more than a couple of stages of a bill at any one time wasn't at all frequent."

McAnulty said discomfort with the high use of urgency is reflected in submissions to Parliament's Standing Orders Committee.

Before November's election, the cross-party group will consider the rules for the next Parliament.

"We will take our concerns that much of the use of urgency by this government has been to avoid scrutiny to [the] Standing Orders Committee, but no amount of extending sitting hours will address the harm this government has caused."

Leader of the House Louise Upston said the "vast majority" of bills being considered under urgency had gone through a select committee process.

"Therefore, the only effect of urgency is to allow stages to happen back-to-back, and extend the hours the House can sit."

She said of the bills that had skipped the select committee, only 10 were not Budget-related legislation, or were passed in the first 100 days of government, some to repeal laws enacted under Labour.

"All of these bills had necessary reasons to be enacted as soon as possible. Five of these Bills were supported by Labour at [the] third reading.

"This government has never used urgency for the purpose of skipping scrutiny. Much of the urgency that we use is just to get overtime, to get extra hours, and that is to progress the legislation that the government and the parties in the Coalition campaigned on in the election that we won."

RNZ also approached Chris Bishop - who has been the Leader of the House for most of this Parliamentary term - for comment. His office said Upston would be the most appropriate spokesperson.

Should the rules change?

Parliament's rules require a minister to move a motion in the House to enter urgency, which is passed through a simple majority. When doing so, the minister must give "some particularity of the circumstances that warrant the claim for urgency".

Standing Orders do not define what those circumstances are or allow MPs to debate those reasons, something Geoffrey Palmer told the Standing Orders Committee a submission he wanted to see changed.

He said four-year terms, while putting more safeguards in place, could also be considered.

During the Key government, there was a drop in the level of urgency used between the three years after 2008, and the same period after 2011.

This coincided with Standing Orders amendments allowing pre-arranged extended House sittings on Wednesday or Thursday mornings.

It followed criticism of the Key government's use of urgency after the 2008 election and the Clark government's rapid lawmaking during its final year in power.

Chris Finlayson said the House could consider sitting more often on Friday mornings or abolishing dinner breaks since MPs are not present for all debates anyway.

For constituent MPs who needed to be in their electorates on Fridays, he said they should be allowed to go home.

RNZ asked Finlayson and Palmer to assess MPs' willingness to enact changes for the next Parliament, given political parties tended to justify their own use of urgency while in government, then criticise the other side while in Opposition.

"Everyone said it's the other person's fault. That's just part of politics," Finlayson said.

He was keen to present alternatives, and "less interested in attributing blame".

Palmer said there were instances where urgency was necessary, including when mistakes needed to be corrected quickly.

"The difficulty is that you don't want to make urgency a standard method of making legislation. But it's rather become that in New Zealand in recent years."

Asked about his own government's use of urgency, Palmer said: "There was quite a bit because there was a terrific amount when Muldoon left office.

"There was a terrific mess, and it had to be fixed up with a lot of legislation… There are proper occasions for urgency.

World.title: Inquiry into death of Pauline Hanna to begin today at Coroners Court
World.content:
An inquiry into the death of Pauline Hanna, who died in her Remuera home in April 2021, is set to begin today at the Coroners Court in Auckland.

A jury found Hanna's husband, retired eye surgeon Dr Philip Polkinghorne, not guilty of murdering her after a high-profile criminal trial at the High Court in Auckland in 2024.

The purpose of the coronial inquiry is to establish the cause and circumstances of Hanna's death, including whether her death was self-inflicted.

Coroner Tania Tetitaha - who is in charge of investigating Hanna's death - might also make recommendations to prevent more deaths occurring in similar circumstances.

The first stage of the inquiry, lasting about two weeks, is expected to focus on the 24 hours before Hanna's death and the immediate aftermath, including the police scene examination.

Expert pathology evidence will also be given.

World.title: Diamonds win bronze medal with an eye to greater things for netball
World.content:
There's a sentiment in team sports at multi-sport events like the Commonwealth Games that you lose silver and win bronze.

The bronze medallists get to climb on the podium having won their last match, while second place is coming off a heartbreaking loss, having let gold slip through their grasp.

For the Diamonds, bronze at the 2026 Commonwealth Games is a complicated celebration.

Less than 20 hours after Jamaica ripped their hearts out in the semifinal, the Aussie netballers were back on court at 9am in Glasgow for the first centre pass of their first-ever bronze-medal match.

Diamonds fumble Australia's most anticipated gold medal The Diamonds will miss the Commonwealth Games gold medal match for the first time after a shock semifinal loss to Jamaica in front of a crowd baying for Australia's downfall.

It was hard to bounce back from the loss but they did so against England, winning 65-80.

"We had such a quick time to process what happened, I think a lot of us still feel quite numb," defender Jo Weston said.

"Then you go out and have a game like we did, we're so proud and we know all of Australia have been behind us, so it's been a real rollercoaster of emotions in a very short time frame. But I think the overwhelming feeling is pride and a lot of love for each other.

"It's immensely challenging for us having that mental fortitude to come back out. We have very high expectations of ourselves and we want to do our country proud.

The Diamonds rediscovered their flow to keep their medal-winning streak alive. (AP: Andrew Milligan/PA)

"They always say Diamonds are made under pressure and I think that really showed in us today. Although it's not the colour we were after we're really proud about it."

Coach Stacey Marinkovich said the night between the games was about leaving space for team members to "be vulnerable".

There was no point pretending they weren't gutted, that the loss was anything other than gut-wrenching, but once they left the meeting room it was about moving forward.

"It was very emotional last night, it was still probably lingering today a little bit, so to be able to mentally switch in showed our culture isn't words on a wall," she said.

There were complicated emotions for Australia's bronze medallists. (Getty Images: James Fearn)

"That took a lot of grit to be able to go out there and get that result."

Adding another layer of emotion for these stewards of the game, constantly fighting for eyeballs and recognition, is the more objective flip-side of the loss.

That is those celebrations of the Sunshine Girls after the semifinal.

For the first five Commonwealth Games, only Australia and New Zealand won gold and silver. In 2018, England stunned the Diamonds on their home patch for the Gold Coast title. Four years ago Jamaica beat the Aussies in their group match and made their first final. And in Glasgow, they went even better to take the Diamonds down in a knockout match to fight New Zealand for gold.

"International netball is the best it's ever been, which is so good for the sport, it's what we want to see," Weston said.

Four countries is not an enormous range of winners or even contenders, but in every event around the world there are dominant forces.

It wasn't the colour they wanted or expected, but a medal's a medal. (Getty Images: James Fearn)

With six years to the Brisbane Olympics and a push for the sport's inclusion, the Diamonds' bronze may have been the best thing for game.

"It's great for the sport because we always want the game to grow. Gone are the days where it's just one or two nations really dominating," Kiera Austin said.

"It's disappointing for us to have not gotten to that point ... but Jamaica were far too good on the day and that's great going into Brisbane hopefully getting netball into the Olympics.

"It's a sport we absolutely love, a sport we think deserves a great platform on the international stage and if it means a greater competition, then winning that gold medal whenever we get the chance to again is going to be all that much sweeter."

World.title: Live: Australia finishes with enormous medal haul as flag bearer announced
World.content:
Georgia Baker (centre) prides herself on being a leader and role model in the Australian cycling team. (Getty)

Australian cycling superstar Georgia Baker has just spoken to us, with her seventh Commonwealth Games medal around her neck and a new honour bestowed upon her as the closing ceremony flag-bearer.

Thomas really sprung it on her as she was celebrating the elimination race 1-2 with Alyssa Polites and says she was completely blindsided.

"I wasn't expecting it, I have to say. I think I was in race mode, not really thinking about that and when Petria came over and told me I would be the flag-bearer, I felt like I was in a bit of a dream.

"It was just a really emotional moment. I just reflected straight away of when I was young, watching these ceremonies on TV and seeing my idols carry out the flag. I'm just really proud and it's one of the biggest honours of my career."

And she has every right to stand alongside those idols, now boasting five Commonwealth Games gold medals to sit alongside Anna Meares.

Baker says it was a blur when Thomas told her and she couldn't really remember what she said, but we let her know Thomas's comments that it was not just about her remarkable performances on the bike, but who she is off it.

"I think that's the most important thing. I get so much joy and pride out of seeing the young ones perform, it gives me just as much joy as when I win the gold medal. But to be recognised not just for what I do on the bike but off the bike, that to me is the most important thing."

World.title: Australia's Rhiannan Iffland becomes greatest cliff diver of all time
World.content:
Australia's Rhiannan Iffland has officially become the greatest cliff diver of all time after winning the penultimate event of the season in Mostar, in southern Bosnia and Herzegovina.

The 34-year-old from Newcastle arrived at the historic bridge knowing that victory on Saturday local time from the 21m platform would seal her 10th World Series title in a row and 48th victory of her career.

An estimated 23,000 fans turned out across three days of competition to see Iffland tally 363.20 points, finishing ahead of Canada's Molly Carlson (361.60) and Australian Xantheia Pennisi (345.80) to again lift the King Kahekili Trophy.

Pennisi's 10th career podium came thanks to a personal best total score, while Stella Forsyth (276.15), the third Australian participating, came 10th in the 12-woman field.

Rhiannan Iffland is now a commanding 27 points ahead of her nearest rival in the standings. (Getty Images: Dean Treml)

"I'm super stoked, and I guess it's time to process and then celebrate," said Iffland, who entered the final round just 1.6 points ahead of Carlson in sweltering conditions.

"I knew deep down in my heart that it wasn't going to be an easy one today. I knew Molly wasn't going to leave without putting up a good fight."

Iffland's triumph — her 48th in 59 stops — moved her to 77 points after four of the five stops on tour, an unassailable 27 clear of Carlson, with compatriot Pennisi (35) fifth.

The win — thanks to a stunning inward three somersaults half twist tuck dive into the Neretva River — also moved Iffland ahead of Englishman Gary Hunt on the all-time wins list.

It is the third time she has wrapped up the title with a stop to spare.

Romania's Constantin Popovici (right) joined Australia's Rhiannon Iffland in celebrations after winning the men's event in Mostar. (Getty Images: Romina Amato)

"Forty-eight out of 50-something starts, it's nuts," the five-time high diving world champion added.

"But I guess the recipe really comes down to passion, and drive and hard work. There is no secret recipe to being so consistent. Practice, practice, practice, and it paid off for me."

The men's event was won by Romania's Constantin Popovici, who edged out Britain's Aidan Heslop and James Lichenstein of the United States.

Heslop leads the standings on 68 points, followed by Lichtenstein (57) and Popovici (55).

Divers now have an extended two-month break before the final event of the 2026 calendar takes place in Polignano a Mare, Italy — the home of European cliff diving — from September 27.

World.title: 'Rubbish' costs Rabbitohs as Hynes chases NRL record, Eels beat Tigers
World.content:
South Sydney coach Wayne Bennett has said "rubbish" from his team continues to cost them chances to win games, as the Rabbitohs were beaten by the Cronulla Sharks.

The Rabbitohs started Sunday's top-eight battle brightly, scoring first and then playing against 12 men when Cronulla's Teig Wilton was sin-binned for a high shot on Jack Wighton.

But the Sharks would bounce back with 18 unanswered points before half-time, before kicking on in the second half for a 32-16 win.

Souths were their own worst enemy at times, missing more than 50 tackles as well as conceding six penalties and three six-again restarts.

The loss leaves the Rabbitohs seventh on the NRL ladder with 10 wins and nine losses, just one win ahead of 10th place Manly in the tight race for the top-eight.

After Sunday's 16-point loss to Cronulla, Bennett told reporters Souths' repeated errors were costing them the chance of competing with the best team in the league.

"Our Achilles heel is when we don't execute and then we pay a bit of a price for it," Bennett said.

"We can run deep (in the premiership) any day of the week if we can just get over the rubbish that gets in our game.

"If we can get that right, we can hold our own with most teams in the competition."

Meanwhile, Sharks halfback Nicho Hynes set a new club record by successfully kicking his 32nd consecutive goal.

Entering the day with a streak of 26, Hynes was perfect from his six attempts on Sunday to extend his run and close within three of the all-time record.

Canterbury Bulldogs great Hazem El Masri holds the record when he converted 35 consecutive goals in 2003.

In the final match on Sunday, Parramatta broke the hearts of Wests Tigers fans with a late try to Isaiah Iongi, snatching a 16-13 win.

The Eels led 12-0 at half-time before suffering a shocking second half, camped in their own end thanks to repeated errors, while two defence lapses allowed the Tigers to level the score.

Tigers halfback Adam Doueihi, who returned to the side after refusing to play last week, scored the try to level the scores, and kicked the Tigers ahead with a 72nd-minute field goal.

But a late try to Iongi in the 76th minute sealed an unconvincing win for the blue and gold.

World.title: Glorious athletics campaign ends in an empty stadium near midnight
World.content:
The final moment of celebration in Australia's glorious athletics campaign at the 2026 Glasgow Commonwealth Games was hilariously understated.

Approaching midnight, Lachlan Kennedy, Calab Law, Josh Azzopardi, Rohan Browning and Chris Ius finally walked onto the podium to receive their gold medals for the men's 4x100-metre relay.

The crowd had long since filed out of Scotstoun Stadium when the medal ceremony, which was supposed to happen two and a half hours earlier, kicked off.

The track and field that had hosted seven golds, five silvers and five bronze medals for Australia on a jam-packed day, had been leaf-blown, cleaned and stripped of most of its Games paraphernalia.

The stadium was empty when the medal ceremony took place. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Only a handful of volunteers, family, stadium crew, media members and team support staff remained to applaud the historic relay winners, Australia's first since 1974.

A protest by the initially disqualified Canadian team had finally succeeded, reinstating the Olympic champions to the silver medal spot and cutting short Ghanaian celebrations of bronze deep in the bowels of the Glasgow Warriors' rugby club home ground.

In a credit to organisers, the pyrotechnics still fired, the flags were still raised by military personnel in full regalia, and the anthem still played over the stadium PA.

Lachlan Kennedy, Josh Azzopardi, Calab Law, Rohan Browning and Chris Ius eventually got their moment. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Advance Australia Fair was sung even more drone-fully than usual without the safety of a crowd to hide the nasal tones of the Aussie accent, before the small gathering shuffled off the track.

It was a bizarrely low-key moment for one of the crowning achievements of this breakout meet for Team Australia, equalling the most medals won by the track and field team at a Commonwealth Games on foreign soil.

Of the 12 gold medals, 11 silver, and 11 bronzes, none sums up what the team has and can become more than this relay triumph.

Administrators, cheerleaders and athletes alike have been spruiking this new golden generation for Australian Athletics, which has pumped countless hours and very countable dollars into the nation's relays program in recent years.

Team Australia athletes pose for a photo after the women's and men's 4x100 metres relay finals on day nine of the Commonwealth Games at Scotstoun Stadium. (Getty Images: Paul Harding)

In the past four years, Commonwealth Games Australia invested $11.6 million into the Green2Gold2Great program.

That covered a wide range of athletes, with $500,000 dedicated to relays specifically.

In that time, Australia's teams have found some phenomenal success across a number of events.

In 2025, there were green and gold teams in all six events at the World Athletics Relays for the first time ever and the mixed 4x400m team won silver.

At this year's World Relays, the men's 4x400m picked up an Australian record and bronze.

Calab Law handed over to final runner Rohan Browning with Australia in first place. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

So well drilled are these teams that when it came time for the heats on the final morning of the athletics program, both the men's and women's teams could rest individual 100m medallists Kennedy and Torrie Lewis.

Azzopardi put aside his bitter disappointment at only being brought to Glasgow as a relay runner to contribute to the cause, describing the heats as "a training run".

That is a far cry from the team that missed out in Birmingham because Browning took a tumble in the heats.

They missed the 2024 Olympic final despite running faster heat times than the top three in the opposite heat, mucked up the final change in last year's world championships final, and missed a medal by just 0.24 of a second at World Relays in May.

This gold medal puts the world on notice, and there is still more room to grow.

Lachlan Kennedy, Joshua Azzopardi, Calab Law and Rohan Browning celebrate victory in the men's 4x100m relay final at Scotstoun Stadium. (Getty Images: Ross MacDonald/SNS Group)

It is a credit to the system and their confidence in it that they didn't rush Glasgow 100m finalist Eddie Nketia into the team, even for the heats, opting instead for quick-start specialist Ius to lead off.

Kennedy replaced him for the final, playing his role to perfection, handing off cleanly to Azzopardi deep in the box, before Law and Browning came home in 38.07.

"We knew what we had in us, we're training well, we compete domestically all year against each other, [so] we're pretty used to each other. I think it's a big part of why we're so successful. Train together all year, camps all year," Kennedy said.

Kennedy said there is no first and second squad in their team, but 1A and 1B, described as "green and gold" by Browning, who flagged the looming arrivals of Gout Gout and Nketia once they have more time to train with the team that now carries a golden aura.

"I hope there are kids at home tonight watching this who aspire to grow up and be part of this team," Browning said.

"Not just aspire to the baggy green or the Wallabies or the Australian AFL team, aspire to be part of the Australian relay team."

We have already seen glimpses of it, with former Cronulla Sharks under-17 player Zavier Peacock opting for the track and finishing second behind Gout at this year's junior Australian titles.

Aussies on fire on a night when that should've been impossible Australian athletics lives up to the immense hype on a night of glorious culmination for Lachie Kennedy, Torrie Lewis and their team of track stars.

And veteran Kurtis Marschall was spurred on by their performance.

The back-to-back-to-back Commonwealth Games pole vault champion started his competition first and finished last on a frigid summer's night in Glasgow, getting the chance to watch his teammates pick up medals as he made his way up to a Games record of 5.85m, claiming the last Aussie gold of the program.

"The system is working. The boys' relay tonight was just phenomenal. They inspired me to get over the line," he said.

"We just want to keep pushing this sport along more and more and more. It's the best sport in the world and deserves more eyes, so we're just doing our part."

The whole stadium was watching his crowning moment and while no-one saw "the boys" get theirs, they weren't there to see the work it took to get there either.

World.title: Eagles star in tears after loss, Crows into top four after downing Dons
World.content:
Melbourne captain Max Gawn was inspirational in his team's nine-point win over Gold Coast. (Getty Images)

Melbourne has cemented its top six status ahead of next weekend's clash with ladder leaders Fremantle, defeating Gold Coast by nine points at Carrara Stadium.

In a contest featuring several lead changes, the Demons did just enough in the fourth quarter to claim an 18.6 (114) to 16.9 (105) victory.

After a four-goal display against Geelong last week, Harrison Petty kicked three majors including a crucial after-the-siren effort at the end of the third quarter, while Jacob van Rooyen also kicked three for the visitors.

Melbourne captain Max Gawn was huge for the Demons, notching 25 disposals, 10 marks, 33 hit-outs and nine clearances.

After last weekend's loss to the Cats, Demons coach Steven King was thrilled by his team's ability to find a way to victory ahead of the clash with the Dockers.

"We've already played them once earlier this year, and we got taught a lesson," King said.

"This time we'll be at the MCG and we love playing there but I'm sure they'll come over as a full dress rehearsal for what's in front of them as a footy club.

"It's a privilege to play in big games that count, and we're lucky we grabbed our opportunity today and can still be relevant in this competition for what's ahead."

Jed Walter kicked three for the Suns, all in the first half, as Gold Coast was unable to prevent slumping to its 10th straight defeat in what was Christian Petracca's first match against his former club.

Petracca, whose impact at the Suns had been under the spotlight throughout the week following an on-field argument with young gun Leo Lombard in the loss to Carlton, had minimal impact on the contest with 16 disposals and two clearances.

Instead it was John Noble (34 disposals, seven tackles, 10 marks) and Matt Rowell (30 disposals, nine tackles, eight clearances) who led the way for the Suns, with coach Damien Hardwick lamenting a similar display to previous defeats.

"It's just frustrating because a lot of those things are absolutely within our control, and it's the stuff that we need to eradicate," Hardwick said.

Gold Coast slumped to its 10th straight loss, a feat unthinkable at the start of the season. (Getty Images)

"I've got to coach harder and tougher because otherwise we don't move forward.

"So we've learned a lot of lessons like that this year, unfortunately, but not getting the result we're after."

Both teams had injury worries with Sam Collins (ribs) and Blake Howes (wrist) sent to hospital for X-rays after coming off in separate incidents.

Melbourne set the template for their accuracy in front of goal early, kicking five straight in the opening term to hold a three-point lead at the first break.

Bailey Humphrey's goal after the siren at the end of the second quarter, despite a question mark over whether he ran off the line of the mark as he came into kick, had the hosts in front heading into the main break.

And the Suns extended that lead to three goals during a high-scoring third term, kicking four goals alone from free kicks.

The Demons, however, kicked two goals in the last 30 seconds including another after-the-siren major to Petty to snatch a one-point lead heading into the final quarter.

Howes' nasty looking fall early in the last term didn't deter the Demons, who kicked four goals to three to secure the points.

While the Demons host the Dockers next weekend, the Suns will aim to snap their losing run in Canberra against GWS.

World.title: After javelin gold, Aussie star heads straight back to hospital work
World.content:
Sydney doctor Mackenzie Little has finally become a golden girl with the javelin as she led one last parade of Commonwealth Games field event medallists in the green and gold.

The remarkable 29-year-old Little, a doctor at Northern Beaches Hospital, can barely even call herself a part-time athlete these days, such is her busy medical life, but she still proved too good for her opponents as she finally lifted a major international title.

She nailed victory with her first throw and then revealed she will be jetting straight back to work on Tuesday as an ear, nose and throat registrar.

On a night when pole vaulter Kurtis Marschall completed Australia's golden track-and-field program by soaring to a Games-record 5.85 metres and a third-straight title, Little's achievement felt even more astonishing.

"I'm so I'm relieved and excited — this is so fantastic. Nailing the first throw is maybe something to do with how my training's been a bit quality over quantity in the last couple of years," she said.

"I wish I could say, you know, that I'm really, really training my butt off, but I'm just having to fit things in around my job. I'm having to make the most of sometimes challenging situations, not having all the time in the world.

"I perform surgeries and see outpatients in clinics and take care of patients who are in the ward sick in hospital. Then in the evenings, I'll get to training, but I've had to change my training locations this year to stay within 30 minutes of the hospital. When you're on call, you need to — overnight and in the evenings — be within 30 minutes of the hospital in case of emergencies.

"I'm gonna go and fly home straight away and get back to work."

On a tricky night for throwers in the Scotstoun Stadium on the last evening of track and field competition, Little believed her technique of throwing low and hard to cut through the wind helped her to a season best 61.88m with an opener that no-one else threatened.

New Zealand silver medallist Tori Moorby hurled 60.08m in the third round to grab the silver, while Kenya's Irene Jepkemboi took the bronze.

Kurtis Marschall reacts after securing his third Commonwealth Games gold medal in the pole vault. (Getty Images: Dean Mouhtaropoulos)

Marschall, winner at both the Gold Coast and Birmingham Commonwealth Games, finished the night in style by becoming only the third Australian ever to win three titles in a row in the same event, and ending with a leap that surpassed his hero Steve Hooker's 5.80m in Melbourne 20 years ago.

Entering the competition late, the hot favourite from Adelaide held his nerve to defeat South African silver medallist Kyle Rademeyer and England's bronze winner Owen Heard (both 5.70m).

It was the latest big achievement for the 29-year-old, who earlier in the season handed a once-in-a-blue-moon defeat to the sport's modern-day legend, Armand 'Mondo' Duplantis.

"I just wanted to solidify myself in the record books, like I already did with the gold medal, but I definitely wanted to jump that 5.85 and take it off Steve," Marschall said.

Brooke Buschkuehl in action and on her way to bronze in the long jump. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

Melbourne's Brooke Buschkuehl, the indefatigable 33-year-old mum, also made it a hat-trick of medals, but again missed out on the one she really wanted as she added a bronze in the long jump to go with her two silvers from Gold Coast and Birmingham.

Promising Wollongong teenager Delta Amidzovski, the 19-year-old world junior long jump champion, finished fourth, just five centimetres off a podium place.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.
